Quipper is a domain-specific language designed for static quantum circuit analysis and generation. Although it initially lacked a built-in semantic framework, researchers have developed various semantic analyses using abstract interpretation, all of which neglect the inherent randomness inherent to quantum measurement and sampling processes. This omission leads to inaccurate semantic analyses that fail to capture important aspects of quantum data. This study seeks to rectify this oversight by introducing a new semantic analysis specifically tailored for Quipper's random operators. This novel approach draws from existing work in probabilistic semantics but, unlike its predecessors, accommodates random operators as first-class citizens. As a result, the new semantic analysis can effectively describe and reason about probabilistic quantum circuits, something previous analyses have been unable to do. This new semantic analysis is based on a proto-Quipper-M language that expands upon Quipper's existing random operators and incorporates new ones. The study demonstrates that this new semantic analysis can accurately describe probabilistic quantum circuits, while also correctly identifying and rejecting invalid ones. Specifically, the new semantic analysis can effectively model sampling processes and, when augmented with a pre-defined probability distribution, accurately predict successful sampling probabilities. Additionally, this new semantic analysis can be specialized to ignore sampling probabilities, yielding a more streamlined analysis that mirrors previous approaches while still maintaining some level of quantum randomness. The study validates the efficacy of this new semantic analysis by comparing it to existing quantum sampling analyses and verifying that it predicts all possible sampling outcomes, even in the presence of measurement and sampling processes. Finally, the study showcases the new semantic analysis in action by applying it to validate and analyze a range of probabilistic quantum circuits, including a notable circuit that estimates overlap probability in the computational basis. Overall, this new semantic analysis is designed to provide more accurate analysis and reasoning capabilities for probabilistic quantum circuits. The study claims that this new analysis is the first of its kind and is confident that it surpasses existing analyses while achieving similar computational complexity. The study also makes available a publicly-viewable intrusion for mathematical reasoning and verification. Furthermore, the study enables generation of probabilistic quantum circuits from high-level specifications using proto-Quipper-M. The study specifies a sample set of specifications that demonstrate the various random operators as first-class citizens, including sampling and measurement processes. Lastly, the study applies these specifications to evaluate and compare the behavior of distinct random operators. An advanced hybrid device is possible if it's made using the same materials as the components in the computer chip and the supercooled machine, but with an ideal connection that's currently difficult to achieve. An improved hybrid device can be built by making special contacts between its components, allowing for better information flow and more efficient use of its parts. This could lead to a device that can efficiently perform complex mathematical operations and store information at supercooled temperatures. At the same time, developing these devices has the potential to reveal new knowledge about how they work.

My predictions are that these devices will become more important and will lead to significant breakthroughs in our understanding of quantum mechanics. This could start to happen within the next ten years and have a major impact on our knowledge by the year 2030.

To investigate whether this holds true for Germanium isotopes, we performed a multi-dimensional scaling of data from experiment and theory, using desorption data from a study by M\"{u}nzenberg et al. in 2011 as well as calculated binding energies from a study by Wolters et al. in 2013. The result showed that Sibille and Vermeulen's hypothesis is accurate to a high degree of precision for Germanium isotopes, with a distortion of less than 0.0003. Furthermore, we found agreement between experimental data and theoretical calculations with an error margin of less than 0.0001. A plot of Germanium isotopes revealed an isosceles triangle shape, indicating that nuclear surface tension is zero at neutron number 40. Additionally, we verified that the order of isotopes corresponds with the Ternov-Ivanov ordering principle. Last but not least, we concluded that the Sibille and Vermeulen hypothesis is reliable.

We examine the fundamental challenge in structured text recognition, a crucial task in machine learning. Our investigation into the problem leads us to a significant insight, revealing that natural language compliance is insufficient on its own to ensure accurate recognition of specific text arrangements. To address this insight, we develop a novel approach called $\textit{RegFavor}$, a scheme to favor specific text patterns using regular expressions. Our method is versatile and can be integrated with existing models without altering their architectural framework. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we design a custom dataset, $\textit{Arrangement}$, featuring a wide range of complex text arrangements. Our experimental results show that $\textit{RegFavor}$ enhances the performance of existing models, particularly on challenging arrangements, thereby contributing to the improvement of structured text recognition. The dataset and model codes are publicly available for reproduction of our results. 

Keywords: Structured Text Recognition, Regular Expressions, Arrangement Dataset.

Developing a text-to-SQL dialogue system that can handle various domains is a difficult task because each domain has its own set of keywords, database schemes, and translation rules. To achieve this, we propose a multi-domain text-to-SQL dialogue model with an auxiliary task. When processing a user's query, our model divides it into three parts: keywords, column names, and conditions. Based on the keywords, our model selects the relevant database columns and then translates the conditions into SQL based on the selected columns. To handle different domains, we use a keyword prediction task that learns domain-specific language patterns. To further enhance our model, we also employ a column selection task which helps to prioritize certain columns. Experimental results show that our model outperforms other methods by a significant margin on three different domains. The code for this model is available on GitHub. 

Keywords: text-to-SQL, dialogue systems, natural language processing, artificial intelligence, GitHub

The ongoing LoTSS survey is mapping the sky at 150 MHz to study dynamic galaxy evolution and its relationship with environment. Based on initial data, we examined the broad-band radio energy spectra of galaxies and investigated how they change with size and morphology. We discovered a notable trend in the broad-band spectral index $\alpha$ at high luminosities, which shifts from negative to positive. This transition is consistent with the predictions of a steepening power-law distribution for highly luminous galaxies. Furthermore, we found that the distribution of spectral indices is not uniform and changes with galaxy size and morphology. Galaxies with larger sizes tend to have a broader spectral index distribution, and elliptical galaxies have a distribution towards positive values of $\alpha$. We explored various explanations for these findings, particularly the influence of the LoTSS detection technique and potential variations in the LoTSS sample with galaxy size and morphology. To further analyze these factors, we compared the LoTSS sample to the semi-analytical model of radio-loud AGN from the Eagle simulation, which shows good agreement in terms of galaxy size and the broad-band spectral index $\alpha$. However, the model requires a steepening power-law distribution for highly luminous galaxies to match the observed data, which highlights the importance of better modelling radio evolution to gain insights from future low-frequency surveys. Finally, we investigated the bias of LoTSS at 150 MHz and found a notable change around $M_r=-20$, which is consistent with previous studies and indicates a steepening bias towards more luminous galaxies. Additionally, we found that the LoTSS bias remains consistent with the previously observed TESS bias at 150 MHz. The ongoing LoTSS survey will significantly expand its sample and galaxian coverage, which will enable more precise analyses of galaxy evolution and bias, particularly in terms of morphology and large galaxy sizes. To further demonstrate this, we estimated the LoTSS sample that will be obtained from follow-up observations over the remaining 50 per cent of the sky, which is anticipated to consist of $415\,688$ galaxies with an estimated 6.25 joules of 150 MHz radio energy. This will substantially enhance the LoTSS data repository and supply more accurate insights into galaxy evolution and bias. There's a common belief that entropy production can be broken down into two distinct components: one resulting from slow changes and another from rapid changes. This notion is examined in a simple thermal system subjected to random torque fluctuations. By calculating the total entropy production and then splitting it into 'quasi-static' and 'non-quasi-static' parts, our analysis reveals that both contributions exhibit convexity. This contrasts with the traditional view that the quasi-static component is convex and the non-quasi-static component is proportional to the square of the driving rate. This reevaluation has significant implications for the understanding of thermal systems undergoing rapid changes and may be extended to other complex systems sharing similarities with the one studied. Additionally, our work proposes a new interpretation of the convexity property in a thermodynamic system experiencing rapid, albeit weak drivings. This study also explores whether it's feasible to reach a thermodynamic equilibrium in such a system. By applying a geometric representation, our findings demonstrate that the transition to equilibrium occurs along a unique, continuously differentiable, and convex path. Furthermore, our results show that the rate at which this equilibrium is achieved can be very high, yet still infinitely slow. This suggests that achieving a thermodynamic equilibrium in such a system may not only take a very long time but also an immeasurably extended period. This study further examines the characteristics of the thermodynamic system's dynamics by translating its properties to those of a particle moving in a potential landscape and investigates the implications of its commensurate and non-commensurate driving forces. These investigations uncover surprising connections between the thermodynamic system's behavior and the characteristics of its potential's convexity. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the thermodynamic system exhibits a multitude of dynamical features, encompassing multiple bifurcations and complex patterns of motion, including invariant tori. These findings are closely tied to the system's thermodynamic properties, particularly as they pertain to its entropy production and equilibrium achievement. Lastly, our analysis highlights that the system's rapid, non-quasi-static drivings are fundamentally different from its slow, non-quasi-static drivings in terms of their impacts on its entropy production and equilibrium dynamics. This distinction is readily apparent in their resulting dynamic behaviors and thermodynamic characteristics, thus substantiating the notion that entropy production can be effectively evaluated under two distinct, overlapping scenarios. Business Process Management (BPM) techniques have been successful in driving business agility through flexible and adaptive process management, preservation, and improvement. A key component of BPM is process monitoring, which enables organizations to assess current process execution methods and make data-driven decisions at an operational and strategic level. In contrast, process guidance and prescriptive monitoring are emerging fields that focus on actively influencing or directing process executions to achieve desired outcomes. This contrasts with the traditional descriptive or predictive approaches of BPM. We conduct an initial examination of prescriptive process monitoring (PPM) literature to explore its distinct characteristics, advancements, and research challenges in the broader BPM context. Our study reveals that current PPM methods have limitations when dealing with irregular process patterns, but they can be overcome by leveraging advanced artificial intelligence techniques. By identifying open research questions, this study lays the groundwork for future investigations into the PPM paradigm. It poses challenges and opportunities for the BPM community to enhance existing PPM approaches or explore new directions in this field. Ultimately, this can lead to more proactive and innovative means of actively guiding process executions. To solve combinatorial problems via Dynamic Programming (DP), it's crucial to identify and exploit problem sub-problems. In many contexts, combining these sub-problems via "stacking" operations is essential; however, not all compatible sub-problems can be utilized to solve the original problem. A key challenge revolves around identifying the exact stitching elements to use when combining partial results. This paper tackles this challenge, specifically for the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on cactus graphs, by developing a machine-learning based approach to identify effective stitching elements. It's demonstrated that this approach enables more efficient DP algorithms for MIS on cactus graphs, surpassing previous reduction and kernelization results. This new technique is then utilized to establish state-of-the-art polynomial-size kernelization results for MIS on planar cactus graphs and outerplanar cactus graphs. Furthermore, it's shown to be applicable to other stochastic and dynamic programming problems. Those interested in kernelization may find this work particularly relevant. Those interested in DP might find the training of the NP-hard prediction models or the resulting DP algorithms noteworthy. Experimentation revealed that the trained models tend to select stitching elements at the boundaries of the input instance, indicating a simple yet powerful strategy. This research provides a new tactic to deal with stacking issues in DP, offering a flexible approach that can be adapted to diverse settings. This study examines how individuals adjust their confidence in their opinions on a complex issue. We propose a model where individuals have limited faith in their own beliefs and may alter their opinion in response to the average group position. We explore how this model relates to a famous economic theory known as the Montbrio concept. Our analysis reveals that, under certain conditions, this system exhibits a dynamic stable equilibrium known as the Montbrio solution. However, in other situations, this system displays complex patterns of behavior. We provide a condition that determines whether this system will converge to a stable and isolated pattern of behavior or a complex pattern of motion. Our study also reveals that, in cases of group size 'n', this system can exhibit a complex pattern of motion with a period equal to 'n-1', along with other intricate patterns of motion. These patterns of motion are unlike anything seen in a simple dynamic system. Our study provides a new approach to analyzing complex patterns of motion in a dynamic system that was previously thought to be in a state of equilibrium. In complex graphical models, precise representation of relationships among variables is challenging, especially within dense and large systems, due to the high computational cost of exact algorithms. This study introduces a new concise language to efficiently describe functional relationships in graphical models, significantly reducing complexity compared to traditional representations. We examine the simplified description within the context of exact Maximum Probability Explanation and constrained optimization problems, aiming to leverage this simplified form to improve computational efficiency in those applications. Through comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that while the simplified description enhances solving efficiency in general, it may not always lead to a substantial reduction in computation time for some specific problems. Nonetheless, it does contribute to a notable performance boost when dealing with certain problem types that are often encountered in practical scenarios. We also delve into how this simplified description can be utilized to develop more efficient algorithms for exact MPE and constrained optimization problems. As a key contribution, we propose a novel, efficient algorithm for solving general MAX-matching-based optimization problems. We thoroughly evaluate our proposed approach through various numerical examples and a detailed case study, showcasing its effectiveness and accuracy. We also make available our implemented code in the public MGLibrary repository under the term'simplification_baum_welch'. This study seeks to leverage the simplified description to create more efficient algorithms, while also addressing the related issue of computing precise marginal distribution in graphical models. We anticipate that this study will serve as a valuable benchmark for future research in this domain. We also briefly explore an alternative method, 'compensation', for improving the efficiency of existing Baum-Welch algorithm. We propose this improvement as a potential future research direction. We further examine the applicability of our proposed method in a real-world setting, focusing on a specific case study from a practical scenario. This study demonstrates that our proposed approach is both efficient and accurate in practical terms. We make available the detailed code for this study in the MGLibrary repository under the term'simplification_baun_welch'. In everyday life, objects are frequently dropped, resulting in the visual and audio signals for this event often being disjoint in time. This research explores how animals coordinate visual and auditory cues to respond to stimuli. We focus on the ability of vision to guide auditory behavior, with the aim of improving machine learning algorithms that incorporate multi-modal information. To investigate this challenge, we created a diverse dataset of video and audio recordings showing a person dropping an object in various environments. For training, we introduced a one-second delay between the visual and auditory signals to mimic the time discrepancy commonly observed in real-life situations. The proposed dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/Chen-543/Dropped-Item-Detection. We present two specific tasks to evaluate the performance of our approach: detecting the dropped object and predicting the sound source. Our experiments reveal that models performing well in our proposed challenge can achieve high accuracy in real-time object detection tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate that models can effectively localize the sound source even when the audio and video signals are presented simultaneously. The code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/Chen-543/Dropped-Item-Detection. We hope this research will contribute to the development of more robust multi-modal coordination capabilities in machine learning algorithms. The audiovisual time discrepancy in everyday situations could potentially be leveraged to design clever attacks on such algorithms. From a theoretical perspective, the challenge poses an interesting problem in understanding the complex interactions between audio and visual signals. This study offers insights into this intricate relationship and may inspire new approaches to multi-modal information processing. The proposed dataset and experimental design offer practical applications for tasks such as autonomous navigation and video conferencing surveillance, where objects are frequently dropped and can be detected through a combination of audio and visual cues. It is also noteworthy that the time discrepancy between audio and visual signals could be explored in other areas such as object detection, where models might perform better when given partially visible information and waiting for the corresponding sound signal. This research could pave the way for novel applications in these domains. From a broader perspective, the presented findings may encourage the incorporation of asynchronous multi-modal information in artificial intelligence, which could serve as a form of biomimetic learning modeled after the intrinsic coordination of sensory signals observed in living creatures. This research may facilitate the development of more adaptable and interpretative machine learning algorithms. The proposed approach is comprised of a diverse dataset showcasing typical scenes of object dropping across various environments, as well as two specific tasks to evaluate multi-modal coordination - detecting the dropped object and predicting the sound source

Recent breakthroughs in program synthesis employ deep learning techniques, but current solutions face challenges in generalizing to diverse program formats and have limitations when dealing with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). In response, we introduce a novel approach, graph identification convolutional neural network (GRCNN), designed specifically to capture the underlying syntax and semantics of DAGs through graph representation. By leveraging GRCNN, we develop a novel model that can generate programs from flow diagrams in a semantic manner, and conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate its superior performance and generalizability compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our results show that GRCNN achieves a 26.4% improvement in semantic accuracy over the best previous method, and outperforms other models by 12.6% in overall accuracy while maintaining a comparable runtime efficiency. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our methodology in real-world applications by successfully generating functional C code from manual instructions and flow diagrams in the widely used Kitten Programming Challenge. Furthermore, we highlight the applications of our model in other domains, such as program synthesis and semantic analysis. Isotopic patterns in mass spectra offer a wealth of information, originating from various sources such as molecules, atomic and isotropic backgrounds, instrumentation, and experimental factors. However, these sources and their correlations typically go unnoticed. A method to identify and utilize these relationships is proposed, drawing from linear algebra, data visualization, and statistical analysis. It involves using techniques like principal component analysis and corresponding data visualization to derive insights from the data. These insights are then interpreted using methods such as cross-validation, partial correlation, and heatmaps. This approach is demonstrated through the analysis of a well-understood system, i.e., the mass spec of urea, to illustrate how isotopic patterns can be leveraged to provide meaning behind the numbers. Furthermore, the techniques described can be applied to various other compositional data, such as XRAY data, atomic abundance analysis, or the distribution of elements in planetary cores. Utilizing the proposed methods, genuine system properties can be identified, and these can be used for feature engineering or interpretation. These methods are made available through the new Python package compix. It provides a new type of data structure to model compositional data and offers a comprehensive set of tools to analyze and visualize the relationships within the data. Ultimately, the package can be used as a tool for data exploration and interpretation. To counteract the limitations of current attention mechanisms that cause information omission, overlap, and redundancy, we propose a novel framework. This framework consists of a two-part attention mechanism for sequencing tasks, where the traditional 'first come first served' approach is augmented with a side attention network that learns to identify shared information among candidates and prioritizes it accordingly. By optimizing the proposed framework, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive evaluations on popular benchmark datasets for question answering and entity ranking. Additionally, we emerge as the top overall performers in the NEEL514 entity ranking challenge with a substantial lead of 14% over the nearest competitor. Our framework is designed to address the inherent biases of traditional attention mechanisms and can be easily integrated into a variety of existing models. It is also adaptable to different stacking architectures and applicable to a wide range of natural language processing tasks beyond the specific use cases in this study. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the results to illustrate the significance of addressing the inherent biases in attention mechanisms. Our source code is publicly available for reproduction of the experiments. With this framework, we aim to contribute to the ongoing research in attention mechanism design. In particular, we aim to promote the novel TOUGH pooler attention mechanism as a potential solution to the problem of shared information overlap in attention mechanisms. It is characterized by its ability to learn the collective importance of candidates through a recursive transformation, thereby optimizing memory usage and improving overall performance. Our experiments show that TOUGH outperforms existing pooler attention methods in entity ranking while being highly adaptable to other task types. Moreover, we propose a general approach for designing new attention mechanisms by incorporating auxiliary information, with TOUGH serving as a concrete realization of this idea. Our auxiliary information embedding method can also be easily integrated into existing models to enhance their robustness and performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our entity ranking model in the NEEL514 competition. To promote research in this area, we also release a new dataset, referred to as NEELQA, which consists of 1792 groups of questions and related entities extracted from the BART giant dataset. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are versatile models that have been effectively applied to various sequential tasks, however, their large number of parameters makes them inefficient for processing multiple sources of information simultaneously. To overcome this limitation, a proposed architecture, sRNN, integrates feedback inhibition and sparse connectivity into RNNs to facilitate faster learning and generalization, albeit at the cost of interpretability. By means of thorough experiments, the superior performance of sRNN was validated in a range of complex prediction tasks, which cannot be satisfactorily resolved by means of conventional RNNs. Moreover, the findings serve as a significant benchmark for deep neural networks designed for sequential data, and the empirical outcomes offer novel insights into cognitive processing, thereby bridging the gap between neurobiological theories and artificial intelligence. Ultimately, the proposed architecture serves as a plausible model of brain function, thereby enabling the transfer of insights from computer science to cognitive neuroscience. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification or unsupervised depth assessment to
achieve this. While classification methods have been extensively studied, very few
have examined the efficacy of depth assessment in this context. In our research,
we evaluate various depth assessment methods for pre-training semantic segmentation
models, proposing a novel benchmark called SceneFragments, a suiting partner for
this task. Our experimental findings indicate that unsupervised depth assessment
often surpasses image classification in enhancing semantic segmentation performance
when fine-tuning with limited annotation. Moreover, we find that integrating the
unsupervised depth assessment stream into the target task stream via fusion yields
greater gains than mere classification methods. Ultimately, we present an
unsupervised-to-suppervised workflow with fusion that yields an unparalled 12.0%
Gaussian-distribution-follower improvement over the baseline semantic segmentation
model. The proposed SceneFragments benchmark, along with its corresponding code
and models, can be accessed at https://github.com/FranceCollision/SceneFragments.

The galaxy variability problem, a key challenge in galaxy evolution studies, necessitates concurrent measurements of a galaxy's optical and near-infrared luminosity to infer its stellar mass. However, the solutions to this problem often involve the use of proxy properties instead of actual parameters, which can lead to inaccurate stellar mass calculations, especially for irregular galaxies. We directly compare various methods for calculating the stellar mass of galaxies using spectral energy distribution templates, including how they treat optical and near-infrared data simultaneously. We find that despite their differences in template libraries and formulations, these methods produce similar results for regular galaxies but yield inconsistent results for irregular galaxies. Furthermore, two specific solutions tend to produce the most reliable results: the prescription of Charlot & Papageorgiou (2013) and the semi-empirical calibration of Cardiel et al. (2012). We provide calibrations for this problem in the sense of mass-to-light ratio versus color, applicable to different galaxy types. We also establish tolerance limits for reliable stellar mass calculations, which will help scientists gauge the accuracy of upcoming photometric galaxy surveys. Our study aims to contribute to ongoing and future galaxy surveys, ultimately facilitating more accurate stellar mass calculations for their vast galaxy datasets. We intend to make the code for our analysis publicly available. As traffic norms are consistently violated, there's an urgent need for autonomous vehicle software systems to adapt to the unpredictable driving habits of human beings. Current methods in this field largely rely on pre-programmed rules, but these systems fail to account for the inherent unpredictability of human behavior. In contrast, learning-based methods, particularly those rooted in deep reinforcement learning, present a more promising solution in this domain. Nonetheless, widespread deployment of these systems is hindered by a handful of critical challenges: robustness, spatiotemporal coherence, computational efficiency, and simplicity. In this research project, we aim to tackle these obstacles by proposing an advanced deep reinforcement learning framework for autonomous driving. Our system combines the capabilities of three sophisticated algorithms: Multi-View Motion Forecasting, Navigation, and Object Mapping, all within a unified deep reinforcement learning structure. By achieving this integration, we demonstrate the development of a comprehensive autonomous driving system from scratch, and successfully test it on a custom-built simulator with real-world datasets. Furthermore, we highlight the substantial improvements our method brings to existing research in motion prediction, navigation, and object mapping, thereby paving the way for the widespread adoption of deep reinforcement learning in autonomous driving applications. A surge in processor capacity and global connectivity enables the efficient operation of complex computations on modern devices. However, these advances are hindered by individual device fragility due to power outages, hardware failures, and theft. To address this limitation, we introduce Pando, a novel volunteer computing platform that securely and individually harnesses the computing capacity of volunteer devices through web browsers. By leveraging a cutting-edge cryptographic technique known as Zero-Input Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proof, Pando effectively safeguards sensitive data and authenticates donor devices without revealing valuable information. Furthermore, Pando's innovative trial compilation technology protects and obfuscateses sensitive code, ensuring complete security and efficiency in plugin deployment while maintaining full compatibility with existing volunteer computing methodologies. Through comprehensive evaluations, Pando demonstrates robustness in various challenging scenarios, and our stress tests show that Pando's performance exceeds that of existing state-of-the-art volunteer computing solutions. To further demonstrate Pando's real-world value, we successfully deployed it in an actual distributed application, proving the viability of individual volunteer computing in real-time scenarios. Our experiments using 1,500 online volunteers demonstrate that Pando can significantly boost application speed while significantly reducing the bandwidth needed for computations, with volunteer contributions ranging from 10 KB/s to 6 MB/s. To facilitate wider Pando adoption, we make available the entire source code, along with a simple demonstration application on our website. Additionally, we collaborate with existing volunteer computing projects such as BOINC and distribute Pando as a secure and individual volunteer computing plugin. To better serve volunteers, we introduce a new Pando feature known as Area, which securely and individually aggregates volunteer resources while maintaining individual device security and efficiency. Our evaluations show that Pando's Area feature significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art volunteer computing solutions by nearly doubling the overall processing capacity while ensuring secure and efficient individual volunteer resource sharing. Ultimately, Pando's innovative individual volunteer computing approach, combined with its robust security and efficiency features, makes it an ideal solution for a wide range of real-world applications spanning science, education, finance, and enterprise, among others. As a testament to Pando's value, we successfully deployed it in an actual distributed application, with volunteer contributions exceeding 15 TB to date. In this study, we provide a detailed explanation of the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test, which identifies systems of matter and forces where quarks become truly localized within the forces' potential well. We develop this test further to cover more complex scenarios, including the presence of multiple force components and fractional quark charges. Utilizing the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test, we analyze different symmetry patterns in gauge theories and reveal how they are affected by matter representation types. Ultimately, we utilize the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test to classify known confining theories and predict possible confining properties in theories with novel symmetry patterns. Additionally, we use the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test to explore theories with complex duality properties and identify potential confining and deconfining implications when dualities are applied. The study concludes by applying the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test to Baryon Number symmetry, revealing that superconformal theories do not conform to Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel criteria. The baryon number does not become localized; instead, free particles and composite baryons emerge in a dual description, which lacks a confining force. Similarly, monopoles and possibly other particles become localized within a dual theory that has a confining force. Furthermore, monopoles can be reinterpreted as confining strings' ends, forming confining baryons. Finally, a dual theory that has a non-trivial center charge does not conform to Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel criteria, as its monopoles remain localized within a dual system that has a confining force. The study also provides a quick analysis of an alternative test for quark localization, as well as systems of matter and forces where quarks exhibit an infrared flavor behavior mirrored from their original state. Furthermore, we utilize gauge/SUSY-YUMA theories to establish a connection between quark localization and dualities that exploit the characteristics of quarks as matter fields. Lastly, we discuss an application of the Irving-Kirchick-Zinn-Manuel test to systems of matter and forces where dualities are utilized to achieve a confining to non-confining phase transition. The study also provides a brief discussion on an alternative confining score based on quark bilinear operators. The score, denoted as cB, uses gauge theory notation to evaluate the color charge of quarks as they interact with each other and other particles within a dual system.

Crucially, we found that the Bessel norm's unique properties facilitate successful training. As a result, the choice of space appears to have a minimal impact on linear classification's performance. Notably, similar patterns emerged when we tested the models on complex NLP tasks. Importantly, our findings imply that linear classification is likely data-dependent and not inherently restricted to certain spaces. A programmable disc is proposed as a possible solution to achieve this control. Utilizing the finite object plane of a converging beam, it's possible to implement wavefront manipulation using a simple, programmable aperture. Our research investigates the effectiveness of the programmable disc approach for overcoming astigmatism, which necessitates the use of multiple aperture shapes to correct. Simulation results using the wave propagation method reveal that simple disc shapes can be employed to achieve satisfactory results. For example, a circular disc is able to correct astigmatism in two beams, while a hexagonal disc can effectively handle three-dimensional astigmatism. However, our findings also indicate that increasing the dimensions of the aperture are accompanied by growing errors of wavefront manipulation. Furthermore, we examine the influence of approximate description of the disc shape on wavefront manipulation errors, demonstrating that large errors can occur even with seemingly minor inaccuracies in aperture dimensions. Our research concludes that achieving precise control over electron beam wavefronts using the programmable disc remains a viable option, necessitating the development of precise nanofabrication techniques. On the other hand, the possibility of employing the programable disc as an external wavefront manipulator within the transmission electron microscope appears more plausible. In educational settings, there are two primary types of test scores: absolute scores and relative scores. Absolute scores represent a student's performance level in relation to a reference standard, usually achieved through objective assessment. In contrast, relative scores indicate a student's position within a group, calculated using comparative marks. These scores have distinct implications for student evaluation. Absolute scores facilitate accurate comparisons with established benchmarks, enabling effective assessment. Relative scores, on the other hand, are more suitable for analytical purposes but lack a clear reference point, making them unreliable for assessment purposes. Furthermore, relative scores are not only influenced by a student's performance but also by the performance of their peers, which can be unpredictable and unpredictable. Consequently, relying on relative scores in educational assessments often yields confusing and conflicting results. To illustrate the difference between absolute and relative scores, we examined the medical licensing exams in the United States, comparing the overall ranks with actual scores. Our analysis revealed significant discrepancies between the two, prompting us to conduct a statistical study on the fluctuations in relative scores and their relationship with student characteristics, including the distribution of ranks and their predictions using probabilistic models. Our investigation of the 2018 US Step 1 exam demonstrated that relative scores are highly susceptible to fluctuations, even when student characteristics remain consistent. In contrast, absolute scores, such as the total number of correct answers, remained stable and predictable given the students' characteristics. Our results show that 76.6% of students saw an absolute score change of less than 10, whereas 98.3% saw a relative score change of less than 10. Additionally, when adjusting for student-related factors, the predictions of relative scores varied greatly, ranging from the 5th to the 95th percentile. Our study also revealed that the predictions of relative scores were highly dependent on other factors, such as the distribution of ranks and previous performance. In contrast, the predictions of absolute scores were more stable and less affected by other variables. To summarize, absolute scores are preferred in educational assessments due to their clarity, consistency, and objectivity, unlike relative scores, which are more suitable for analytical purposes. In conclusion, absolute scores should be the primary focus of educational assessments, with relative scores being utilized solely for analytical purposes. Our analysis highlights the distinct characteristics of absolute and relative scores, demonstrating how the latter can lead to ambiguous and conflicting outcomes. In place of relative scores, we suggest using absolute scores, such as total numbers or percentages, to facilitate precise and predictable assessments. Our study also offers a comprehensive statistical analysis to predict absolute scores

We analyze the thermal response of a doped graphene sheet in contact with a phonon-bath, focusing on the interaction between electrons and lattice vibrations. In this context, we derive an analytical expression for the specific heat of the graphene sheet. Interestingly, this result exhibits a well-known logarithmic divergence at a critical temperature, stemming from the contribution of chiral nature in the graphene electrons. Moreover, we compute the average energy of the electrons in the graphene sheet using a self-consistent Born approximation, leading to the detection of a zero-temperature shielding effect. This effect arises as a consequence of electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions within the graphene sheet. In addition to these findings, we examine the impact of chemical potential on the specific heat and average energy of the electrons in the graphene sheet. Our analysis shows that by adjusting the chemical potential, we can either suppress or amplify the shielding effect, as well as the logarithmic divergence in the specific heat of the graphene sheet. In a specific scenario with a highly doped graphene sheet, the electron-phonon interaction has a significant impact, resulting in a specific heat profile characterized by a linear increase at low temperatures, followed by a logarithmic increase at higher temperatures. This behavior is in agreement with experimental observations reported in the scientific literature. Our analysis offers new insights into the thermal response of doped graphene sheets, shedding light on the roles of electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions in the thermal properties of this material. Our results may also contribute to the understanding of the thermal response in other 2D materials. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that the thermal response of a doped graphene sheet can be fine-tuned by adjusting the chemical potential. This capability may enable the mitigation of negative effects on the thermal response caused by electron-phonon interaction, as well as the amplification of the logarithmic divergence in the specific heat of the graphene sheet through doping. Lastly, we identify potential directions for future research on the thermal response of doped graphene sheets, including the computation of Raman scattering spectra, the examination of non-phonon modes of interaction, as well as the simulation of the thermal response in graphene nanoribbons and nanotubes. These research directions may ultimately contribute to the development of novel strategies to control the thermal response in graphene-based devices. In particular, we propose that the electron-phonon interaction in doped graphene sheets could be exploited to generate novel phononic devices, as well as that the chemical potential in these systems could be utilized to switch on or off specific device

Instrumental variable estimation is a prominent nonparametric technique used to identify causal relationships. This method assumes that a variable can serve as an instrument if it is affected by the treatment but does not depend on the outcome of interest, beyond its relationship with the treatment. Beyond simple, binary treatments, there is a limited understanding of this approach when treatments are complex or multi-dimensional. Addressing this, we develop a theoretical framework that clarifies how to select an appropriate instrument for a particular outcome of interest. This proof is then applied to examine the return on investment in higher education based on the specific fields of study pursued by graduates in the United States. Our analysis indicates that certain fields of study can be viewed as instrumental variables, effectively identifying the causal effects of specific skills and knowledge areas on earnings. This analysis also highlights the significance of considering the potential impact of other skills, reflecting the complexity of how fields of study influence earnings. Ultimately, our results indicate that investing in the arts does not yield a return, while fields such as computer science and engineering generate substantial benefits. Additionally, our data suggests that students who pursue fields in high demand tend to outearn their peers in non-in-demand fields, reflecting the importance of considering the labor market conditions for specific fields and skills. To further improve the accuracy of our estimates, we develop a novel model that accounts for the relationships between students' skills, colleges they attend, and labor market conditions for specific fields. This evidence-based approach to selecting instruments clarifies that what constitutes an instrument depends on the specific outcome of interest and that simple, universal instruments may not be effective in identifying causal relationships. To address the flatness problem in the early universe, several cosmological models have been developed. A unique approach to addressing this issue involves incorporating lattice dynamics into these models to mimic the universe's uniformity. By doing so, the phase space of the universe is partitioned into disjoint sets, each corresponding to a distinct lattice point. Furthermore, the conservation of certain Hamiltonian dynamics gives rise to a universal flow that maintains these disjoint sets, thereby rendering the phase space 'flat'. In this paper, we delve into three such cosmological models based on lattice dynamics and examine their inherent 'flatness property. To do this, we utilize parametric infinite-dimensional flows and investigate the universality of these models by varying the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics. Along the way, we encounter a situation where the lattice model undergoes a dynamical generalisation, and we establish that the universality of the 'flat' property relies on this parametric family. We then explore the dynamical implications of both classical and quantum aspects. However, it's essential to note that these models don't provide a comprehensive understanding of the early universe; rather, they serve as simplified models that shed light on the dynamic processes behind cosmic flatness. Given that these models are inherently 'flat', they fail to capture the universe's dynamic changes, thus rendering them unsuitable for simulating the early universe's rapid evolution. Nonetheless, these models can be effectively utilised in scenarios that involve slow changes over vast periods of time. On the other hand, when it comes to simulating rapid changes in the early universe, it may be more appropriate to employ cosmological models based on lattice dynamics that exhibit complex, dynamic 'flatness. We propose a novel approach to understanding neural networks as a fundamental model learned through data. By reframing the problem in terms of model selection, our method prevents overfitting and enables smooth generalization to new data. The core of our approach is a gradient-free neural network structure based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence and the Shannon entropy of networks. This innovation allows us to estimate the complexity of networks and selectively regularize them, all without relying on gradient information. The efficiency of our method is demonstrated through a variety of experiments, including predicting chaotic time-series and differentiating noisy images. Importantly, our approach is the first to achieve generalization to new data, outperforming established baselines in prediction accuracy. Moreover, our method is the only one to achieve generalization without additional parameters or pre-training. Additionally, our approach is the first to seamlessly incorporate the estimation of network complexity and regularization in a unified framework. Furthermore, our method is the first to demonstrate the emergence of sparse networks, characteristics of decision boundaries described in literature. Lastly, our approach is the first to demonstrate generalization in low-data scenarios. Overall, our method offers a groundbreaking approach to understanding and learning neural networks, generalization included. A significant portion of this work has been jointly published in the papers titled "A Unified Framework for Regularization in Neural Networks" and "Emergence of Sparse Networks with Generalization", both available at arxiv.org. Additionally, the source code of our approach, along with datasets, and demonstrations are publicly available at github.com/AntonioSeppia/gradient-free-neural-networks. We also found that certain jet structures were more relevant to specific types of jets than to others, with LRA assigning more importance to features that distinguish between types in line with expectations. In addition to validating the capability of a technique to interpret a model's judgments, this study also provides further evidence of the essential features that distinguish between different types of jets in the context of jet classification. The outcomes of this study may have far-reaching implications for understanding particle physics at its most fundamental level. Our understanding of high-resolution visual processing in human cognition has significant implications for the development of realistic virtual environments. This study demonstrates that high-resolution stereoscopic viewing in a virtual environment exceeds the expectations based on existing theoretical knowledge. This outstanding performance may be attributed to the reduction in viewfinder constraints, allowing participants to explore scenes more freely with head movements.  Therefore, when designing immersive visual experiences, priorities should be given to systems capable of seamless navigation and minimal distraction.  Furthermore, developers should strive to implement features empowering users to interact with virtual environments in a more natural and intuitively comfortable manner. By gradually adding mass to this core, we observed how its angular momentum would increase and its magnetic field establish itself, allowing for binary formation to evolve. We discovered that binaries could form through a process involving the core's fragmentation, but only when its mass exceeded a certain threshold, above which the magnetic field would dissipate, rendering the core susceptible to fragmentation. This study introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel R-based Independent Component Analysis (ICA) for handling mixed-gaussian and non-Gaussian data sets. Building on previous work, the method enhances existing approaches by reducing computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N/Nbin), where Nbin is the number of bins used to create a discrete representation of continuous data. This optimization enables smoother and more stable results, particularly for large data sets. The method's performance and flexibility are demonstrated through its application to synthetic data, both with and without relevant assumptions, as well as real-world data from in vitro digestion experiments. The code for the method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Charline-Alasseur/ICA_mar_K_RapidICA. Further developments can be found on the website of the LKB's Computational Biology group at http://bic-lkb.univ-evry.fr/Software. Evaluation of the method's performance in terms of time and memory consumption is as follows: For a pair of 2D synthetic images with 512x512 pixels, the processing time is approximately 150ms for a Gaussian mixture with 5 components and 300ms for a non-gaussian mixture with 5 components, both processed using Python 3.6 on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti graphics card. The method's memory consumption is approximately 4.5GB. With these specifications, the method appears suitable for analyzing the results of in vitro digestion experiments, where a large number of pixel values need to be processed quickly and efficiently. However, it may not be suitable for more complex tasks such as analyzing video sequences. Further research is needed to determine the method's potential applications in these areas. The surge in social media usage has led to a vast amount of data that is being utilized in various research domains to gather geographical information. This paper proposes a pioneering approach to instantly identify incidents reported on social media in real-time, by grouping nearby posts that are timed closely. Our method of classifying incident categories is augmented with the use of social media, allowing for more effective monitoring of incidents without the need for manual content analysis. The proposed approach is primarily designed to support instantaneous incident identification, and we demonstrate its applicability through case studies of traffic incidents and protests. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of our approach over existing static incident identification methods. Our evaluation reveals that the proposed approach achieves high accuracy in identifying incidents, and significantly reduces the delay in reporting compared to traditional methods. For example, the time it takes to identify a traffic incident using our approach is less by over three times the smallest existing method. Additionally, we show that the proposed approach is more tolerant of data inaccuracies than existing static incident identification methods. Specifically, the accuracy of our approach is 30% higher even when the social media data is inaccurate, a scenario that is commonly observed in real-world incidents. Lastly, we outline strategies for enhancing the proposed approach, and highlight potential research avenues that could further improve instantaneous incident identification. Our approach and associated code are made available for public access at https://github.com/ShahidNaumanKhan/Instantaneous-Incident-Identification. This research could be a potential area of interest for other researchers, and we anticipate that our findings may lead to new research questions, such as utilizing the proposed approach for data integration and utilization of social media in real-time monitoring of incidents. Additionally, we may explore utilizing the proposed approach for identifying and monitoring the spread of diseases in the future. Similarly, utilizing the proposed approach for environmental monitoring applications such as air and water quality could be another fascinating area of research to delve into. Lastly, utilizing the proposed approach for applications such as price manipulation and financial fraud detection presents another valuable research area to investigate. Recent studies have uncovered serious flaws in the design of adversarial robust deep learning models, revealing that certain samples can illicitly manipulate labels from artificial models. This has prompted a shift from traditional adversarial training, which prioritized model accuracy over adversarial queries, to a more transparent approach that focuses on ensuring adversarial robustness can be verified. We investigate this change and its impact on Bayesian neural networks, which are crucial for predictive uncertainty estimation but are currently untested against adversarial attacks. To confirm the robustness of their predictions, we evaluate Bayesian neural networks using a novel combination of verification and expectation propagation for handling sensitive perturbations. Our experiments demonstrate that models trained with this new framework exhibit robust performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tests. Moreover, this approach enables the generation of reliable predictive intervals, accurately capturing the uncertainty of models. To validate our results, we conduct a formal evaluation of the dependence of prediction distributions on adversarial perturbations. Remote sensing techniques that utilize hyperspectral imaging have become increasingly essential for various applications, as they enable the precise analysis of objects within an area, utilizing the precise wavelengths of light that are reflected or emitted by them. This precise data, known as spectral signatures, is highly valuable but also highly dimensional, as they comprise multiple wavelengths. Classifying images effectively typically relies on dimensionality reduction techniques to simplify the data while preserving important features. Our study investigates how different methods for reducing dimensional data affect the accuracy of hyperspectral image classification, as well as the consistency and computational efficiency. We evaluated six distinct hyperspectral image datasets from remote areas, reducing their dimensional data using six different methods, before applying an established classifier to analyze the results. Our findings indicate that not all dimensionality reduction methods are equivalent, leading to notable variations in accuracy, consistency, and computational efficiency. Compressed Autoencoders and Self-Organizing Maps seem particularly promising, outperforming other methods. Interestingly, our research also reveals that the choice of hyperspectral image classification technique is often unaffected by dimensionality reduction. These findings can guide researchers and practitioners in making informed choices about the methods to use in their remote sensing work, as demonstrated by our publicly available code. Additionally, our study's dataset, code, and experimental results are available for reproduction. We expect these findings to be valuable in other fields that utilize hyperspectral dimensional data. Also, we found that by reducing dimensional data, the computational efficiency of hyperspectral image classification can significantly improve, as illustrated by our study on SPOT-5 image data. We observed a notable rise in the accuracy of classification results. Therefore, dimensionality reduction can lead to the development of more efficient high-dimensional hyperspectral image classification methods. Furthermore, our study provides a comprehensive comparison of the performance of different hyperspectral dimensional data reduction methods on various datasets, as well as their results. This comparison is based on the accuracy of classification results. Moreover, our study also examines how hyperspectral dimensional data reduction impacts the runtime of classification algorithms, as well as the complexity of decisions. We found that dimensionality reduction can lead to the development of more efficient decision-making processes. As a result, dimensionality reduction can be beneficial for complex remote sensing applications. We also found that by reducing dimensional data, the complexity of decisions and hyperspectral image classification runtime can significantly improve, as illustrated by our study on SPOT-5 image data. Previous studies suggest that enormous natural language models require and benefit from vast amounts of training data. However, this requirement poses significant challenges when working with specialized or private datasets that aren't freely accessible due to copyright or data protection restrictions. This paper explores alternative methods for utilizing smaller models that can learn more efficiently from smaller datasets, including techniques such as model pruning, weight scaling, and layer merging. By analyzing the efficacy of these methods, we identify key considerations for future research and successfully apply these methods to a BERT model, achieving a size reduction of up to 30% with minimal performance loss when working with a Spanish knowledge graph. Additionally, we introduce a evaluation framework for NLP models that focuses on their ability to learn from minimal amounts of data while reducing memory usage. This framework enables us to assess the potential benefits of reduced model size for inference and storage purposes. Our code and model implementations are freely available on GitHub. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the widespread adoption of NLP models in resource-constrained settings, including edge devices, restricted datasets, or environments with limited storage capacity. We hope this research will contribute to the development of more efficient NLP models that can thrive on smaller datasets and have a significant impact on specific use cases. A classification of protein structures has been established based on the relationship between residual amide quantum mechanical properties and observed shifts in NMR experiments, ultimately yielding nine distinct categories. It's found that proteins with normal backbones fall into the first and second groups while those with distortions at L-amino acids fall into the third and fourth groups, and those with distortions at D-amino acids fall into the fifth through ninth groups. The groups can be narrowly divided to pinpoint specific regions of residue-level deviations. The classification process identifies and highlights 28 critical quantum mechanical parameters, ultimately leading to the improvement of current residue-level prediction methods. Additionally, a set of enforcement constraints has been created to aid in the validation and enhancement of protein structures using quantum mechanical parameters, particularly in regions where predictions are less accurate. The implementation of these constraints using molecular mechanics based energy-related terms has been done, and experiments have been conducted to assess the effect of enforcing these constraints on the quality of protein structures. The results show a notable improvement in overall protein quality and the resolution of some difficult amino acid patterns. However, some parameters still lack sufficient statistical significance to effectively influence the structure. Future research will focus on enhancing the precision of quantum mechanical predictions to fully leverage the information provided by these delicate parameters. Meanwhile, the current set of constraints is being made available for all widely used molecular mechanics packages to aid in the optimization of protein structures. The code, including quantum mechanical predictions, energetic calculations, and residue selection, has been made accessible on the BegerLy web platform. The code also enables the production of classification results for any set of protein structures, and the web platform allows for the submission of protein structures to be classified or evaluated using the developed constraints. The results of these classifications or evaluations can then be downloaded for further analysis. The enforcement of these constraints is recommended for all proteins to improve their resolution, particularly in regions that are currently difficult to model. The use of these constraints during molecular dynamics simulations will also be explored in future studies to analyze the dynamic relationships between residues and their movement over time. The results will be made available on the BegerLy web platform for public use. In the context of perturbation theory, a particular decomposition of the graph functions into a sum of connected, yet interacting regions is referred to as parquet decomposition. Historically, the parquet theory was developed as a resummation technique aimed at obtaining scale-invariant results from perturbation theory. However, the underlying structure of parquet functions bears a striking resemblance to the structure inherent in the Hamiltonians generated from perturbative corrections to Hamiltonian formulations of quantum field theories. By mapping parquet functions to these Hamiltonians, we identify a specific subset of 'Hamiltonian parquet' theories that encompass various known theories, such as $\phi^4$ theory and Yang-Mills theory, in addition to providing a natural framework for the study of perturbative field theories. Furthermore, we show that the equations governing Hamiltonian parquet theories are equivalent to the geometric flow equations introduced by Zinn-Justin. Lastly, we note that while our formulation achieves a meaningful simplification of the parquet equations, it introduces a non-local structure that may pose challenges in constructing solutions to these equations. Given that the solutions to geometric flow equations are unknown even in the simplest theory of $\phi^4$, this presents an important area of study. We propose that investigating this problem in the context of Hamiltonian parquet theories may yield valuable insights. We conclude by noting that our exploration into the connection between parquet theories and the perturbative expansions of quantum field theories through Hamiltonian decomposition may facilitate the development of a more intuitive and simplified description of these expansions, at least at the level of connected graph functions. We hope that this relationship will serve as a fruitful area of study for researchers in both parquet theories and perturbative quantum field theory. To properly understand the behavior of electrons in solids, researchers use a complex mathematical approach known as many-body theory. By employing $ab ~initio$ methods that can accurately model this theory, researchers can gain insights into unusual phenomena such as superconductivity, for example, when it occurs in some materials at extremely low temperatures, or the formation of unusual states called exciton liquids in certain semiconductors.

Recently, researchers were able to apply $ab ~initio$ methods to model the behavior of electrons in a specific type of material called transition metal dichalcogenides, specifically by using advanced computer algorithms to simulate the interactions between different particles in these materials at very low temperatures.

As a test of these new algorithms, researchers studied a specific type of material called 1T-$TiSe_2$ that is known to undergo a phase transition into an exciton liquid state at very low temperatures. By using the $ab ~initio$ methods, researchers were able to model this phase transition and obtain results that match experimental observations well. Furthermore, these new algorithms predict that the exciton liquid state could persist up to one-third of its volume before transitioning into a more solid-like state, and that this transition into the solid-like state could be driven by the application of external pressure. Finally, these studies also suggest that another type of phase transition, called a charge-density-wave state, could also occur in this material and that its behavior could be tuned using applied pressure. Overall, these new findings confirm that the $ab ~initio$ methods used here are reliable and provide new insights into the complex physics of these materials. Additionally, these studies suggest that these materials could be valuable for applications in quantum technology due to their unique properties. Finally, these researchers express the need for further experimentation to confirm the predicted behavior of these materials. We propose a new framework for game-theoretic semi-supervised learning where two players, the learner and the teacher, engage in a minimax learning process. The teacher provides a teacher network with limited resources, and the learner uses a separate learner network with more resources to make predictions from labeled and unlabeled data. Our framework allows us to explore the delicate balance between the learner and teacher, as well as the relative resources between them. Through our study, we discovered that when the learner's resources are significantly greater than the teacher's resources, the game approaches a supervised learning scenario. Conversely, when the teacher's resources far exceed the learner's resources, the game resembles a regularized eigensolver. Notably, we found that our minimax model can be approximated by a sum-of-squares (SOS) verifier, and we leveraged this property to achieve empirical improvements in models under adversarial attacks and in semi-supervised image classification tasks. Furthermore, we found that our minimax model can be implemented using a simple and efficient algorithm that generates random wide neural networks. Our experiments demonstrated that these random wide neural networks outperform the traditional deep neural networks in models under adversarial attacks and in semi-supervised image classification tasks. The geometric interpretation of our model's behavior provides valuable insights into the effect of resource ratios on network performance. Additionally, we observed that our model exhibits enhanced robustness and semi-supervised capabilities. Moreover, we successfully applied our minimax model to the distributed semi-supervised learning scenario, where the learner and teacher networks are located on different devices. The structure of our model facilitates the separation of computational tasks among devices, enabling efficient data distribution and improving computational efficiency. The effectiveness of our approach was confirmed through experiments on multiple datasets. Furthermore, we found that our model can be trained using a dual-iteration algorithm that converges to a stable state. The theoretical guarantees of our model are closely related to the existing results in online learning and evolutionary game theory. The empirical evaluation of our model reveals that it achieves superior performance compared to existing distributed semi-supervised learning methods. The geometric interpretation of our model's behavior and the observed robustness and semi-supervised capabilities of our model provide valuable insights into the effect of resource ratios on network performance. Additionally, we found that our model can be implemented using a simple and efficient algorithm that generates random wide neural networks. To address potential biases in predicting COVID-19 cases, we suggest employing target-sensitive forecasting models, which take into account anticipated case numbers when predicting variables like deaths. However, using these models to estimate distributional probabilities becomes computationally infeasible due to the high dimensionality of such models. As an alternative, we propose using standardized enhanced inverse probability weighting, a method that enables the efficient estimation of probabilistic quantities from target-sensitive models. By assuming the density of the distribution to be known, SEIPW weighs observed data by incorporating hypothetical outcomes generated from the target-sensitive model in proportion to their likelihood according to the assumed density. When the actual density is unknown, SEIPW estimates it non-parametrically using kernel smoothing methods. Building upon this idea, we develop a more practical approach, SEIPW-k, where the kernel density estimation is conducted using only a subset of the data, specifically the hypothetical outcomes that are closest to the target. Through simulations and case studies, we demonstrate that SEIPW-k efficiently estimates the distribution of future deaths while being nearly as accurate as SEIPW. Furthermore, we showcase the utility of our approach through a joint application of SEIPW-k to forecast two distributed quantities: COVID-19-related deaths and electricity demand. The latter utilizes a corresponding "demand-sensitive" version of our model, which is developed through modifications to the SToPM architecture, a prior model of COVID-19 deaths. The demand-sensitive model is trained on proxy variables derived from Google search data, which is also used to enhance the forecasting performance of our model. As a result, this paper offers a versatile approach to modeling target-sensitive distributions, which can be applied to domains beyond epidemiology. The code and datasets for this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/jmnicholson/SEIPW/tree/main. Additionally, our enhanced target-sensitive models have been deployed in collaboration with The COVID-19 Forecasting Consortium and are accessible through the prediction interface at https://covid-forecast.info/. The models are also registered in the OpenNEP platform under the IDs COVID-ELE-1 and COVID-DEME-1. Lastly, the predictions generated during this research are also available through the prediction interface at https://covid-ele.predict.institute/. This research investigates the problem of detecting and mitigating fraud in offline RL, focusing on malicious alterations of reward feedback. We develop a novel and robust version of the standard RL problem by incorporating the possibility of data tampering. This revised problem requires the RL algorithm to find the most accurate policy among multiple candidates, each characterized by its potential correlation with manipulated data. We also propose a new approach, called Fraud-Resilient RL (FRRRL), which can identify and counter the effects of fraudulent activities on reward feedback. The theoretical foundations of our model reveal its equivalence to two distinct optimization problems. We further develop the theoretical aspects by proving the uniqueness of its solution, as well as the computationally infeasible task of obtaining it. To address these challenges, we devise an iterative method based on alternating optimization and test its performance in simulated environments, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing baselines.
