This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability results for one-dimensional heat equations featuring dynamic boundary controls. Furthermore, we establish the exact expression of the control cost in optimal problems involving such heat equations, which in turn allows us to determine the exact threshold for exact controllability in the one-dimensional heat equation with dynamic boundaries. Ultimately, we prove a version of logarithmic sub-Levelt convergence for the L^2-norm of the control cost in optimal control problems. To support these findings, we present a detailed estimate of the control cost using a Lagrangian formulation. The analysis is then validated through a numerical example that demonstrates a level of accuracy in the computed solution. In addition, we use the obtained estimates to analyze the behavior of a sequence of optimal control problems with moving targets, which we previously introduced. The analysis yields several interesting observations. Firstly, we confirm that the sequence of optimal controls is convergent. Moreover, we find that the limit of the control cost is given by the integral of the positive part of the control cost cost function. Finally, we show that the logarithmic sub-Levelt convergence property holds for the L^2-norm of the control cost cost function. The study begins by noting that in the case of controls acting directly on the interior of the domain, the issue of impulsiveness arises naturally. However, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can also occur when the control acts on the boundary of the domain, which leads to the concept of boundary impulsiveness. The study then focuses on determining the exact threshold for exact controllability in the one-dimensional heat equation with dynamic boundaries, where the control acts on the boundary of the domain. The result shows that the exact controllability in the L^2-norm can be achieved if the support of the initial condition is smaller than the controllability constant. Furthermore, we find that the optimal cost in the L^2-norm is proportional to the time of controllability and the square of the space controllability constant. The study also establishes the exact expression of the control cost in the L^1-norm. Moreover, we prove a logarithmic sub-Levelt convergence property for the L^2-norm of the control cost cost function. The study uses several log-concave functions, including specifically tailored versions of the heat kernel and the control cost cost function, to derive these estimates. The exact expressions of the control cost cost functions are then used to analyze the behavior of a sequence of optimal control problems with moving targets, which we previously introduced.

In the realm of dialogue systems, the out-of-domain text category receives relatively little attention, with most research focusing on in-domain text. However, out-of-domain text can be further subdivided into misleading and plain varieties. This paper seeks to clarify the distinction between these two subcategories, providing a set of criteria to assess and compare their prevalence across various domains. Moreover, this study endeavors to contribute to the development of effective out-of-domain detection methods by introducing a novel benchmark, specifically tailored for domain change scenarios, to evaluate and improve existing techniques. In addition, two novel methods are proposed to analyze and improve current research in out-of-domain classification. The proposed benchmarks, data sets, and code are freely accessible for reproduction and further study. Our research reveals that existing models are more adept at identifying plain out-of-domain text than misleading text, and that pre-trained language models perform well on out-of-domain detection tasks when fine-tuned with domain-specific data. Nonetheless, they often generate ambiguous responses that conceal the conversation's intention, highlighting the need for further advances in out-of-domain text classification. In a related area, this study investigates the prevalence and characteristics of another distinct text type, self-contradictory text, and explores its potential connection to plain out-of-domain text. The analysis indicates that self-contradictory text can be effectively identified through pre-trained language models, but they struggle to pinpoint plain out-of-domain text, which appears to be more accurately classified by models fine-tuned with domain-specific data. Unlike out-of-domain text, self-contradictory text does not exhibit a consistent distribution across various domains. Moreover, this study finds that existing models often fail to recognize misleading text, which might be partially attributed to the limited presence of misleading text in the training data. Consequently, this study proposes two new methods to aid out-of-domain classification and provides a unique dataset combining text that is out-of-domain, self-contradictory, and plain domain change types, dubbed the ODLC data set, consisting of 15 domains, with associated labels and corresponding data sets provided for each domain. Traditionally, molecular engines are modelled as undergoing thermal equilibrium with their surroundings, utilizing thermal fluctuations to generate work. This study proposes a different dynamics where the engine and its environment are in a state of non-equilibrium known as Brownian molecular dynamics. In this framework, the engine is in contact with an electron bath, allowing for one-electron transfer between the two. Although this transfer is highly unlikely under normal conditions, it occurs frequently at high temperatures, enabling the conversion of thermal energy into directed motion. A numerical simulation of a molecular motor shown to be driven by this process, has been successfully tested and demonstrated to replicate the behavior of actual nanomachines. Furthermore, the engine can be designed to display diverse modes of motion, such as stationary, linear and circular trajectories, as well as oscillatory and rotational movements by adjusting its structure. Additionally, the engine's motion can be made to display memory effects, reciprocity and non-Newtonian forces. Lastly, an analysis of the engine's entropy has revealed that far-from-equilibrium systems like this one can still exhibit reduced entropy production compared to a system in thermal equilibrium. In other words, systems in non-equilibrium can actually display reduced entropy production than systems in thermal equilibrium. This has been observed in scenarios such as an active swimmer in a fluid, driven by internal forces, also displaying reduced entropy production. This study has successfully distant-furred the notion that reduced entropy production is an exclusive property of systems in thermal equilibrium. Additionally, this study has proposed the development of a thermal molecular machine that could convert thermal energy into mechanical work, a concept based on tunneling dynamics, which could have practical applications in the development of molecular engines. It has also provided a theoretical explanation for the reduction in entropy production observed in certain systems by identifying a common denominator - the directed motion facilitated by tunneling. In this research, we introduce a novel method to enhance dynamic mode decomposition's (DMD) ability to accurately capture complex flows while minimizing errors caused by nonlinearity. Our approach, Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), uses kernel regression to remove nonlinearity from DMD equations, thereby recovering the true linear dynamics governing complex systems. By leveraging LANDO, we can separate a flow's linear and nonlinear effects, achieving two main goals: eliminating nonlinearity's influence on DMD's estimated dynamics and using nonlinear information to improve accuracy. Our results demonstrate that LANDO can recover the true linear dynamics in highly nonlinear systems (e.g., Kleckner-Durin flow) and enhance DMD's accuracy in moderately nonlinear systems (e.g., Kelvin-Helmholtz instability). Additionally, LANDO can be used to provide a linear low-order model for high-dimensional data, such as that obtained from magnetic resonance imaging of blood flow in the human brain. Our findings illustrate the significant impact LANDO can have on understanding complex physical systems, whether that involves quantifying error caused by nonlinearity or utilizing nonlinearity to achieve higher accuracy in modeling dynamic systems. A open-source implementation of LANDO is available at https://github.com/aim-uidot/lando.git. This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, spin rates, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarves within binary star systems, extracting parameters through the computational modeling of this collapse and its resulting neutron star. The stochastic simulations of binary evolution allow us to identify distinct evolutionary pathways, one of which corresponds to the origin of millisecond pulsars. Our findings on the parameters of these pulsars align with observational data, yielding a notable match for the distribution of spin periods. Additionally, our simulations predict an accompanying stellar system evolution, resulting in a distinct separation between the birth locations of the millisecond pulsars and the broader population of neutron stars. Our analysis offers new insights into the origin of millisecond pulsars, and their subsequent displacement from their parent star systems, giving rise to the gap between the MSPS and ENS populations. Our work may contribute to an improved understanding of the overall MSP population properties and the eventual fate of these systems, potentially leading to supernova events that expose heavy-element rich matter. The research also paves the way for analogous applications in the study of other compact objects, such as magnetars and black widow pulsars. Three-dimensional model retrieval techniques are usually based on using computer to create three-dimensional models. However, this limits the amount of data that can be used for retrieval. Our research explores an alternative approach where three-dimensional models are derived from virtual drawings created by users in a three-dimensional virtual environment. This novel method enables the creation of large datasets for 3D model retrieval, as well as novel applications such as generating three-dimensional models from sketches. Our current results show that the effectiveness of our approach is comparable to established methods using computer-generated models. Additionally, we discovered that the virtual drawing environment enhances the user's creativity. Our future work will focus on further refining our approach and applying it to more complex drawing tasks. We will also extend our model retrieval framework to include semantic information to facilitate more advanced retrieval capabilities. This will involve developing new features and testing them against existing benchmarks. Our ultimate goal is to enable effective retrieval of three-dimensional models from virtual drawings, as well as to introduce new methods for creating three-dimensional models. This will have significant practical implications in various fields such as architecture, product design and animation. Specifically, developers may use our drawing-based model retrieval technique to allow users to find similar 3D models in games and applications based on sketches drawn in three-dimensional virtual reality environments. In the field of computer-aided design, designers may utilize our retrieval technique to identify and select relevant 3D models during the design process. Furthermore, bigner may use our approach to enable users to reproduce and modify existing 3D models as a starting point for their projects. To achieve these applications, we will continue to refine our virtual drawing method and evaluate its performance in comparison to existing computer-generated models. Our preliminary results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach, as well as its potential for various applications. This paper presents our current research outcomes and serves as a foundation for our future work in this domain. Specifically, we contribute novel methods for evaluating the performance of 3D model retrieval tasks, as well as new applications and approaches that combine virtual drawings and three-dimensional model retrieval. Additionally, we make available our implementation of the virtual drawing method, as well as the created datasets and experimental results for reproduction and further evaluation. Our code and datasets can be accessed through the following repository: https://github.com/I6-ASU-VRR/3DVRDT3DModelRetrieval. This repository includes the implementation of our virtual drawing method, as well as the created datasets and experimental results. We make these research outcomes publicly available for reproduction and further evaluation

HD80606b, a gas giant in the L2 plane, is notable for its highly eccentric orbit and unique properties, making it one of the few planets like this in terms of mass and size that is also well-characterized. As the planet transits its host star every 111 days, researchers have the opportunity to study its atmosphere using space-based telescopes. To make the most of upcoming observations by the James Webb Space Telescope, it is crucial to have an accurate understanding of the planet's orbital path. This is particularly important since the most effective times to schedule a particular observation are when the planet is on the far side of its orbit and passing in front of its star. To this end, a team used a network of small telescopes, involving 236 volunteers and the Z-TESS network, to gather new data on HD80606b's orbital motions. Analysis of the resulting data confirmed that the planet's characteristics are consistent with previous findings, indicating a mass of approximately 5.15 times that of Earth and an atmospheric pressure of about 10 bar. With its new ephemeris, scheduled observations using the James Webb Space Telescope were then adjusted to take place at the optimal times, based on its orbital cycle. This involved using a data analysis algorithm to select the most useful sets of observation dates, ultimately resulting in a revised list of preferred dates for the James Webb Space Telescope. This study serves as a model for collaborative research, highlighting the effectiveness of working together on a small scale to achieve scientific goals, using available resources and available data, as seen in the success of the Z-TESS network in gathering 215 new transit times for the planet using 138 different telescopes. Further research using the James Webb Space Telescope is now set to take place, with a focus on understanding the atmospheric chemistry of HD80606b by observing it at various points in its orbit. This could help reveal whether the planet's unique atmosphere is similar to those of other planets with similar properties. To make the most of these observations, it is essential to continue using the telescope network to gather new data on HD80606b's orbital motions. This will involve ongoing efforts by the team, as part of the Z-TESS network and other similar initiatives, to monitor the planet's transits and share their findings. This is likely to be a crucial strategy for future research, as the team continues to study the planet using a network of small telescopes, with a focus on understanding the details of its orbit and the characteristics of its atmosphere. A significant issue in robotics is the efficient learning of tasks. Current methods either simplify the complex end-effect objectives or use them in a crude manner, despite acknowledging their importance. We take a different approach and propose a framework that drives motor learning towards a precise target by regularly assessing the outcome of imagined movements. This innovative system uses simulated collisions to quickly determine movement outcomes without actually moving, allowing it to optimize a task more efficiently than other methods that rely on actual movements. We test this framework in a diverse set of simulated and real-world experiments to understand its impact on learning dynamics and movement patterns. The results show that this framework expands the learning landscape to include more precise and varied end-effect objectives, and that it achieves faster learning times than other methods, often in a fraction of the original time. Additionally, the results suggest that this framework produces more localized and efficient movement patterns during learning. The code for this research is openly available on GitHub at the link provided. Furthermore, a video showcasing the results can be found on the arXiv platform. The compactified Poincaré group, a subgroup of the Lorentz group, is the full three-dimensional rotational symmetry group $SO(3)$'s covering. It possesses a nonlinear momentum operator, whose application in constructing a relativistic quantum theory is intriguing but also poses a significant challenge. Researchers are still trying to find a suitable quantum action for this momentum operator. We discover, however, that the quantum action for the relativistic Poincaré group's momentum operator is the covariant Klein-Gordon action. This result stems from our finding that the covariant Klein-Gordon action is the unique classical action for Poincaré group's momentum operator that is both covariant and classical. We utilize a novel method to determine the action, an method which could be applied to other groups as well. We also establish that the covariant Klein-Gordon action is the general solution to the issue of finding a suitable quantum action for the relativistic Poincaré group's momentum operator. We further prove that this action gives rise to a nonlocal quantum momentum operator. We show that the relativistic Poincaré group's action leads to a novel method for obtaining the conventional Einstein-Hilbert action through an extremum variation procedure. We also establish that this action gives rise to conventional de Rham degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we use the relativistic Poincaré group's action to develop a novel method for obtaining the conventional Klein-Gordon action through an extremum variation procedure. Additionally, we show that the extremum variation procedure gives rise to a novel method for obtaining first-order conventional gravity actions. We established that these methods are legitimate. We also use these methods to investigate various types of action, including Yang-Mills action, Einstein-Yang-Mills action, and Born-Infeld action. These methods give rise to various types of classical actions, including Einstein-Yang-Mills action, Einstein-Yang-Mills-Born-Infeld action, and Yang-Mills-Born-Infeld action. Furthermore, we show that the extremum variation procedure gives rise to a novel method for obtaining a class of action that generalizes Yang-Mills action, Einstein-Yang-Mills action, and Yang-Mills-Born-Infeld action. Finally, we establish that the extremum variation procedure gives rise to a novel method for obtaining Einstein-Yang-Mills-Born-Infeld action. We have developed efficient algorithms to solve NP-complete upward planarity problems, which ensure that graphs remain vertically oriented in a tree-like structure. Our methods work by reducing the problem to a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) problem and leveraging previous research on linear parameterized complexity to develop efficient algorithms. Specifically, we've developed parameterized algorithms for finding a rooted upward planar subgraph and identifying the rooted center of a graph. Our techniques also allow us to develop new FPPT algorithms for the center problem and maintaining upward planarity in directed acyclic graphs. To achieve this, we've defined new parameterized tractability criteria, extending previous research on linear parameterized complexity and exploiting structural properties of ordered graphs. As a result, we've developed efficient algorithmic solutions for these challenging graph problems. Our research also provides new FTPT methods for converting sequences of graphs into a single graph with upward planarity properties. which, given a set of processed data, may not always understand the meaning of
its inputs. Inspired by human learning, we have investigated how an agent can use

the most informative past memories are often ones that are related to the current

In this article, we take a quantitative approach to examine the progress of tiny cell research from 4G to 6G. We start by defining tiny cells and the roles they play in supporting various applications. Next, we break down the evolution of tiny cell technology into distinct eras, highlighting 4G tiny cell and the underlying challenges, as well as the advancements made in the ongoing 5G era. We then look to the future, discussing the tiny cell developments that will shape the emerging 6G technology. To track tiny cell research advancements, we propose a visualization method utilizing a network knowledge graph, where similar research topics are clustered and linked. We update our knowledge graph annually to facilitate comparisons across different eras. The analysis of our knowledge graph reveals that tiny cell research has witnessed substantial growth in recent years, as seen in the figure created using this analysis. By studying the research outcome attributes, such as metrics, models, and applications, we identify trends and propose future research directions. The knowledge graph and associated code are publicly accessible for reproduction and future validation. Our research aims to provide a comprehensive perspective on tiny cell research, enabling researchers to navigate the field, identify gaps, and explore new areas for future investigation. The data, code, and graph are available at https://tiny-cell.github.io/. The empirical evaluation of our proposed method is detailed in our previous articles [1,2]. This article may be updated to keep pace with recent research developments, with the current version reflecting our analysis up to 2021. We plan to conduct further updates in the future.

The presence of a Hoyle state, $^7$Li, is established through its unique decay pattern. Recent experiments at RIKEN [1] and iNSPIRE [2], investigating the decay of $^7$Li from a TPC, support its existence. Our calculation demonstrates that nearly medium-free $\alpha$ and $^3$He spectroscopies can confirm the characteristics of the Hoyle state without being overwhelmed by its dense surroundings. At the RIKEN QCD Research Center, where $^7$Li production is feasible, the detection of its direct decay in a TPC should be feasible even in the dense environment. Our simulation indicates that the density of the surrounding medium has a minimal effect on the detection of the $^7$Li decay, implying that the dimensions of the detector should be sufficient to cover the full decay pattern of the Hoyle state. Consequently, the medium does not substantially alter the determination of the $^7$Li gamma-decay branching ratio. Our simulation aligns with the findings from the iNSPIRE experiment that the detector can fully contain the $^7$Li decay pattern. At the RIKEN facility, where the $^7$Li beam is available with a relatively low intensity of 10^8 particles per second, the decay of the Hoyle state can be fully detected within a time frame of around 100 seconds. In a dense environment, the signal associated with the Hoyle state is primarily affected by its direct decay into three helium nuclei, rather than other possible decays. At the RIKEN facility, where the $^7$Li beam is available with a relatively low intensity of 10^8 particles per second, the decay of the Hoyle state can be fully detected within a time frame of around 100 seconds. In a dense environment, the signal associated with the Hoyle state is primarily affected by its direct decay into two alpha particles and a neutron, rather than other possible decays. A graph G is considered soluble if it can be accurately located based on the knowledge of the distances between any pair of vertices. A set S of vertices is known as a location set if the distance between each vertex in G to every vertex in S is uniquely determined. The minimum number of vertices needed in S to make G soluble is referred to as the metric dimension (cd(G)) of G. A subset S is known as a 2-solver if for any two distinct vertices in G, the distance between them is uniquely determined as either less than or equal to the minimum distance between the two vertices in S. The minimum number of vertices needed in S to make G soluble is referred to as the 2-metric dimension (2cd(G)) of G. In this research, 2cd(G) is studied for finite graphs by proving that it is equal to the minimum number of vertices needed in S to make G soluble where the distance between each vertex in S and every vertex in S is at least 2. The result is further generalized to the concept of t-metric dimension of a graph where a vertex's distance to every other vertex in the graph is at least t. Machine learning models are widely applied but often rely on supervised training, which assumes labeled data and a clear goal, but in reality, objectives and labels are frequently uncertain. This problem is particularly common in areas like medicine, where data is stained and decisions are difficult to define. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework for training machine learning models in ambiguous environments. Our approach, Indecision Forests, utilizes uncertain objectives and data, relying on arguments to establish connections between input and output. By applying arguments from examples and goal descriptions, our model learns to make decisions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by creating a decision forest that navigates ambiguous medical diagnostics, showing that Indecision Forests outperforms traditional machine learning methods in ambiguous settings. Additionally, our framework is designed for human interpretation, eliminating the need for explicit probability distributions or model ensembles to capture ambiguity. This novel feature enables our approach to tackle problems that are inherently uncertain, providing a valuable tool for applications in ambiguous environments. More information is available at https://pralab.mit.edu/indecision-forests. A publicly available Python library for Indecision Forests can be found at https://github.com/atalukta/indecision-forests. This work is currently being extended to address uncertainty in model reasoning, which will be presented in a companion paper. Experiments have shown that the current approach is efficient but can benefit from further optimization, particularly in terms of scalarization schemes. Future research will focus on developing new techniques that reduce computational complexity without sacrificing performance. Additionally, we aim to apply our approach to other domains beyond medical diagnostics. It is possible that the primary contribution of Indecision Forests lies in its potential to tackle entirely new applications, which we have not yet identified, due to its unique ability to capture ambiguity in objectives and data. The DTW distance is commonly applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and retrieval tasks, often outperforming other distances. Nonetheless, its time complexity hinders its practical use in large datasets. To address this limitation, a optimized DTW distance variant, referred to as PrunedDTW, was developed. PrunedDTW significantly reduces time complexity by discarding irrelevant sections. However, its early discarding strategy may lead to suboptimal results in certain situations. To address these issues, we introduce an improved PrunedDTW distance, referred to as PrunedDTW-ED. This variant employs an enhanced early discarding strategy, reducing the number of discarded intervals and improving results. To confirm the effectiveness of the improved technique, we compared PrunedDTW-ED with existing approaches in a comprehensive experiment consisting of three similarity retrieval tasks. The findings reveal that PrunedDTW-ED surpasses the existing PrunedDTW approach, as well as several other efficient DTW based approaches, in two out of three tested scenarios. Additionally, we present PrunedDTW-ED as a open source implementation for future use. To validate the robustness of the proposed approach, we employed comprehensive robustness tests, confirming that PrunedDTW-ED consistently delivers better results compared to existing approaches. The robustness tests also revealed that PrunedDTW-ED consistently outperforms the existing PrunedDTW approach, as well as several other efficient DTW based approaches, in early discarding based PrunedDTW variants. Effective testing is crucial for any software project's success, yet many students struggle with it. Current evaluation methods, such as direct measurement through code review, often provide immediate feedback but lack context. This leads to students focusing solely on testing technique, rather than its purpose. This study presents an alternative approach, inquiry-based testing, which incorporates real-world scenarios and practical problems. To confirm its efficacy, we compared IBT to traditional methods in a testing course, and found that IBT performed better. Not only did IBT achieve higher grades, but it also received higher feedback ratings from students. Our results indicate that IBT can provide more accurate, timely, and fair evaluation, as well as promote better understanding. Therefore, we suggest considering IBT as a viable option for testing education. If necessary, a hybrid model combining IBT with other methods can also be effective. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a popular choice for graph-based data analysis. They merge the benefits of convolutional neural networks, commonly used in image processing, with the power of graph models. This fusion of techniques has led to GCNs being effectively applied to a range of tasks, including graph classification and node classification. However, in our investigation, we observed that GCNs can often achieve comparable or even superior performance to state-of-the-art models on specific datasets. Despite this achievement, we recognize that GCNs can be interpreted as incorporating an over-blurred feature extraction process. This process involves the substitution of a given node's features with an average of neighboring nodes' features, weighted according to their connection strength. Our analysis highlights how this feature substitution technique contributes to the success of GCNs in graph-based learning applications. Additionally, we propose a novel improvement to standard GCNs, known as Multiple-Aggregation Graph Convolutional Networks (MAGCNs). In MAGCNs, each node's features are replaced by a combination of neighboring nodes' features, using various aggregation methods. This enhanced approach surpasses the performance of standard GCNs, according to our experimental results. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of the MAgCN model, aiming to explain its success. In particular, we investigated the impact of distinct hyperparameters on the model's behavior, as well as the model's response to synthetic data manipulation. Our systematic evaluation of the model, through extensive experiments, confirms its efficacy on 7 publicly accessible datasets, surpassing the performance of GCNs in node classification tasks. Specifically, the model achieved improved accuracy, augmented feature extraction insights, and reduced model size, compared to GCNs. Additionally, we found that the model effectively addresses 'over-blurring' in GCNs by incorporating an average of neighboring nodes' features. Furthermore, we explored the model's behavior when applied to pre-trained models, demonstrating its ability to improve results. Ultimately, our investigation contributes to the understanding of GCNs as an 'over-blurred' feature extraction technique and proposes MAGCNs as a valuable improvement to standard GCNs. Achieving single-crystalline Heusler films is crucial for their integration into spintronics and energy conversion technologies. This study investigates the epitaxial behavior of Mn$_2$Av and MnAv$_2$ (Av = Ge, Si) films on graphene/sapphire using ab initio and empirical methods, focusing on the importance of epitaxial relationship and chemical bonding. It's discovered that chemical bonding plays a significant role in determining the epitaxial relationship, whereas epitaxial mismatch has a minor effect. Film growth is found to be a remote epitaxy versus van der Waals epitaxy versus islanding process regulated by the epitaxial relationship, epitaxial strain, and chemical bonding. The results indicate that remote epitaxy and van der Waals epitaxy are not mutually exclusive, and that van der Waals epitaxy can occur even with a perfect epitaxial match. Additionally, it's found that the remote epitaxy is associated with a higher energy barrier, but also offers the advantage of minimizing contamination during growth due to reduced interaction with the substrate. The study suggests that the van der Waals epitaxy could be a useful strategy for achieving single-crystalline Heusler films, and that growing films with a lattice parameter closer to that of graphene can improve epitaxial quality by minimizing epitaxial strain. The research provides a new perspective on Heusler film growth and suggests new approaches to realize single-crystalline Heusler films. The findings have broader implications for the development of other epitaxial films, and could help to overcome common challenges in epitaxial growth, such as achieving single-crystalline films, reducing contamination, and minimizing disorder. Internet Service Providers have long been plagued by the issue of revenue disparity, generating just enough income to cover their costs. Content Providers, on the other hand, are willing to pay Internet Service Providers for guaranteed Quality of Service. Our proposed model revolves around a revenue-sharing agreement, where Content Providers compensate Internet Service Providers for both their initial investment and a predetermined Quality of Service level. We break down the scenario into two distinct cases, where either the Content Providers or the Internet Service Providers decide on the pricing model. Our analysis yields closed-form expressions for revenue distribution and achieves two key objectives: ensuring both parties pay a positive amount and preventing overpricing by either party. Our model can be generalized to accommodate multiple Content Providers and is applicable to various Network Service Models. We illustrate our approach using numerical examples and make our associated code available on GitHub. Our experiment results validate the efficacy of our suggested model, supporting the feasibility of revenue sharing as a means for healthy cooperation between Content and Internet Service Providers. Ultimately, this leads to improved network quality and a fair pricing model. The source code for the numerical examples is available at https://github.com/wesamalhanash/Revenue-Sharing-model. The $\alpha$-attractor inflation model is a popular choice among inflationary scenarios.  In this class of models, the transition from inflation to the de Sitter phase is closely linked to the stability of certain quantum systems.  Recent research has made significant contributions by refining these models:  first, inequalities were derived to ensure the stability of quantum systems, which in turn set boundaries for viable $\alpha$-attractor models;  second, new inflationary configurations were identified, which often fail to satisfy previously proposed consistency conditions.  Our goal is to provide an exhaustive list of these new configurations, evaluate their potential for detection using upcoming observations, and examine the implications for field interaction in these scenarios.  The new configurations fall into three distinct categories:  constant-field configurations, cosine potentials, and more complex scenarios with polynomial forms.  The constant-field configurations are notable for predicting a scalar field value at $m_{Pl}/\alpha$ upon re-examination, while cosine potentials and polynomial forms require a different approach, which is based on the characteristics of attractors.  The new models also make distinct predictions for field dynamics upon re-entry into the de Sitter phase.  Ultimately, our analysis suggests that observations may be able to differentiate between these different configurations, which in turn will help to further refine our understanding of $\alpha$-attractor models.  The potential for future detection was assessed by running Nssflood, a simulation-based forecast, which showed that $\sim$3000 observations may be required to tell these different configurations apart from one another.  Therefore, while these new configurations may not yet be distinguishable from each other, upcoming observations may be able to help clarify their relative merits. Heart disease is a significant global concern, and proper diagnosis depends on heart sound analysis, which is complicated by varying noise levels and variable heart positions. To address these challenges, a new method is proposed that utilizes an autoencoder-based feature extraction approach paired with a robust classifier. To mitigate the effect of noisy signals, a signal filtering technique is applied, and to account for varying signal configurations, a flexible activation function in the autoencoder is designed. Experimental results on a custom-built database demonstrate the superiority of the proposed system over existing approaches. Additionally, the findings highlight the significance of addressing positional variations and the potential for further improvement through employing more advanced classification techniques. The developed system shows exceptional performance, achieving classification accuracies of 92.08% for clean signals, 88.75% for moderate noise, and 85.51% for strong noise. Humanity's greatest achievement, cooperation, is the last unexplained phenomenon in the natural world. Despite its significance, cooperative behavior has been largely absent from scientific studies, with social sciences focusing on it through complex theoretical models. Our approach is unique in that we believe cooperative behavior is inherent in society and can be described using laws similar to those of physics. By analyzing this phenomenon using complex network analysis, we find that human society's resilience and ability to adapt are remarkable examples of the system's ability to self-organize. However, the current climate crisis threatens the planet's very existence, and our inability to cooperate is a critical obstacle in addressing this global challenge. To mitigate climate change, we need a fundamental shift in how we view cooperation, and by applying physical laws to social dynamics, we can unlock the system's potential for rapid and significant change. This presentation will discuss our research on cooperative behavior and the urgent need for a societal transformation to save the planet. We will explore how applying physical laws to social dynamics can reveal a world where climate action is both necessary and achievable. Specifically, we will focus on the critical role of time in social dynamics, with an emphasis on how our understanding of the historical context of climate change and the failure of the Tragedy of the Commons can be distilled through physical laws into a clear and actionable plan for a sustainable future. Our approach is built on a deep understanding of Stephen Hawking's cosmology and the inherent properties of human society, and it offers a hopeful perspective on the system's future evolution. We believe that by applying physical laws to social dynamics, we can overcome the current climate crisis and create a more cooperative and sustainable world for all. We invite you to join us on this journey of discovery and exploration, and we hope that together, we can uncover the secrets of a wonderful and resilient planet. This study offers an empirical examination of the trust-building dynamics in a sequence of sequential auctions where bidders' abilities are unknown, and their earnings are rewarded based on their performance in each auction. Our results reveal that bidders refine their assessment of others' trustworthiness as experience grows, and this is achieved through reduced uncertainty about others' types. ADHD is a prevalent psychiatric condition, and recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of algorithms capable of accurately diagnosing it using resting-state fMRI data. Nevertheless, the success of these models heavily relies on employing comprehensive brain regions, which are often obtained through pre-defined templates rather than individually identified areas. This study demonstrates that by selectively removing crucial regions from the brain, the performance of the rFMI-based classification model is severely impaired. The most significant regions were found to reside in key areas, including the left CADP and right ICA14. Furthermore, we explored the potential of noise-induced variations in rs-fMRI data to simulate the effects of target brain lesions on ADHD diagnosis, revealing that some models are resilient to such perturbations, while others significantly decline in accuracy. By investigating the spatial distribution of these models' sensitivity to brain lesions, we aimed to determine whether they preferentially agree on the locations most affective to diagnostic accuracy. Our results demonstrate that some models exhibit a unified agreement on the importance of regions like the left CADP and right ICA14. This study establishes that these areas are indeed instrumental in accurate ADHD diagnosis through deep learning algorithms. The findings of this research may have implications for understanding the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of ADHD, as well as its diagnosis in clinical practice, which could be improved by targeting these critical regions for validation. Additionally, the observed behavior of these models in responding to brain lesions may be useful in designing new algorithms capable of differentiating individuals with ADHD by identifying variations in rs-fMRI patterns indicative of pathological changes in these critical regions. In distinct-time networks, connections between nodes are created at specific times, forming subgraphs of isolated components. When a node becomes infected, it only transmits to nodes within its own subgraph. We're investigating an epidemic SISI model where infected nodes follow an SI dynamics within their subgraphs and an SIS dynamics when interacting with uninfected nodes. By applying a first-step Taylor approximation to the generating function of the epidemic equation, we've established an approximation for the epidemic equation itself. Our approach involves linearizing the approximate epidemic equation and using the resulting system to simulate distinct-time epidemic spread. We compare these simulations to the results from a corresponding continuous-time network, showing that the approximate epidemic equations accurately model small and medium-sized networks, with errors increasing slightly for larger networks. Additionally, we've found that the time it takes for an epidemic to spread through a network is roughly the same whether we use the distinct-time or continuous-time models, except for cases where infection spreads across multiple subgraphs. We've also established conditions under which the epidemic spread is delayed in the distinct-time model compared to the continuous-time model. Our findings provide valuable insights into how epidemic spread behaves in distinct-time networks, offering potential applications in modeling the spread of diseases in networks with time-varying connections. Moreover, they raise an important question about the time it takes for an epidemic to spread: is it inherently dependent on network properties or can it be influenced by the network topology? Our work answers this question for the SISI model, with potential implications that extend beyond this particular model. Lastly, our approximations offer a simpler approach to simulating the epidemic spread in large networks, which could be useful in practical applications. We've made both the code and the network generator used in our study openly available. Anyone can access these at the following link: https://github.com/sopar3/dist-time-epidemic-model. In various documents and conversations, abbreviations are frequently used.
However, their meanings are unclear without corresponding expansions.
MadDog is an open-source online tool that helps users decode and
interpret the meanings of abbreviations in given text input. It was
initially developed as a project for the DIP course at the Knowledge
Graphs and Data Mining laboratory in the Informatics Department at
Technion and is now available at http://kd.i2s.technion.ac.il/maddog. 
MadDog utilizes a classification model based on the BERT framework to
recognize potential abbreviations in a given sentence. Following this,
it identifies relevant expansion candidates from a comprehensive domain-specific dictionary. 
Finally, MadDog implements a logic-based algorithm to resolve ambiguity
and provide a single, accurate interpretation of the abbreviation in a given context. 
MadDog's approach is versatile, allowing it to be applied to domains
with established standardized terminology or those with less structured
terminology usage. While it is primarily designed for acronym
interpretation, MadDog is capable of recognizing and managing other types
of abbreviations. MadDog's online interface enables simple interaction
and provides instant results, and the system is now accessible at http://kd.i2s.technion.ac.il/maddog. 
MadDog was introduced approximately one year ago and has processed over
190,000 sentences, providing over 120,000 accurate interpretations of
abbreviations. Moreover, the system has an overall accuracy rate of 92.9%
in detecting and expanding abbreviations, with up to 98.4% accuracy in
cases where the abbreviation has a single valid expansion. This systematic
approach to acronym recognition and interpretation makes MadDog a valuable
resource for a wide range of natural language processing tasks. 
Additionally, the system includes a detailed explanation of its logic
for users who wish to learn more about its logic or report discrepancies. 
MadDog's results are further validated by comparisons with existing
related systems, where it demonstrates superior performance in specific
aspects. MadDog is now available for use at http://kd.i2s.technion.ac.il/maddog. 
In accordance with the instructions, the MadDog code is publicly hosted at
https://github.com/avnerbmadDog/madDog/tree/master/madDog_api.

Our proposed technique addresses two significant issues in DNA storage: the structural layout of data on the DNA molecule and the time-consuming process of refreshing updated data. Current methods using linearized, base-paired DNA molecules store data in a sequential order, which leads to a high number of unnecessary base pairs in the storage mixture. Additionally, when updating this data, the entire DNA molecule must be recovered, modified, and then re-synthesized to extract the updated files. To solve these problems, we present a novel approach that utilizes a hierarchical DNA storage layout consisting of multiple levels of structured DNA units, each containing a portion of the total storage capacity. This allows for efficient data refreshes, as only the modified files need to be re-synthesized and integrated into the existing structure. To assist in optimizing hierarchical DNA storage layouts, we developed a simulation tool that determines the best partitioning of the storage levels to minimize the time spent refreshing and retrieving data. This paper showcases several word embedding-based techniques employed to enhance the exploration of visual data with Ontodia, utilizing the knowledge base Wikidata. We identify suitable word embedding properties for mapping concepts to Ontodia entities, focusing on the disambiguation challenge. To address this issue, we develop and implement two methods: one utilizing hyperedges from Wikidata to create tailored embeddings for specific concepts, and another leveraging Hyperlex to incorporate the context of surrounding texts in the embedding generation process. Our implementation is built upon the Wikidata property edge network to facilitate efficient hyperedge generation. We investigate how these embeddings can be utilized to improve the automatic assignment of labels to nodes in Ontodia and discuss the practical implications of applying such embeddings in the context of knowledge graphs like Wikidata. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we provide visual examples illustrating the improvement achieved through Hyperlex-based embeddings over standard Wikidata embeddings. We anticipate that the techniques presented will pave the way for innovative applications that combine natural language processing and knowledge graph domains. Furthermore, the project's source code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/semantic-m2mmlk/ontodia-word-embeddings. To ensure full reproducibility, we also provide a publicly accessible Wikidata Hyperlex dataset at https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidata/latest/hyperlex/wikidata_hyperlex_20210224-165255.json.gz. Additionally, the Hyperlex dataset can also be downloaded from is.datahub.io/hyperlex/wikidata. We expect this dataset to be useful not only for the purposes mentioned in this paper, but also for other potential applications of Hyperlex technology. Moreover, a public demo of the proposed solution is available at https://demo.semweb4life.org/ontodia-word-embeddings. We intend to continuously develop and expand this project, incorporating user feedback to further refine the embedding properties and apply them to other Ontodia use cases, as well as exploring new directions such as the extension of Hyperlex to knowledge graphs like DBpedia. Within the cell's crowded interior, proteins and RNA molecules self-organize into membraneless droplets influenced by electrostatic interactions, often participating in various biological processes. However, the inherent focus on a single type of molecule in theoretical models has hindered a comprehensive understanding of condensate formation. To address this, we develop a generic theoretical framework that accounts for interactions between multiple components lacking specific information. Utilizing experimental data on RNA-based droplet formation, we demonstrate that our model is capable of explaining observed behaviors. Furthermore, we investigate how droplet properties are affected by variations in ingredients and environmental conditions. The outcomes reveal both collective and individual contributions from different components, leading to diverse outcomes and, consequently, different types of droplet behavior. To verify our approach, we compare our results with existing experiments on mixtures of proteins and RNA. Our findings suggest that even minor changes in droplet composition can lead to significant and distinct behavioral outcomes, and that tuning components and environmental conditions can induce various types of droplet behavior. This research provides a broad theoretical application for analyzing multimolecular interactions and their implications in understanding biological processes and developing therapeutic strategies. Based on our analysis, we propose several experimental interventions that could leverage droplet behavior to manipulate and regulate cellular processes. Our study opens up a wider scope for theoretical modeling in condensed phases and may inspire new approaches to understanding and manipulating droplet behavior in cells. Additionally, we explore the possibility of engineering droplets with desired properties by selectively introducing new components. Our research indicates that a droplet's properties can greatly differ from those of its constituent molecules, and that their interactions are more complex than simply summing the interactions of individual components, and that varying environmental conditions can also affect these interactions. We also find that our results are comparable to existing experimental data on mixtures of proteins and RNA. We propose several new experiments that could further validate our approach and explore the behavior of droplets in cells. We investigated numerous freeware tools to facilitate our analysis and chose to utilize SDO's sunspot tracking tool, which enables detailed analysis of sunspots, to examine the behavior of sunspots in NOAA AR 11429. On February 25, 2012, a major X-class flare occurred, triggering a significant decrease in long-wavelength seismic signals and altering the sunspots in NOAA AR 11429. These changes marked a'revolution' in the sunspots, characterized by rapid movement, distortion, and shape changes associated with the solar activity. We observed similar sunspot revolutions in response to lower-level flares, albeit with less severe consequences, indicating that smaller events can also produce these effects. To investigate the cause of these movements, we analyzed the longitudinal magnetic field of the active region using Helioseismic and Magnetic Implant, which revealed that the areas surrounding the sunspots experienced noticeable reductions in magnetic strength. These findings suggest that the solar activity leads to a temporary decrease in the magnetic strength of the surrounding areas, which may provide new insights into the solar structure. Furthermore, our study indicates that the solar activity can cause significant changes in the solar atmosphere, which may have implications for understanding the solar interior. These findings also imply that the solar activity can produce ripple effects in the solar elastodynamics. Given a smooth manifold, M, with a map, f, sending it to N, 
the feeble b-principle asserts that given suitable bundles on M and N, 
any obstructions to configuring them consistently with f arise from 
obstructions forming a feeble b-relativistic structure, 
defined as a morphism to a groupoid with a compact, smooth base space. 
The feeble b-principle further claims that this feeble structure can be dispensed 
with under certain conditions on the maps and bundles involved. 
The feeble b-principle has been extended to non-smooth manifolds, 
with "smooth" replaced by "Mumford", meaning they satisfy a certain 
topological condition known as Mumford's conjecture, which has been proven by 
Corbett and Roberts. 
The feeble b-principle for smooth manifolds relies on the simplicial version of 
Mumford's hypothesis, while its extension to non-smooth manifolds relies on 
the original form of this hypothesis. 
The feeble b-principle has several implications, including generalising 
Mumford's hypothesis to certain types of manifolds and proving a 
topological version of a theorem by Gromov's principle.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model, particularly for low molecular weight values. By extensively applying the Lozowski-Carleman estimate and related techniques, we demonstrate that any globally smooth solution remains so over any positive time interval, and its key quantities exhibit limited growth in time. Concurrently, we show that solutions with moderately high initial conditions exhibit oscillatory behavior around an equilibrium state, characterized by zero velocity and varying density, depending on the molecular weight. In the low molecular weight limit, these solutions converge to a state of hydrodynamic equilibrium. This work also includes an analysis of the long-term energy behavior for globally smooth solutions. Notably, for sufficiently low initial energy levels, solutions converge to an equilibrium state with zero velocity and constant density, and in the low molecular weight limit, these solutions converge to a state of hydrodynamic equilibrium. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, which can adapt to emerging tasks or skills. To accelerate the development and evaluation of these methods, we introduce L2Explorer, an open-source framework and benchmark environment designed to support lifelong reinforcement learning research. L2Explorer encompasses a set of navigation tasks across 15 different state spaces, which require agents to navigate towards objectives in varied layouts. These tasks are structured to simulate real-world scenarios where agents might encounter new situations, such as expanded layouts or hidden obstacles, which could be viewed as emerging tasks. Our benchmark includes evaluations of several established continual learning methods as well as novel approaches, showcasing the challenges of adapting to these dynamic situations. The challenge server will be updated with more evaluations and new methods will be added through contributions from researchers. Finally, the source code of our framework is publicly available for reproduction of our results and customization of our environment for novel evaluation protocols. Our framework, including the code, can be found at https://l2xplorer.github.io/.

This behavior contrasts with the original Euler equation's conservative form, where such disturbances would remain stationary and equidistant from the equilibrium state. Additionally, these accelerating waves can take on the form of highly localized features, known as "waterwaves". A second key finding is that, given sufficient distance from the equilibrium state, such waves will always decelerate and converge, resulting in the accumulation of energy in a smaller area and ultimately leading to a singular state in the flow. These analytical findings validate and expand upon previous numerical studies examining the dynamics of such waves in this specific setting. Furthermore, it is shown that the dynamics of these waves can be effectively modeled by a related equation in "conservation form", where certain properties of the wave remain stationary, underscoring the theoretical importance of this equation. A related study by Chouza et al. provides a dynamic description of the equilibrium state itself, leading to a dynamic equation for the energy of the wave, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the accelerating waves' behavior, particularly with respect to their interaction and the ultimate singular state in the flow. The COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa was characterized by a significant delay in data collection, leading to a critical shortage of reliable, real-time data needed to guide policy decisions. To mitigate this issue, we explored alternative approaches to supplement the lack of data by leveraging accessible, non-specialized sources such as social media and online news platforms. This analysis focused on provincial COVID-19 incidence rates in South Africa, using both unstructured social media posts and news articles, in addition to existing surveillance data. Our results showed that incorporating social media and news data allowed for more accurate forecasting and reduced errors in estimating incidence rates, particularly for provinces with limited data availability. However, incorporating non-specialized data sources also introduced bias associated with representation bias and the potential for data quality concerns. The team discovered that even simple initial conditions could lead to long-term diversity in the complex systems they created. In our study, we build upon the work of Dow and Muller by examining the mathematical equation that governs the transition to long-term stability in these systems, specifically in the case where all state variables are equal. Our analysis reveals that a previous proposed solution, known as the ABS H2 formula, is actually incorrect and can be corrected through our method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this new solution is unique and valid for all types of irregular initial conditions. Lastly, we acknowledge that the proposed solution may not directly apply to all cases of irregular initial conditions due to the associated computational complexities. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that the underlying equation that governs the transition to long-term stability in these systems remains solvable. Moreover, they struggle with recognizing shifted patterns, which are prevalent in real-world images. In response to these limitations, deep neural networks with message passing capabilities have been developed for image classification. Although effective, these models rely on predefined message transfer functions that cannot be adapted to new scenarios. This has led to the exploration of new architectures that can learn their message transfer functions. Despite these advancements, we are the first to propose a new model, Active Graph Message Transfer Networks (AGMTN), which can learn both the nodes and edges of the message transfer graph. Specifically, we leverage the advantage of graph neural networks in image recognition and propose an algorithm that automatically generates the message transfer graph for any given image recognition task. Efficient hardware implementations of Circulant Matrix Valued Functions (CMVFs) are crucial for various signal processing applications, such as extension of 1D convolution operators and exploration of new ideas in deep learning. In this paper, we tackle the complex issue of CMVF hardware realization by developing an efficient construction method that allows for implementation of any CMVF with a size that scales sub-quadratically with the data size, based on a previous efficient construction of Bunse-Garzoni et al. improving a lower bound from O(N^5) to O(N^3) for matrix sizes N^2. This new construction leads to significant cost savings, under a specific assumption, leading to notable hardware area savings of up to 87\% and 65\% over previous efficient constructions for matrix sizes 256x256 and 512x512, respectively. The proposed architecture has been successfully verified on an Advanced Edge Platform with a Partial Reconfigurable Capability. Additionally, this paper explores the Concept of Spectral Similarity in CMVFs, an informal criterion that identifies potentially useful functions for further exploration. The study manually examines spectral characteristics of over 300 million CMVFs, revealing that only a tiny fraction less than 10^-6 possess exceptional spectral properties, while a significantly larger fraction approximately 5.96e-4 is proximally similar to known valuable functions, such as Laplacian of the 2D Gaussian, revealing potential applications and suggesting new directions for further research. Furthermore, this paper develops a novel Hardware Efficient Approximation Algorithm (HAIA) able to derive approximations of CMVFs at 2-4 bits accuracy, reducing approximate filter area by up to 12.65 times the original size, while still maintaining an acceptable 0.76 dB approximation loss. Finally, this paper introduces a novel Algorithm for Selecting CMVF Approximations (ASCA) able to identify suitable approximations of valuable functions, such as Bessel thinman filter, reducing approximate filter area by up to 6.97 times the original size, while maintaining an acceptable 0.57 dB approximation loss. The proposed HAIA and ASCA algorithms exhibit significant performance improvements over existing efficient constructions, achieving substantial hardware area savings of up to 87\% and 65\%, respectively. Furthermore, these algorithms demonstrate robustness in various challenging scenarios. The study also confirms the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed HAIA and ASCA algorithms through thorough performance evaluations on several benchmark scenarios. We have determined the generalized dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various contexts: neutrally charged, charged in a background fluid, and charged in a background electromagnetic field. By establishing the linearized equations for relativistic hydrodynamics with charge and electromagnetic field effects, we showed that the field contributes to stabilizing sound waves and allows for the reconstruction of a relativistic Navier-Stokes equation from first principles. Our analysis for the neutral fluid aligns with existing findings, but our results for the charged fluid reveal stability in certain orientations and the presence of Rayleigh-Plateau instability in specific setups. Furthermore, the presence of electromagnetic fields leads to novel features in dispersion relations, and we found that some modes exhibit dissipationless behavior. Our study also offers a method for deriving the Navier-Stokes equation solely from hydrodynamic principles, an achievement that was previously considered infeasible. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the structure of the linearized hydrodynamic theory is more intricate than initially thought, influenced by aspects like charge conservation and the metric tensor. Finally, our findings indicate that the canonical variation of relativistic hydrodynamics fails to accurately represent the linearized theory, particularly due to inaccuracies in energy-momentum tensor constructions. Conversely, the covariant form of relativistic hydrodynamics appears capable of capturing the complex dynamics of relativistic fluids. These conclusions emerge from our analysis of various instability conditions, such as the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, which reveals that the conventional description of relativistic fluids through Navier-Stokes equations, and by analogy the covariant and canonical formulations, do not accurately represent the linearized theory. The theoretical notion of dark matter, since the 80s, has not been directly observed despite numerous attempts. A hypothetical state, taking the form of microscopic black holes resulting from primordial matter in the early universe, has been proposed as an explanation for this mysterious matter. These black holes, due to their extremely low mass, would have formed shortly after the universe's creation and would still exist, given that their lifetime is tied to their mass. They would emit radiation with very low energy frequencies, such as gamma rays, upon accretion of surrounding matter. This hypothesis presents a possibility of linking cosmic background noise to dark matter, offering a tangible connection between theoretical dark matter and an observable phenomenon. Moreover, the spectrum and spatial distribution of this background noise could provide insights into the universe's early conditions and the formation of primordial black holes. Recent studies using gamma ray data in searching for signals from these black holes are ongoing. They, however, face competition from background noise, primarily stemming from cosmic rays and meteor showers, which need to be distinguished from the hypothetical signal. In this research, we investigate whether these charged cosmic rays could also produce radio-frequency signals, similar to those generated theoretically by primordial black holes. We simulate these charged particles within a model of the Earth's magnetic field, observing their energy loss and distribution across various frequency ranges. The simulation results suggest that electron bombardment produces more significant signals below 100 MHz frequency range, while proton bombardment dominates higher frequency ranges. We propose that detecting weak, short-duration signals above 100 MHz could offer conclusive evidence of microscopic black holes, given that protons are more efficient at producing high frequency signals. Additionally, we discuss how distinguishing low from high frequency signals could provide a tangible indication of whether dark matter is comprised of black holes or particles. Lastly, we explore how our finding that low frequency signals are primarily produced by electrons could be verified through GPS measurements, as GPS systems are sensitive to low frequency magnetic fields. Therefore, we suggest that checking the GPS data records could provide a tangible sign of microscopic black holes. We also discuss how our finding that high frequency signals can be produced by probing the Cherenkov radiation produced by protons, which could be investigated through particle accelerator experiments or by detecting the Cherenkov radiation produced by protons in the atmosphere. Recent advances in self-supervised learning have led to the development of substantial knowledge from vast amounts of pretraining data, which can be exploited in downstream tasks with limited annotated information. The underlying mechanisms of modern language models, such as ELMo, RoBERTa, and BERT, primarily focus on unlabeled text representation learning. This work delves into two key aspects: unsupervised text analysis and few-shot classification. It evaluates various representation learning strategies and task-specific fine-tuning methods on comprehensive datasets to identify the most effective approaches. Specifically, this research examines how different token representations contribute to text classification in the two analysis scenarios, and it identifies suitable configurations for achieving high performance in both unsupervised analysis and few-shot classification. Additionally, this research explores ways to reduce computational costs associated with fine-tuning large language models from scratch and proposes a novel initialization technique for embedding matrices that leverages pretraining outputs. The proposed technique, which relies on the division of text into segments and the assignment of labels to groups of adjacent tokens, enables efficient fine-tuning and significantly reduces the time required to train each iteration. Overall, this research aims to contribute to the development of unsupervised and few-shot analysis methods based on pretraining, and it provides a comprehensive comparison of the evaluated approaches to facilitate the reproduction of its results. In this research, we examine whether near-infrared images are necessary for urban scene segmentation. We ask, "Can near-infrared images exclusively lead to accurate semantic segmentation of various city scenes?" To investigate this question, we focus on the Hyperspectral Phase Change (HPC) image feature, discovering that it makes significant contributions in certain situations. Nevertheless, its value can be diminished by other image features. This leads us to conclude that near-infrared images carry essential information vital to accurate semantic segmentation of complex urban scenes. We demonstrate this through a straightforward, segmentations-only approach based on ensemble learning and the integration of multiple image features. The effectiveness of our approach is shown through its high semantic segmentation accuracy on the Cityscapes dataset. Additionally, we observe that the HPC image component can improve the existing state-of-the-art semantic segmentation models, ultimately reaching new heights in performance. The code for this research is openly accessible on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/UCSTA-CVIT/HPCNet. We also provide the trained models for evaluation purposes. Note that the HPC images were generated using the open HSImageGeometric toolbox at https://github.com/UCSTA-CVIT/HSImageGeometric. It is noteworthy that the HSImageGeometric toolbox is an innovative technology that seamlessly integrates hyperspectral image analysis and geometric deep learning, yielding outstanding performance in urban scene segmentation. As such, the HSImageGeometric toolbox is suited for applications in advanced navigation systems and robotic platforms that require seamless integration of hyperspectral imaging and geometric learning for enhanced object detection. Hence, we believe the HSImageGeometric toolbox holds immense promise for the advancement of various computer vision tasks and applications. Lastly, we hypothesize that the incorporation of the HPC image component can lead to groundbreaking advancements in other computer vision tasks, extending beyond semantic segmentation. We intend to explore this possibility in our future research. To facilitate this, we have openly released the HSImageGeometric toolbox, allowing other researchers to build upon our work and investigate the vast potential of hyperspectral imaging in computer vision. The HSImageGeometric toolbox is now openly accessible at https://github.com/UCSTA-CVIT/HSImageGeometric. We look forward to seeing the innovative applications that other researchers will develop from this powerful tool. In particular, we expect the HSImageGeometric toolbox to lead to cutting-edge technology in autonomous navigation and robotic vision, ultimately benefiting various industrial and technological communities. We establish that, in addition to the already valid linear combinations, the RAM model can execute constant-time nonlinear operations such as taking the square root, along with various other operations. To facilitate effective session-based suggestion, users need relevant information quickly, so a fast and accurate recommendation algorithm is crucial. Since users typically view sessions as a whole, ignoring session boundaries can lead to subpar suggestions. To address this, we developed an enhanced co-training graph-based recommendation system, or LGST, which treats entire sessions as nodes in a graph and uses user interests to enhance suggestion quality. To ensure accurate recommendations, we enhanced co-training with a self-guided learning strategy, leveraging both user and item information. We also added guides to help nodes exchange information and enhance global representation. As a result, LGST surpasses traditional algorithms in multiple datasets and outperforms the standard graph-based and co-training methods. Notably, LGST improves recommendation accuracy by up to 11.5% with a significantly lower computational cost of 85.6%, making it a more efficient option. The code for LGST is available on GitHub at https://github.com/cuiyh05/LGST. Experimental evidence confirms that LGST is a reliable and efficient method for session-based suggestion. It consistently outperforms the standard graph-based and co-training methods in multiple datasets, and has a lower computational cost while achieving better performance. The code for LGST is also easily accessible, so developers can use it to create efficient session-based suggestion algorithms. A code is called LCD code if the cross permutation operation maintains its invertibility within the code. Additionally, if a code satisfies this condition and the cross permutation combined with a cyclic shift has an invariant property, the code is referred to as a group LCD code. The present research focuses on group LCD codes, both non-cyclic and cyclic, made up of monomials whose degrees are relatively prime. It is demonstrated that group LCD codes, both non-cyclic and cyclic, have a higher minimum distance than regular LCD codes. The study also establishes a connection between group LCD codes and semigroups of functions with the 2-shift property. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions for group LCD codes to achieve the maximum possible minimum distance are proposed. The existence of cyclic group LCD codes with any desired minimum distance is proven, while the non-cyclic group LCD codes' capacity is determined. The paper presents various examples of group LCD codes, highlighting their superiority over regular LCD codes in terms of minimum distance. Finally, several open issues and recommendations for future research are provided. The contribution of this research is validated through the creation of an open-source MATLAB script, available at https://github.com/NYUWireless/Group\_LCD, used to generate group LCD codes of any size. We identify discrete invariants, referred to as 'graph polynomials,' that possess unique properties. These polynomials serve as fundamental elements in the development of the mentioned complexes and enable the creation of differential operators, resulting in a differential structure on each complex. We then focus on an important type of graph polynomial called the'supercover polynomial,' stemming from work by Enomoto, Eto, and Tsuru, which has strong connections to combinatorial topology, algebra, and the integration theory of Feynman graphs. In various object classification tasks, several attributes of objects can be categorized and grouped.  The hierarchical nature of these categories is reflected in the connections between them - lower-level categories are linked to higher-level ones. This study examined how recurrent neural networks (RNNs), used for object classification, organize information about object attributes in their internal states, considering the structural relationships among these attributes. We found that on top of encoding attribute information, RNNs also represent the relationships among attributes, with stronger connections between categories that are closely related. Furthermore, the internal states of RNNs contain information about specific attributes only when that information is independent of other categories, not when it is determined by other categories. Additionally, connections in RNNs are not simply needed for basic object classification but are essential for solving dependent object classification tasks. We conducted experiments using twin RNNs, where we trained them to classify objects using either structural or dependent information, and found that dependent information is processed in a category-organised manner in internal states of the RNNs. These results are supported by numerical analysis of the matrices governing the flow of information through the RNNs, as well as by observations of the internal states at different points in time. Overall, our study indicates that RNNs utilise hierarchical category structures when training for object classification and that this structural representation is essential for solving object classification tasks that depend on the structural relationships among objects. It is this structural representation that enables the efficient flow of information through the connections in the RNNs. The efficiency of information flow in the RNNs, as well as their performance in object classification, significantly rely on the level of dependency among object attributes. We found that processing information in a hierarchical manner, considering the structural relationships among object attributes, leads to better performance in object classification compared to treating each attribute in isolation.
