In one-dimensional systems with correlated electrons, we investigate how non-Hermitian point-gap topology is diminished. By means of numerical cluster diagonalization, we examine the reduction of topological content in a one-dimensional non-Hermitian Hubbard model featuring on-site interactions and multiple correlated electron exchanges. It is demonstrated that increased correlations cause a decrease in the point-gap topology score, an assessment based on the parity of the local many-body wave function under site permutation. Specifically, two-body correlations see a substantial decline in the point-gap topology score, an effect that is contrasted with three-body correlations producing more nuanced variations in this score. Ultimately, our findings emerge against the backdrop of reduced electron transport capacity and enhanced localization within the system. Moreover, our research reveals that under certain conditions, four-body correlations can give rise to a revivification of point-gap topology, thereby exemplifying the intricate role of correlations in determining the topological content of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems. Ultimately, our research may enable the utilization of correlations in controlling the point-gap topology of one-dimensional systems. Four distinct families of Golay complementary pairs of orthogonal functions are developed and two more families are developed up to a scalar multiple. These sets exhibit intermodal isolation in multi-phase signals and anti-isolation in single-phase signals. A proposed measure quantifies the degree of isolation between different frequency components within a multi-phase signal. Several design methods are presented to create Golay complementary sets with specified properties, including a novel approach using a symmetric argument for constructing Golay sequences. Furthermore, a theoretical framework is provided for identifying all possible multi-phase periods that can be utilized in a Golay complementary pair. A quantity is established and shown to be a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a Golay complementary pair with a given multi-phase period. This research also presents a quantity that controls the size of Golay sets with prescribed properties, providing a tradeoff between size and isolation. Ultimately, a range of Golay complementary pairs with distinct multi-phase periods is presented, and their corresponding Golay sets are displayed in a visual format for easy reference. It is shown that some of these sets achieve the optimal size possible, given the available multi-phase periods. Several applications are presented that highlight the utility of the proposed Golay sets, including a novel solution to the general problem of simultaneous signal acquisition. Additionally, these sets are shown to be useful in multi-carrier signal design and the construction of Golay codes in two and multi-dimensional spaces. These findings demonstrate that silicon, with its integrated and disconnected quantum components, offers a versatile platform for the development of complex quantum processing schemes. Furthermore, we theorize that silicon's complex atomic structure could provide a mechanism for disabling and re-enabling a qubit, effectively acting as an all-electric gate in silicon-based quantum computing systems. These observations open new avenues for the optimization of silicon's performance as a quantum computing material, particularly with regard to efficiently coupling and switching qubits. The proposed research path will greatly contribute to developing efficient quantum processing schemes for applications in quantum computing. single-crystalline diamond in a three-dimensional framework. Our research utilizes
synthetic single-crystalline diamond in the Ivanov phase with two types of scintillator
materials to monitor charge transport over a large volume. We use the transient-current
profiles and compute the charge generation rate to map out the spatial distribution of
electronic and hole transport. Our experiments are accompanied by finite element modeling
in three dimensions to investigate the influence of light-absorbing scintillators and the
effect of varying charge mobility on our findings. SBTIM offers a versatile method for
investigating charge transport in diamond and other semiconductor materials over a
large volume.

In this thesis, I investigate charge transport in single-crystalline diamond using
the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current technique. To achieve this, I design
and implement experiments utilizing diamond in the Raman phase, as well as in the
Ivanov phase, utilizing two different scintillator materials and mapping out charge
transport in a three-dimensional framework. 

As part of this research, I also develop a computational model to simulate charge
transport in a large volume, as well as the effect of light-absorbing scintillators and
different charge mobility on these findings. To model charge transport, I use the finite
element method to analyze the spatial distribution of charge and the rate of charge
generation in a three-dimensional environment. To verify our model, we compare it to
experimental data and find that by adjusting parameters, we can match the shape and
movement of charge transport observed in experiments. 

These findings validate the use of the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current
technique to investigate charge transport in diamond and other semiconductor
materials over a large volume. To better understand these observations, we map out
charge transport in a three-dimensional environment, compute the charge generation
rate, and use finite element modeling to simulate and analyze these findings.

Social media platforms are facing significant concerns about the spread of toxic content, particularly gender-based hate speech. The severity of this issue is heightened in environments where it is increasingly protected by law, such as in Poland following a recent legislative change. To combat hate speech, effective detection and regulation mechanisms are crucial, primarily through reporting systems that rely on domain experts. However, the translation of text into reports can be hindered by poor quality, including spelling and grammar errors, as well as ambiguous Arabic words with multiple possible translations. To enhance the usability of these systems, it would be beneficial to utilize computer-driven methods for processing and improving the quality of user input. In this research, we introduce a pioneering quality improvement initiative by developing a cutting-edge neural network model to classify Arabic text as misogyny-related or not, while also categorizing it into specific sub-categories. Furthermore, we introduce two novel tasks: hate speech target detection and arson hazard classification to support misogyny detection, leveraging class-imbalance techniques through synthetic data generation via focus loss. To this end, we created the Arab-Hate dataset, comprising 3,114 Arabic tweets marked as misogynous, along with expert-provided reports for reference. The model was evaluated using standard metrics on Arab-Hate and two comparable English datasets, resulting in an outstanding 0.925 F1 score for misogyny detection, alongside high scores for the additional tasks and hate speech target detection. Conversely, we observed relatively lower performance in arson hazard classification, which we attribute to the relative scarcity of relevant data. To address this, we explored data generation techniques using focus loss, achieving promising results. The proposed model significantly outperformed contemporary models, showcasing its effectiveness in detecting and categorizing hate speech in Arabic while contributing to the arrest of the spread of misogynous content. Moreover, it highlights its potential in identifying the targets of hate speech and detecting hazardous, offensive content. Additionally, it demonstrates the feasibility of computer-driven methods in processing and improving the quality of user input for detecting toxic content, primarily through reporting systems that rely on domain experts. We aim to develop flexible and adaptable controllers for complex systems described by nonlinear dynamics, which are subject to sudden disturbances causing state corruption. To achieve this, we develop a probabilistic model-based approach to controller search, which identifies effective policy changes to achieve setpoints in the presence of disturbances. The distortion measure, a metric that captures system uncertainty and disturbance impact, is optimized through a sequence of state estimation and control planning steps, employing a sequential convex programming method. The proposed controller design is demonstrated to be robust against various types of disturbances, including those that may seize system control, as illustrated in a quadcopter simulation scenario. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of our approach on GitHub and showcase related videos on YouTube. Experimental results indicate that our controller design achieves significant performance improvements over existing methods, while also ensuring the safety of system operations. Specifically, our approach reduces the average time to reach setpoints by approximately 30% while preventing costly and hazardous yaw movements. The proposed method is expected to be a valuable tool for developing adaptable control systems in a variety of applications, such as autonomous mobile robots and aircraft. In particular, it has the potential to be implemented on hardware platforms using widely available software tools, further expanding its usability in practical scenarios. Some possible hardware targets for this controller include drones, spacecraft, and lunar rovers. The GitHub repository (https://github.com/frc-utai/quadcopter-jrlsc20) and YouTube videos (https://youtu.be/Jj9b4S9z4sU and https://youtu.be/LoO5MzsGk4Y) associated with this research project have been publicly made available for evaluation. To establish the cancellation of poles of Eisenstein series for $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$ with respect to irreducible automorphic cusp forms, we derive and use several discrete mathematical results. This study provides evidence for the cancellation phenomenon through the analysis of two key components: the growth of matrix coefficient functions and the properties of certain arithmetic functions. Specifically, this investigation demonstrates that the rapid growth of matrix coefficients implies the cancellation of poles, whereas the properties of arithmetic functions are leveraged to generalize from central characters to the general case. Additionally, we discuss the significance of our findings to both the local context and the broader framework of automorphic forms. Although our study focuses on $GL(n, \mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}})$, the underlying reasons for the cancellation of poles can be applied to other groups well. Consequently, this work likely holds implications for spaces of moduli for both abelian varieties and higher-dimensional Shimura varieties. Furthermore, we anticipate that our investigation will contribute meaningfully to ongoing research in the cancellation of poles, such as that of Ginzburg and Rallis, and that it may be potentially generalized to address the third question posed by Langlands. Lastly, we plan to follow up this study with a more in-depth analysis of the cancellation of poles at specific roots, building upon the foundational work of Ginzburg and Rallis. Ultimately, this research aims to establish a mathematical description of the holomorphic part of the automorphic function space, particularly its connection to the Eichler-Shimura relation and the growth of matrix coefficient functions. To achieve this goal, we will need to derive and incorporate additional discrete mathematical results, encompassing the volume estimates of orbits on Grassmannian varieties and the geometric analysis of certain arithmetic functions. Once these discrete mathematical components are in place, we will be able to establish point-by-point correspondence between the spaces of moduli for both abelian varieties and higher-dimensional Shimura varieties, enabling a deeper understanding of both the local context and the broader framework of automorphic forms. This study will likely hold implications for both Fargues-Fontaine's Grassmannian space and the Rallis-Shalika conjecture. Ultimately, we anticipate that our investigation will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing research in the cancellation of poles and the growth of matrix coefficient functions. Additionally, we plan to follow up this study with a more in-depth analysis of both the Eisenstein series and automorphic forms, particularly their connections to both abelian varieties

This research paper focuses on developing a novel security framework for mobile robotic arms using control barrier functions and configuration-aware techniques. A multi-layered control system is proposed, comprising an outer layer that employs configuration-dependent CFs to address changes in arm geometry, and an inner layer featuring a multi-variable quadratic programming-based controller. Additionally, the paper outlines methods for scheduling and switching between these controllers to ensure comprehensive coverage. Key findings include the derivation of a generalized palindromic cone and the establishment of bounds for variable scaling matrices through certificate optimization. A real-world application on a Titan II mobile robotic arm has been successfully used to test and validate the proposed security framework in various operating scenarios. Important outcomes include maintaining stability, preventing escape and tracking target trajectories while considering factors like joint bounds, geometry variations, and actuator limitations. Researchers have been interested in quantum systems that exhibit complex behavior in various contexts, such as identifying characteristics of quantum gates that function reliably or developing all-optical switches that work efficiently.

A practical approach to studying these systems is to use a Bose-Einstein condensate and an optical potential created by laser beams to simulate a nonlinear interaction. By using this method, it is possible to observe the transition from a weakly coupled system to a strongly coupled system that exhibits phenomena like mode locking.

Our research focuses on the application of the nonlinear quantum switch principle in three different scenarios that are typically difficult to engineer in nature: when interactions are not uniform, phase locking is required, or states need to be disconnected. To achieve this, we developed innovative laser control schemes that allow for precise manipulation of the coupling and phase of the BEC.

First, we engineered an all-optical switch that functions reliably even with non-uniform interactions. Next, we developed a system that can adjust the phase of the BEC and simulate quantum gates with high precision. Finally, we created a device that can quickly switch between different states of the BEC.

Our work not only contributes to the advancement of quantum gating technology but also opens the door for further innovation in laser technology and the development of cutting-edge optoelectronic devices. Moreover, it paves the way for the extension of nonlinear quantum switch principle to other areas of quantum communication and use of nonlinearity in quantum processing. Potential applications of the described systems include dispersion-controlled light sources, phase modulators, and various kinds of quantum-connected switches. It is also possible to extend the described concepts to other dimensions and systems, making them suitable for a broad range of applications. However, achieving stability is a significant challenge that needs to be addressed in future research, particularly when dealing with massive systems. It is also interesting to explore the possibility of using our methods in various kinds of fermionic and spin systems. It is also important to investigate whether similar mechanisms can be used in other dimensional systems and whether any of the described innovative laser control schemes can be adapted for use in quantum computing systems with multiple dimensions. Furthermore, it is possible that the described quantum gating schemes could be used for development of various kinds of quantum light sources that rely on different phase and coupling relationships between quantum states. Moreover, it is possible that the described systems could be used for generation of entangled light and its application in quantum communication and use of nonlinearity in quantum processing. It is also possible that the described innovative laser control schemes could be adapted for use in quantum computing

Finding the nontrivial solutions to a polynomial system is a critical problem in algebraic geometry, with applications in coding theory and secure communication. The vanishing set of a polynomial system can be broken down into irreducible components, known as algebraic sets, which can be studied through their degenerations. One approach to identifying these components involves examining signature-changing degenerations, as they offer a clue about the structure of the polynomial system's nontrivial locus. A new algorithm is proposed to compute this locus by analyzing such degenerations and determining the required algebraic sets that define the nontrivial locus. The algorithm is illustrated with a simple example. Moreover, the connection between signature-driven algebraic sets and the polynomial system's nontrivial locus is established in monomial missing degree, showing that these sets contain the desired information in that specific scenario. The study presents preliminary findings on signature-driven algebraic sets and their relationship with the nontrivial locus, with more investigation likely to be explored. The study's results are expected to contribute to the development of the nontrivial locus's characterization, especially in the context of projective polynomial systems. Pulsar wind nebulae, PWNe, are powered by the energetic particles ejected from pulsar jets that interact with local interstellar matter. As a pulsar moves, its jet blows a shell-like structure, capturing gamma-ray emission. These gamma-ray pulsar shells are primarily associated with the relativistic particles within the shell, although a particle transport model may also explain the observed gamma-ray emission.

A comprehensive search for gamma-ray pulsar shells in the Galaxy has been conducted using the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. This search involved examining the gamma-ray emission towards young pulsar birthplaces, as well as isolated pulsars, to identify shell-like structures. A sample of 5 gamma-ray pulsar shells has been identified, with 2 of these representing previously unobserved gamma-ray emission.

The analysis of these gamma-ray pulsar shells has revealed information about the mass of these structures. It was found that the mass of the shells is primarily composed of electrons and positrons, with a typical mass density ranging from $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$. The estimated size of these shells is typically between 10 to 100 pc, with a velocity of around $10^{2}$ to $10^{5}$ km/h. Our research examines how social norms surrounding climate change are established and evolved through the intersection of scientific evidence, institutional influences, and economic interests. Unlike traditional decision theories that view climate change as a factual issue, we acknowledge the significant role of social norms in shaping public perceptions. By incorporating insights from social theory, our model investigates how these norms are created, maintained, and ultimately affect climate change policy. Specifically, we analyze the relative impact of scientific research, institutional factors, and economic considerations on the development of social norms. Interestingly, our findings indicate that even in the presence of perfect information, social norms can diverge from optimal policies. Moreover, policies are more likely to align with social norms when institutions demonstrate a genuine commitment to protecting the environment. Our research also reveals that the pursuit of short-term economic gains can erode social norms focused on environmental conservation. Ultimately, our study highlights the complex interplay between different social norms and suggests that a multi-faceted approach is necessary to address the complex problems of climate change and economic productivity. Given the abstract nature of social norms, our model is best suited for qualitative analysis, and our empirical case studies reveal that the intersection of climate change, economics, and institutional influences is a real and significant one. Specifically, our analysis of the US climate change policy debate and the global economic discourse on climate change illustrates how social norms are established, influenced, and eventually affect policy decisions. In contrast, our examination of the European climate change policy reveals how social norms can be strengthened through consistent institutional support. Our research offers several practical recommendations for policymakers seeking to effectively manage the evolution of social norms and ultimately tackle the pressing issues of climate change and economic productivity. Additionally, our study identifies numerous avenues for further theoretical and empirical research within the field of social norms. Given the distinct methodological challenges of qualitative analysis, our research is particularly suited to inspire theoretical and empirical investigations in the area of social norms. Lastly, our combined approach, drawing on insights from social theory and decision theory, provides a valuable framework for understanding the complex interplay between different social norms and offers a valuable tool for qualitative analysis in the field of social norms. Ultimately, our study highlights the critical need to examine the distinct roles of science, institutions, and economics in shaping social norms, rather than simply viewing them as a collective force. Moreover, our research demonstrates the significance of exploring the underlying structures that produce and evolve social norms, rather than relying on generic assumptions. Lastly, our study stresses the importance of employing a multi-faceted approach to understand the intricate relationships between different social norms

We employ digital twin technology to model and regulate soft grippers. To do this, we use a model-based approach that relies on the Koopman operator theory to capture the behavior of these complex systems. This methodology allows us to utilize widely available data to generate a simplified representation of the gripper's dynamics, enabling efficient and flexible control strategies. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we perform open-loop experiments in a controlled environment, and then replicate the results in a digital twin environment with high accuracy. This digital twin can be used to implement various control algorithms, including model predictive control, to optimize the gripper's movement and ensure precise object manipulation. Our method has several key benefits, including improved computational efficiency and enhanced flexibility, making it well-suited for use in multi-fingered grippers and other complex soft robotic systems. Additionally, we demonstrate the digital twin's potential for use in tasks such as trajectory planning, followed by a demonstration of its application in a real-world setting, where we use it to guide a soft gripper in grasping and manipulating a flexible tube. This research presents a significant advancement in the control of soft robots through digital twins. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time this approach has been successfully applied to the soft gripper domain. Our model and associated software tools, including the Python package Koopgan, are freely available online at the specified URLs. The extreme radio halo, J2102+6015, at a redshift of 4.575, was studied using high-resolution observations from SIMBAD and CARMA. Its source, 20GM25, was examined as part of a study on radio halo phenomenon. Data from SIMBAD and CARMA both support that the emission originates from a compact radio galaxy. The emission from distant radio sources in J2102+6015 was subtracted and its total flux was then calculated as 2.3 Jy. Its spectral index was found to be 1.3 between frequencies 4.0 and 8.5 GHz, and 1.5 between frequencies 8.5 and 20 GHz. The absence of radio halo emission was confirmed, and its flux upper limit was set at 0.23 Jy. We discuss two possible theories for the halo emission: a plasma halo and a foreground active galactic nucleus. Research into computer-assisted diagnosis methods has shown promise, yet systems relying solely on CT scan data have limitations due to the relative simplicity of radiological information. Our objective is to enhance computer-aided diagnosis by integrating multiple imaging modalities, specifically CT and PET, to improve non-small cell lung cancer prognosis prediction. Through exploratory data analysis, we identified correlations between imaging, clinical factors, and survival rates. These findings guided the development of a deep learning model that combines multimodal information. By integrating PET data into the model, we observed a 6.9% absolute improvement in AUC score and enhanced its robustness through ensemble methods. The experimental results confirm our theoretical findings, which state that a universal vocabulary should not be used for causal inference in semantic communication. This work develops an innovative framework to predict undefined word pairs using latent knowledge and Naive Bayes, leveraging word embedding distributions to estimate unseen word relationships. E-commerce platforms use session-based recommendations to suggest products based on a user's browsing history. The primary goal is to present relevant products to users by grouping similar sessions together and suggesting relevant products to maintain engagement. Most current approaches focus on providing one product suggestion at a time, but aim to replace or complement the user's current interaction. This strategy may not be sufficient in making the most of each browsing session, particularly when users interact with multiple items. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a novel session-based suggestion method that purifies sessions from distracting information and utilizes product similarity representations to make tailored suggestions. The suggestion method is an ensemble of two phases: the first phase involves joint recommendation with candidate rank representations to identify essential items within each session, and the second phase uses a neural network to suggest additional products based on the refined session profile. To evaluate the suggestion method, researchers developed custom datasets by combining product lists with historical user interactions from two well-known e-commerce platforms. The method's performance in terms of suggestion quality, session purity, and relevance was compared to that of baseline methods, including resource augmentation, which involved integrating external e-commerce data into neural item recommendation models. The results showed that the two-phase suggestion method and a resource augmentation baseline that involved candidate rank representations outperformed other baseline methods significantly, while also meeting the requirements of e-commerce suggestion tasks consistently. To summarize, a novel session-based suggestion method with two phases has been developed to enhance e-commerce suggestion quality by grouping similar sessions together and suggesting relevant products to maintain user engagement. The method uses refined session profiles to make tailored suggestions, which was achieved by processing each session as a unit and using candidate rank representations to identify essential items and suggest additional products. Furthermore, the method's performance in terms of suggestion quality, session purity, and relevance was compared to that of baseline methods using customized datasets from two leading e-commerce platforms and was found to outperform them consistently. Thus, a novel session-based suggestion method with two phases has been developed to enhance e-commerce suggestion quality by grouping similar sessions together and suggesting relevant products to maintain user engagement. We examine the movement of fluids through three-dimensional fracture networks, where the fractures are treated as distinct entities, and the surrounding rock is modeled as a porous medium. By combining the fracture mesh with the porous rock mesh, we create a comprehensive model that can accurately represent fluid flow between the fractures and the rock matrix. Through the application of the continuity equation, we derive a linear system that represents fluid accumulation or loss, and by incorporating the effects of flow conductions, we develop a detailed model of fluid behavior. A three-dimensional example mesh is used to demonstrate how our model handles complex fracture networks, and the consequences of neglecting flow between the fractures and the rock matrix are also illustrated. Furthermore, the extension of our model to model chemical reactions between the fluid and the rock is a potential area of future research.

The optimal regulation issue is a critical problem in control theory, and it's particularly challenging when subjected to constraints on control and state variables. In our research, we primarily focus on the mean-field optimal regulation problem of stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion, subject to separate constraints on control and state variables. Through the introduction of a penalty function, we transform the original problem into a path-cost optimization problem, and then utilize the variational calculus approach to establish the necessary and sufficient optimality conditions. Notably, we introduce the fractional Stochastic Maximum Principle (SMP), an innovative method tailored for fractional Brownian motion, to facilitate the analysis, and apply the variational calculus to derive the maximum principle, thereby establishing a key equation. Furthermore, under the stabilizability and detectability conditions, we successfully prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the mean-field optimal regulation problem. Our study presents the first application of the fractional SMP in control theory. In addition, it bridges the gap between classical optimal regulation theory and modern stochastic control, while also generalizing the mean-field optimal regulation theory. The main advantages of our approach are its simplicity and use of minimal mathematical tools. The study provides a numerical method to solve the mean-field optimal regulation problem, and we present an example to demonstrate its effectiveness. The extensive information housed in Wikipedia's database is comprised of nearly 50 million articles, nearly two-thirds of which require revision or are of questionable quality.  Wikipedia's meticulous quality assessment process enables editors to identify and improve individual articles, fostering a vibrant, actively involved community.  However, changes are frequently made by users who leave no record, known as "secret editors," accounting for approximately 20% of all edits.  Through our analysis, we demonstrate that secret editors' behavior is significantly different from verified users in several key areas, notably in article quality, linguistic proficiency, and patterned editing habits.  By identifying distinct patterns in secret editors' behavior, we aim to develop a proprietary algorithm capable of accurately classifying articles into "low quality" categories based on editing habits, an area of research previously unexplored in Wikipedia studies.  Through our evaluation, we achieved an impressive 96.67% precision, 93.47% recall, and 94.03% F1 score, surpassing existing methods and solidifying our findings, ultimately concluding that secret editors can serve as a proprietary label, uniquely positioned to enhance Wikipedia's quality assessment efforts.  Furthermore, this study sheds light on the behaviors of secret editors, identifying significant discrepancies between their actions and those of verified users.  Ultimately, this research not only contributes to the ongoing Wikipedia research community but also reveals the substantial influence secret editors can have on enhancing article quality.  Moreover, we propose several future directions, including employing our training data to develop algorithms capable of automatically assigning low quality labels and leveraging secret editors' behavior to facilitate other Wikipedia tasks.  Additionally, we pose the question of whether secret editors can be induced to apply labels, potentially incorporating their perspectives into Wikipedia's quality assessment processes, an area of research we intend to explore in the future.  Specifically, our future work will concentrate on addressing the ethical considerations and challenges that may arise from applying our proposed algorithm in practice. As critical infrastructure systems continue to evolve digitally, managing their complex governance structures becomes a daunting task due to diverse and fragmented knowledge sources. To address this challenge, we develop a novel decision-theoretic framework for capturing the intuitive decisions made by stakeholders during knowledge transfer processes. This framework leverages utility functions to simulate decisions from both rule-based and unknown reasoning patterns, thereby enabling the identification of common ground among different knowledge sources. To maintain agility in decision-making processes, our framework employs a real-time learning approach based on reinforcement learning. This approach allows it to adapt to new decision-making models and update its beliefs about others' reasoning patterns. Ultimately, our framework facilitates the implementation of novel strategies for zero-shot knowledge transfer through black-box algorithms. To illustrate the efficacy of our framework, we conduct two case studies one exploring knowledge transfer within an organization, and another examining the governance of smart cities. The presented work has been partially inspired by the KDK 2022 challenge in knowledge-driven computer science. More information about the challenge can be found in the reference provided.

In Co-Observation Learning, two agents take turns making observations to gather information about a topic, with one agent sharing their findings with the other.  By iterating between these 'look-then-share' cycles, the observing agent uses the shared observations to refine their understanding.  Notably, this process allows the observing agent to learn a topic as well as the other agent, all without direct access to the topic, simply by analyzing the other agent's new observations over time.  In our research, we reduce Co-OCL to a well-studied problem in computer science, allowing us to analyze its learning capabilities using tools from information theory.  In particular, we find that two agents can learn a topic under the same conditions that allow a single agent to learn the topic through repeated rations.  Building on this result, we propose a novel algorithm for distributing observations between agents in a way that maximizes learning efficiency, with our algorithm capable of adapting to changing environments and yielding performance that is within a constant factor of the best possible performance.  When compared to existing methods, our research shows that these constants can be small, with our best estimate being a constant less than 8.  To validate our results and examine the performance of our algorithm in real-world settings, we conduct a series of experiments using data from the observational learning application, emergency medicine.  In these experiments, we find that our algorithm is capable of efficiently distributing data between two agents, with our results showing that the performance of our algorithm can be up to 30% better than existing methods.  Additionally, our research highlights the importance of considering the information collected by observations when distributing this information between agents, with our algorithm capable of improving performance by up to 70% in certain scenarios.  Taken together, our research indicates that Co-OCL can be a powerful tool for building collaborative machine learning systems, with our algorithm capable of producing results that are close to the best possible performance in a variety of settings. The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and 6300 square degree coverage at a depth of 24.8 mag. Our analysis utilizes the ShapePipe workflow to produce precise galaxy shape data for 63.3 square degrees, incorporating 3719 distinct galaxy clusters from the CFIS catalog, and has successfully implemented the MagLim cosmological program to generate accurate weak lensing maps, ultimately achieving a 2% bias in lensing signal retrieval. Through the lensing analysis, our research has obtained robust evidence for the cosmological constant, with a best fit model corresponding to $\Omega_m = 0.262 \pm 0.033$ and $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.738 \pm 0.033$ at 68% confidence, also detecting a statistically significant correlation between galaxy position and lensing signal at a 5.6$\sigma$ level. Furthermore, our research has estimated the average richness of these galaxy clusters at around $\bar{\Lambda}_R=151\pm6$, along with obtaining lensing-derived redshift distributions for the galaxy clusters, demonstrating good agreement with the expected distributions based on photometric redshifts, with our lensing-derived $f_\sigma$ shape parameter matching the photometric redshifts at 7.1$\sigma$ and 7.4$\sigma$ for early and late-type galaxies, respectively. The article also explores the trade-offs between undervolving levels, the area of SRAM cells, and the randomness extraction overhead. This study examines the interconnections among cryptocurrencies with a
top-down approach, starting with a comprehensive network that includes all
cryptocurrencies and transaction durations. Initially, the trade volume-based
method is employed to construct a cryptocurrency trading market network, where
nodes represent cryptocurrencies, and edges represent the statistical connection
between them. Analysis of the resulting networks over time reveals a significant
stability in the patterns of cryptocurrency relationships. Specifically, it is
found that the structure of the networks tends to be led by leading cryptocurrencies
such as Bitcoin, and that the relationships among the secondary cryptocurrencies
are influenced by their similarity in market performance. Furthermore, our
research reveals a higher-order effect, where the relationships among groups of
cryptocurrencies are also meaningful. By investigating the correlations between
these higher-order structures and the characteristics of the involved
cryptocurrencies, our results indicate that a good performance in the market
often leads to the formation of a cluster consisting of similar and performing
cryptocurrencies. Finally, our findings from a large set of transaction data
using time-resolved trading fractions instead of actual transaction amounts also
reveal a stable pattern in the patterns of cryptocurrency relationships, and
that the relationships among the secondary cryptocurrencies are largely influenced
by their similarity in market performance. Our research provides a new
understanding of the complex relationships among the vast number of
cryptocurrencies, and how their relationships are influenced by the market
performance. Our results may also be useful for the design of new investment
strategies, and provide a new perspective on the characteristics of cryptocurrencies. Several optimization methods in various machine learning tasks rely on transforming problems with constraints to simpler forms by relaxing them. This work investigates how techniques from algebraic topology can be applied to analyze the differences between original problems and their relaxations. Specifically, we utilize the concept of effective homotopy type of non-expansive functions to streamline this analysis. By leveraging multi-dimensional persistence to study these differences, we are able to observe changes in the optimal solutions as the parameters of a problem are adjusted. Furthermore, we apply our methods to the space of group-equivariant non-expansive functions, which provides a general framework for our analysis, and illustrate their effectiveness with several key examples. These include a multi-class classification problem and a task of recognizing shapes based on their outlines. By using techniques of algebraic topology to study these recognition tasks, we are able to compile a detailed description of the spaces of group-equivariant non-expansive functions and establish connections between their properties and the geometric structures of the underlying recognition pairs and spaces of test functions. This knowledge allows us to compute compactified versions of these spaces using multi-dimensional persistence and study how these spaces are related to the underlying geometric structures. In particular, we show that the computationally expensive step of computing a Quillen equivalence between the space of group-equivariant non-expansive functions and a space derived from the recognition pair can be bypassed by applying multi-dimensional persistence to the recognition pairs and spaces of test functions. This allows us to exactly calculate the compactified spaces of group-equivariant non-expansive functions for our key examples. Our methods also provide accessible ways to approximate these spaces up to a specified level of precision for any other examples. Several open problems and potential areas of further research are also identified. They involve applying the techniques of effective homotopy type, multi-dimensional persistence, and compactification to other optimization problems with constraints that are non-convex or involve additional complications. Additionally, we explored but did not complete the tasks of computing multi-dimensional compactified spaces derived from the group action on the spaces of group-equivariant non-expansive functions and establishing whether these spaces are homeomorphic to the spaces derived from the recognition pairs and spaces of test functions. These are left as the subjects of further study. This work presents significant advancements in using techniques from algebraic topology to analyze non-expansive optimization problems and provides concrete examples of effective homotopy type and multi-dimensional persistence in action. Our investigation reveals that geometric complexity serves as a significant regulator of this phenomenon. In our experiments, we created over 26,000,000 synthetic datasets and found that the average size of the model and its training loss correlates strongly with geometric complexity. The regularizing effect of geometric complexity is influenced by several factors, including model size, data size, problem type, and the presence of external regularizers. Our findings hold true across seven different scenarios, and we make our code available for replication. We demonstrate that the Apples and Oranges effect, which describes situations where simple models outperform complex ones, can be found in nearly all scenarios of geometric complexity. Conversely, we identify specific situations, termed Lemons and Peaches, where complex models outperform simple ones. The relationship between geometric complexity and deep learning effectiveness is multifaceted, and our work does not preclude the existence of other regularizing effects. However, we contend that the interplay between geometric complexity and the structure of deep learning models is a significant unexplored area that warrants further research. Potential avenues for future investigation that could lead to a deeper understanding of this phenomenon include the regularization effect of dropout, the role of feature representation, and the bridging of gaps in the landscape of geometric complexity, particularly between parameter space and model size. Furthermore, our work does not completely dismiss the significance of other regularizing effects, such as overfitting and the curse of dimensionality, which continue to be pivotal in deep learning. Nevertheless, our findings do suggest that their significance can be partially generalized and that the training process is not entirely dependent on them, as previously thought. Instead, we propose that the regularizing effect of geometric complexity is a more comprehensive and fundamental phenomenon that can provide additional insights into the deep learning landscape. Moreover, our work does not contradict previously established results, such as those demonstrating the utility of geometric complexity in feature representation, but rather builds upon them by exploring its role in deep learning regularisation. Additionally, we hypothesize that the regularizing effect of geometric complexity may also be beneficial for model interpretation, as simple models may exhibit reduced variability in feature importance and attribute assignments. We introduce an interesting metric, space toughness, for solving linear equations. It represents how resilient a linear system remains under partial noise. This metric leads to a new understanding of the stability of solvers in the presence of noise. It also challenges the common belief that solvers with high condition number robustness also demonstrate high space toughness. To illustrate the significance of space toughness, we examine its value for several popular solvers, including Neumann series and Richardson's methods. Moreover, we show that space toughness can be infinite, indicating that no solver can perfectly solve equations with a specific property. This understanding prompts the investigation of solvers with optimal space toughness and their design. Specifically, we demonstrate that solvers with optimal space toughness can outperform Neumann series and Richardson's methods in certain scenarios. To facilitate this, we introduce solvers, dubbed CNE and CNR, which utilize neural networks in solving linear equations. We show that space toughness is an appropriate regularization term for training these networks, leading to solvers that outperform Neumann series and Richardson's methods. Furthermore, medical data is frequently fragmented and treatment decisions are increasingly grounded in a complex mix of scientific, clinical, and personal considerations. Optimization techniques have been widely used in motion planning to tackle a molecule's conformational changes. Overcoming the exponential complexity of convex optimization is a crucial challenge here. One approach to address this issue involves using data-driven approximations such as the McCormick envelope to reduce the optimization problem's dimensionality. Although these approximations are versatile, they are largely heuristic in nature, making it difficult to guarantee the optimality of solutions. This study develops a new multi-stage optimization framework that incorporates data-driven McCormick envelopes in a systematic manner to ensure problem optimality. This framework relies on a probabilistic model of atom-atom van der Waals interactions to establish a rigorous bounds on the optimal solution through the theory of mixed-integer programming. This theoretical framework is applied to an energy-based motion planning problem, where the objective is to find the most stable molecular conformations through optimization. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this approach leads to near-optimal solutions that are also consistent with experimental observations. These simulations also highlight the precision of our approximations, showing deviations of less than 5% compared with exact solutions obtained through quantum chemistry methods. The proposed optimization framework, named COMPO,, significantly outperforms other planning methods, such as CEDAR,, particularly when dealing with large and complex molecular structures. The study concludes by highlighting potential applications of our approach in related optimization domains. There are various instances where it's impractical or too costly to perform a certain quantum operation, so it's essential to explore its probabilistic version instead. However, there's no universal approach to guaranteeing the success of such probabilistic operations, leading to the emergence of the concept of transformability: a source with one set of states can be transformed into another source with a different set of states through a series of probabilistic operations. We identify a crucial condition, known as the hybridity condition, for a source to be transformable: specifically, each state within a given subset must be closer to a reference state than another state in the same subset is. This condition turns out to be a strict limitation on the evolution of quantum systems during probabilistic interactions with an uncontrolled environment. Our findings demonstrate that certain sources are unreachable through probabilistic operations, even if the target source has lower purity than the initial source and the environment's purity is arbitrarily small. We also present a geometric interpretation of the hybridity condition and illustrate its relevance through examples from quantum channel transformability. We investigate how the parity-time symmetry in a finite lattice affects the light-matter interaction model based on the Purcell effect, using a rigorous mathematical approach. By employing the measure-theoretic paradigm, we define and differentiate between open and closed systems, and identify the essential conditions for parity-time symmetry in a finite lattice to be realized. Furthermore, we develop a strict mathematical representation of the radiation rate and prove its measure-invariant property with respect to any unitary transformation preserving the parity-time symmetry. This generalizes and reinforces the invariance of the radiation rate under spatial reflections and complex conjugation, as previously established findings. We further demonstrate that this invariance holds not only for the tight-binding model but also for any model based on a first-principle tight-binding framework. We illustrate the validity of our approach through a numerical example, where we calculate the radiation rate for a dimer model positioned within an infinite and a finite waveguide, and show that despite a visible difference in the system's wave function, the measure-invariant theory predicts a comparable radiation rate in both scenarios. This theoretical framework provides a precise and generalized interpretation of the parity-time symmetry in the context of light-matter interactions, and we anticipate that it will significantly contribute to the development of innovative optical devices. We also envision that this theoretical framework will enable the exploration of new ideas in optical engineering, where the concept of a 'effective Hamiltonian' may no longer be applicable, as traditionally assumed based on a first-principle tight-binding model. Ultimately, we anticipate that this theoretical framework will enable us to devise new strategies for controlling and engineering the light-matter interaction, perhaps by deliberately introducing a finite waveguide and selecting its dimensions in a way that maximizes the radiation rate and achieves a specified order of magnitude. Such a design approach could potentially lead to the creation of innovative devices, such as those for nanoscale laser development, that would be impossible to achieve based on the existing understanding of parity-time symmetry. In summary, we believe that the measure-invariant theory of light-matter interactions presents a novel and interesting perspective on this topic, and that it presents numerous opportunities for the development of innovative optical devices. We anticipate that this measure-invariant perspective will be particularly useful in exploring new orders of magnitude in optical interactions, and that it may no longer be applicable to our current understanding of devices, such as antennas and photonic waveguides. In that regard, we believe that the measure-invariant theory of light-matter interactions presents a new and interesting paradigm for optical research and development

To identify which particle collider is best suited to determine if the Standard Model is unstable, we developed a numerical analysis method based on theoretical predictions of signal and background rates. The approach involves comparing expected accuracy in measuring the Standard Model, specifically at proton-proton, lead-lead, and electron-positron colliders, as well as considering the impact of various experimental factors. The results reveal that proton-proton and electron-positron colliders are more likely to reveal instability in the Standard Model, while lead-lead colliders are better suited to study strong interactions at very low energies and potential quark-gluon plasma properties at low Bjorken-x. Ultimately, we find that the International Linear Collider, with its high-energy operations and precise Higgs boson measurements, holds the greatest potential for confirming stability in the Standard Model, specifically by measuring its coupling constants and mass. In contrast, we find that heavy-ion colliders lack the necessary capabilities to directly investigate instability, although they offer valuable insights into non-perturbative strong interactions and potential quark-gluon plasma properties at low Bjorken-x. Furthermore, we identify the energy reach and luminosity delivery as the primary factors that determine which collider is best equipped to establish the stability of the Standard Model. In a hypothetical scenario where we assume the presence of an alternative physics scenario at an energy reach of at least 100 TeV, we find that the stability of the Standard Model can only be confirmed by measuring its coupling constants and mass at a collider with an energy reach of at least 100 TeV. Conversely, we find that the stability of the Standard Model can be confirmed with current knowledge and assumptions, specifically at proton-proton and electron-positron colliders with an energy reach of at least 100 fb, without the need for an energy reach of at least 100 TeV. The results of our analysis provide crucial insights for designing future collider projects, specifically whether they should aim to surpass the energy reach of the Large Hadron Collider or focus on delivering high luminosity and precise measurements of Higgs boson and other Standard Model particles. A novel trajectory-based method in molecular dynamics, called sturdy inversion, efficiently generates equilibrium distributions from time-resolved data through a single collective optimization process. This method does not require detailed simulations or model adjustments. Instead, it optimizes a trajectory framework along with relevant distribution parameters in a unified procedure. We demonstrate, through both idealized and realistic simulations, that sturdy inversion effectively recovers accurate results even in the presence of noisy data. Even though it's primarily designed for equilibrium calculations, its general optimization approach makes it adaptable to a broader range of applications, such as estimating non-equilibrium state properties or optimizing active materials performance. The method's performance may be further improved by incorporating higher-order integrator techniques. Additionally, we show that incorporating time-dependent observables into the optimization process, beyond just energy, enhances the method's accuracy and precision. The numerical integration techniques used here have the potential to be more robust, especially in the face of nonlinear forces, and we provide a thorough theoretical justification for the method's convergence. The proposed sturdy inversion method could be a valuable addition to the MD analyst's toolkit, especially for data analysis tasks. A mathematical representation of infinite-dimensional dynamical systems, defined through linear operators, provides a fundamental framework. However, conventional methods requiring finite-dimensional representations or implicit operators with specific characteristics fall short in capturing the full diversity of linear dynamical systems. To address this limitation, we analyze the general properties of infinite-dimensional evolution equations driven by operators, without restricting to particular invariance properties or types of continuity. A well-known representation via Hilbert space and bounded linear operators still struggles to encompass diverse dynamical systems, as shown by counterexamples. To encompass all linear dynamical systems, we establish a theoretical framework based on the concept of epimorphisms within the category of linear partial differential equations. This approach is illustrated by a comparison with the known linear dynamical systems on the plane. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between strong solutions of certain stochastic partial differential equations and the maximal right colimit of a family of linear partial differential equations. To conclude, we consider the geometric implications of our findings on the general theory of linear dynamical systems, potentially offering a more comprehensive framework. In an appendix, we provide a step-by-step construction of a linear partial differential equation representing the right colimit of a family of conservation laws. This representation demonstrates that the general theory of linear dynamical systems can indeed represent all strong solutions of a type of stochastic partial differential equation. Bounded solutions of another type of stochastic partial differential equation are also effectively described within our framework. As an alternative approach, we present a theorem establishing the equivalence between the category of linear strong solutions for a certain class of infinite-dimensional differential equations and the category of linear partial differential equations that satisfy a specific positivity condition. To support these claims, we develop a series of auxiliary results. Furthermore, we discuss how our theory relates to other mathematical representations, such as the infinite-dimensional volume preserving maps and the geometric interpretation of linear dynamical systems, as well as the connections to stochastic analysis and linear thermodynamics. To facilitate understanding, we include a comprehensive bibliography and the definitions of key concepts used throughout the text. Finally, we consider future research directions and potential applications of our theoretical framework. In particular, we explore the applications to linear thermodynamics, volume preserving maps, and stochastic analysis, potentially offering new insights to experts in these fields. Although it's a solvable problem in theory, its computational complexity limits have only been roughly estimated so far. We study two online algorithms that iteratively construct the linear transformation by observing pairs $(p_i, p_j)$ and demonstrate their ability to find a solution with a controlled number of queries. The key to our success is the design of an alternative algorithm to solve the problem, which reveals new insights about the minimum number of queries required to find a solution. Additionally, we propose an early stopping technique for both algorithms to switch to an alternative solution when they encounter difficulties, allowing them to find a solution faster in certain situations. These techniques not only provide new bounds on the minimum number of queries required to solve the problem, but also demonstrate the existence of a complex set of solutions that are difficult to reach from any given solution. We further show that one of the algorithms can solve an important problem in sublinear complexity, thereby expanding the soluble set and improving the previous worst-case bounds on the minimal query size. The other algorithm can also solve this problem, as well as providing a solution to an important problem in quantum computing that we call the "generalized multiplicative linear equation problem." In two-dimensional materials that exhibit parity symmetry, a unique form of light emission can occur, known as bundle emission. Bundle emission happens when multiple quasiparticles combine to emit a single photon, and its emission pattern is determined by the band structure of the material through a process called parity symmetry. To study bundle emission, researchers typically use a framework that accounts for how the material's band structure changes as they move around it. However, since bundle emission is ultimately caused by the interaction between multiple quasiparticles, a more sophisticated approach is needed to fully describe it. 

A new framework, called the Kubo formalism, allows researchers to calculate bundle emission in a more detailed way by considering how quasiparticles interact with each other through their mutual interactions. By applying the Kubo formalism to a specific model based on a honeycomb lattice, researchers found that bundle emission not only follows the traditional bulk emission pattern but also has a polarization that is highly localized and concentrated. Furthermore, this approach has the potential to distinguish between various types of bundle emission, such as coherent and incoherent emission. Unlike typical equations, this particular system behaves differently when posed in spaces with different levels of smoothness. In the $L^p$-theory for $p<\frac{3}{2}$, it has been established that the solutions are equivalent to measures with certain properties, but as $p$ surpasses $\frac{3}{2}$, the solutions' nature remains unclear. Furthermore, we show that in the case of Lipschitz entropies, the solutions with measure-valued initial conditions lead to a unique, fragile, and continuous solution. This approach relies on a novel application of a technique that involves approximating any Lipschitz entropy with a sequence of smooth entropies. Due to the uniqueness of the solution, the solution with the measure-valued initial condition is the sole target of the convergence. In such cases, we show that the solution is continuous and is equal to the limit of a converging series of smooth entropy solutions. Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. In this context, phenotypic variety, referring to the diverse range of solutions produced, is of significant interest. Our study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of phenotypic variety in multi-modal optimization by systematically assessing various factors that influence it. These factors include the number of local optima, their fitness range, the optimization method used, and the criterion by which solutions are evaluated. As a preliminary investigation, we examine multi-dimensional optimization problems with certain characteristics, such as those involving standard functions in evolutionary optimization and Machine Learning algorithms' objectives. Our findings indicate that a wider range of solutions can be discovered through rigorous sampling, and that both evolutionary optimization and gradient-free methods are capable of generating substantial phenotypic variety. Interestingly, our research reveals that the optimal solution may not always be the best representative of phenotypic variety, and that multi-modal optimization strategies are more effective in this regard. Additionally, we find that exploring solutions at various fitness levels can be beneficial in this context. Building on these observations, we propose several theoretical arguments that contribute to our understanding of the relationships between multi-modal optimization, phenotypic variety, and solution diversity. Our study paves the way for further investigation into the phenomenological analysis of optimization, an approach in which phenotypic variety plays a central role. High-performance computing relies heavily on fault-tolerant storage systems that can withstand hardware failures.  In order to ensure data reliability in the event of failure, such systems engage in error-correcting mechanisms like checksumming and raid technologies.  These error-preventing mechanisms generate a checksum based on data being written and compare it with a recreated value following a failure, in order to identify and correct any existing errors.  However, since these error-preventing mechanisms are proactive, they are unable to accommodate a certain level of errors that may occur during failure, known as drop injuries.  In the case where a failure occurs and is corrected through error-preventing mechanisms, the system may treat drop injuries as non-existent, thus leading to data corruption.  In this study, we propose the concept of crash reliability, in which we tolerate a certain level of errors that may occur during failure, without engaging in error-preventing mechanisms during the failure event.  By doing so, we are able to draw a boundary around data corruption and control it through the use of non-performance affecting overheads that become active only after the failure event has occurred.  In order to achieve this, we would need to use an algorithmic approach that uses consistency checking to monitor data corruption, as well as uses advanced techniques to detect and accommodate drop injuries.  We use an example from the field of quantum computing to illustrate the benefits and challenges of this approach, and test it against various fault-tolerance techniques used in high-performance computing systems.  Our results show that this approach is able to offer both faster recovery times and improved efficiency over traditional fault-tolerance techniques, while also providing significant reductions in overheads.  In particular, we are able to achieve a reduction of up to 57% in overheads, as well as faster recovery times of up to 40%.  We conclude by discussing possible areas of improvement and future research directions that could further enhance this approach. Investigations into the $J/\psi$ decays reveal that the nuclear modification factor is not substantially different for central and peripheral events, which suggests the influence of mechanisms that reduce $J/\psi$ production in Pb-Pb collisions is effective throughout. Estimates of the $J/\psi$ production that excludes contributions from prompt hadron decays yield a nuclear modification factor that is larger in central events than peripheral ones, which indicates that non-prompt $J/\psi$ production is subject to the same modifying processes as $J/\psi$ production in general. Consideration of the nuclear effects on $D^0$ mesons, which are produced through fragmentation processes, reveals that the reduction in $J/\psi$ production relative to expected $D^0$ production is more pronounced in central events, which suggests that about half of the charged particle production that affects $J/\psi$ production in Pb-Pb collisions also influences non-prompt $D^0$ production or other contributions to $J/\psi$ production. Estimates of the average $J/\psi$ and $\psi_{\rm B}$ multiplicity in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV are provided, along with predictions for $J/\psi$ production in events with zero and high multiplicity, which are based on the prompt $J/\psi$ spectrum and the $k_{\rm T}$-diffusion model, respectively. Finally, simulations of the $J/\psi$ distribution in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV using the IPhub model, which incorporates effects of diffusion and energy loss, reveal good agreement with experimental data for the average $J/\psi$ multiplicity and zero-to-high multiplicity distributions. Our research aims to optimize the test case selection algorithm used within this framework by leveraging parallel computing capabilities. By applying parallel sorting, we show that the number of test cases and their identifiers are crux factors in algorithm optimization. Our proposed optimization yielded significant performance gains, achieving a 37.65% improvement in processing speed, as demonstrated through extensive experimental testing. With the capacity to process multiple source datasets and incorporate temporal dependencies, SiDeR outperformed existing approaches in predicting suicidal thoughts based on EEG data, with an accuracy of 92.88\% on public datasets, and successfully identified significant features in both EEG and fMRI datasets in a clinical setting. Our study\apos findings highlight the potential of SiDeR in identifying common patterns and predicting suicidal thoughts from multiple source datasets. From a technical standpoint, SiDeR addresses several critical challenges in deep learning, including the optimal use of model parameters, temporal dependencies, and network complexity. Our investigation also demonstrated the significant correlation between predicted temporal dependencies and clinical observations, as well as the distinct features identified in EEG and fMRI datasets. Our investigation of the isolated supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, via the analysis of $\gamma$-rays, shows a significant alignment of X-rays in the north-east to south-west direction with an angle of approximately 110 degrees. This IXPE data, following an extensive search, resulted in the detection of a polarization signal of $(5.1 \pm 1.1)% \pm 1.1%$. We also found evidence of a new gamma-ray feature, designated as a new shell, in the north-east direction with a shell-like structure. We have combined the X-ray findings with detailed spatial mappings across multiple frequencies, providing insight into the overall magnetic field arrangement following a supernova explosion. The total magnetic field strength in the central region was calculated as $\sim 110 \mu G$, while the magnetic ratio of $r_B = B/\sqrt{(B^2 + P^2)/2}$ was determined as $\sim 0.21$. We have also discussed and ruled out alternative explanations for the observed polarization signal. Furthermore, we have estimated the energy stored in the magnetic field of $\sim 1.6 \times 10^{50}$ erg. Our study has extensively examined the uncertainty of magnetic field strength in the central region, ultimately revealing that it is not the primary factor contributing to the overall uncertainty. Lastly, we have concluded that our findings are in line with the scenario of slow shock acceleration in supernova remnant Cassiopeia A. The code used for our analysis is publicly accessible at https://github.com/UoGranthamResearchGroup/CassiopeiaA_XPAnalysis/tree/production_v2.0.0. A new method is introduced to analyze and visualize the intricate structures formed at the interfaces of multi-phase flows, focusing on gas droplets moving through a viscous liquid. This technique generates a minimal representation of the interface, consisting of the skeleton model, to extract vital information about the interface's shape and its overall distribution. By implementing a novel extension of the Rayleigh-Phanse criterion, the method identifies and differentiates the primary and secondary branches of the interface, revealing a distinct phase space for the gas fraction and branch length. This novel information enhances understanding of bubble breakup processes and sheds new light on gas bubble behavior. Furthermore, the method successfully predicts interface shapes that are far away from the initial state, demonstrating good agreement with numerical simulations. This study also provides the first experimental evidence of the generalized Rayleigh-Phanse theory. A comparison between the new method's performance and other existing models shows that it accurately reproduces the same results as these models. This new approach offers a versatile tool for analyzing and understanding the behavior of bubbles in a viscous liquid, and it can be easily adapted for applications involving sinks or forces in the liquid. This technique has vast potential for application in many areas, such as fluid dynamics analysis, machine learning, and the study of biological systems and aquatic animals that produce net sink trajectories in a viscous liquid. A code for this method is available on the GitHub repository at <https://github.com/Stanley-Li/Interface-Skeletons>. Many disk galaxies exhibit unique, S-shaped warps known as U types. This study identifies a novel U type classification system based on three main characteristics: the orientation of the warp's central feature, its asymmetry, and the distribution of its orientation across the galaxy. In a follow-up, we observed that isolated galaxies tend to have less asymmetric U types, whereas those part of a galaxy cluster show more asymmetry. This asymmetry is most pronounced in U type galaxies that reside in groups or clusters. This trend correlates with the collective dynamical influence of nearby galaxies on the spiral galaxies in question. It's possible that cluster galaxies with high asymmetry rates are more susceptible to tidal forces that cause the 'jellyfish' phenomenon observed in numerous spiral galaxies. This suggests a potential link between deformed galaxies and the tidal compression that gives rise to jellyfish galaxies. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed data from the SDSS and NORPAP surveys to examine the relationship between jellyfish galaxies and galaxies classified as U types. Our results confirm that U types with pronounced asymmetry are more likely to exhibit jellyfish-like features. This study paves the the way for future research by establishing U type classification as a valuable tool in understanding the tidal compression that shapes jellyfish galaxies. To further explore this relationship, we selected 54 jellyfish galaxies from the NORPAP survey, and found that their distribution in space does not differ significantly from that of U type galaxies. However, further investigation is needed to establish the tidal origin of jellyfish galaxies. To this end, we propose three key research objectives: Firstly, establishing local tidal environments as a primary factor in the evolution of jellyfish galaxies; Secondly, creating detailed mass models of galaxy clusters to identify specific tidal processes that give rise to jellyfish galaxies; and thirdly, observing the variation in galaxy morphology over extended periods of time to directly demonstrate the tidal compression mechanism. By addressing these research objectives, we can gain a deeper understanding of the dynamic processes that shape galaxy evolution. To this end, we began building a specialized code to model tidal compression, and started gathering data from the NORPAP survey to examine U type galaxies in more detail. Additionally, we conducted early testing of Zentao's Tidal Code by analyzing mock observations of 1000 randomly selected galaxies from the NORPAP survey, and obtained promising results by demonstrating its ability to accurately identify U type galaxies based on their characteristics. This code is an important research tool that may allow us to observe U type galaxies and jellyfish galaxies in a new light

results indicate that electric field correlations in metals have a non-adiabatic
component, which corresponds to the Drude weight, and an adiabatic contribution

in metals. In the absence of scattering, the adiabatic contribution grows like

extending our approach to three dimensions, our results match well with existing
three-dimensional theories. Our work also includes a detailed examination of
Drude weights in various materials across different temperatures and densities.

In 1921, Reynolds noted that high-Re flows are characterized by turbulent motions, which lead to increased friction and heat transfer. This prompted him to investigate the relationship between flow Reynolds number and the critical value above which turbulent motions appear, which he estimated to be around 4000. However, later experiments revealed that the critical value lies beyond what could be achieved in an experiment. In this study, predictions from models of dissipation-range turbulence are applied to an experiment involving a heated plate to clarify the nature of turbulent motions. It is assumed that non-viscous dissipative motions occupy a minimal fraction of the energy spectrum. By assuming an energy cascade process similar to that in an open system, the characteristics of the turbulent motions are clarified, and the possibility of detecting these motions in an experiment is investigated. Our calculations indicate that the highest Reynolds number that could be achieved in an experiment is approximately 100,000. This limits our understanding of the fundamental nature of turbulent motions. It is found that the dissipative motions are isolated isolates from their surroundings by an 'energy barrier', which is a low-amplitude range in the energy spectrum. The appropriate prescription of medications is crucial for healthcare, but certain drugs can be hazardous when taken together. Therefore, it is necessary to assess the safety of medication combinations from the start of treatment to prevent adverse effects later on. Although existing methods focus solely on the initial medication pair, taking into account the entire treatment timeline is essential for avoiding drug interactions. In this research, we present a novel network architecture that can handle long-term information and enable the comprehensive evaluation of medication combinations. Our approach draws on relational deep learning, incorporating properties of Korean medication names and the relationships between drugs to capture the intricate interactions between substances. We also establish a large dataset with 1.63 million pairs of medication combinations and their associated adverse effects, enabling the reliable scoring of drug interactions based on their severity. Our experiments reveal that our model produces the most accurate results alone, outperforming models that incorporate additional information, such as models that incorporate graph models or models that use pre-trained language models. Furthermore, our results show that our model predicts medication combinations that have not been used in real-world practice as having higher interaction scores compared to commonly prescribed combinations. The data and model used in this study can be accessed via dedicated repositories. Additionally, the model has been made available on the M2M Transformer repository as a named entity. Lastly, the model will be maintained as an open model and will continue to provide accurate scoring of medication combinations for others to use. (From the abstract)
