Imitation learning seeks to achieve good performance in tasks by observing human demonstrations in a particular context. However, in many real-world situations, it is difficult to find suitable areas for training as the transfer of observed behaviors from one environment to another becomes increasingly challenging beyond physical and sensory changes. To address this issue, we present CAIO, a novel framework that enables cross-environment imitation learning by integrating multiple source areas for transfer learning purposes. We then examine the effectiveness of our approach through practical applications in two scenarios: navigating grid worlds with different dimensions and mobile robot navigation in realistic simulations. When evaluated in a novel grid environment, CAIO was able to achieve zero-error performance using the learned policies without any further training. Furthermore, we found that CAIO could also facilitate successful navigation in more complex mobile robot environments, where the trajectories obtained from CAIO were comparable to those produced by models trained in the target environment. Crucially, we observed that CAIO was able to generalize to target environments that were constructed by modifying various key features of the source environments, including the shape of obstacles, lighting conditions, and even the presence of novel obstructions. Through these experiments, we believe that CAIO presents an important innovation in the field of imitation learning. We anticipate that our approach will contribute to the development of more robust and versatile mobile robot systems capable of navigating a wide range of diverse environments. Additionally, we expect that CAIO will serve as a useful tool for teaching robots to navigate by observing demonstrations in a variety of contexts. We hope that these capabilities will be leveraged to enhance both the performance and safety of mobile robots. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we openly provide the code, data, and experimental setups employed in our study. We also present an online version of this study, where we continue to explore the effectiveness of CAIO through ongoing evaluations in ever-changing environments. We encourage others to join us in this research and invite feedback on our findings. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves scanning a database to obtain infrequent itemsets, which are then eliminated through successive transformations - such as removal, addition, or duplication - until the resulting itemsets meet a predetermined threshold. To optimize this process, a novel deduction framework called $\mathcal{AS}$ is proposed within this document. This framework incorporates well-known deduction operators while introducing two novel ones: $F_{\text{remove}}$ and $F_{\text{dual}}$. To effectively utilize $\mathcal{AS}$, two key concepts are examined: (i) the first itemset of a sequence and the last itemset of a sequence, and (ii) the least-size base and the smallest-size base of a sequence. These concepts enable the efficient generation of association rule analyses through the application of Fopoulos et al.'s fast deduction operator $F_{\text{size}}$. A mathematical investigation of the first itemset and the last itemset of a sequence is also provided. This includes determining their closed forms, establishing a criterion for their uniqueness, and deriving explicit formulas. Additionally, the study identifies the required size of a base for association rule analysis and proves the uniqueness of the smallest-size base under certain conditions. A practical approach to finding the smallest-size base is then outlined. Finally, two experimental studies are presented to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. In particular, the developed techniques are shown to outperform existing methods in the Apriori algorithm. Furthermore, the proposed methods are demonstrated to generate association rule analyses more efficiently than existing approaches. Several open issues arising from these experiments are highlighted and left to be addressed in future research. This includes the extension of the proposed methods to handling weighted databases. This way, the association rule analysis would be able to incorporate different weights for the database's items. Moreover, the size of the first itemset and the last itemset of a sequence could be optimized using the Deduction Framework $\mathcal{AS}$. Additionally, the proposed methods could be adapted to embed association rule analysis within other Deduction Frameworks. This adaptation could help optimize the size of the first itemset and the last itemset of a sequence under specific framework conditions. Finally, the size of the first itemset and the last itemset of a sequence could be efficiently generated using $\mathcal{AS}$ in conjunction with the fast deduction operator $F_{\text{size}}$. This would help minimize the number of database scans required during the association rule analysis

To address this, some courts now require convicted individuals to undergo therapy as a condition of their sentence.  This innovative approach incorporates mental health treatment into the justice system's operations, eliminating the distinction between justice system care and mental health care. One widespread challenge in statistical analysis is the non-conservative nature of confidence intervals for complex estimators, particularly the median estimator of a parameter from a mixture. Traditional theory focuses on bounding individual estimates but fails to provide a comprehensive assessment of the average performance of these estimators. This study develops a new approach to analyze the average behavior of linear combinations of parameters from mixtures, incorporating randomized sampling designs. By employing a generalized likelihood framework, we establish explicit expressions for the mean and variance of estimators in various mixing scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that, in the central region, the average behavior of estimators is indeed conservative, validating the hypothesis of no bias. To assess the magnitude of bias in the boundary region, we introduce the concept of 'effective complexity'. Our analysis is illustrated by examining the average behavior of six common estimators of parameters from mixtures, including the median, mode, entropy, intensity, and mixture parameters. Our results showcase the versatility of the proposed assessment method, revealing its utility in studying the behavior of estimators in a wide range of statistical analysis problems. Moreover, the study highlights the utility of randomized sampling designs in reducing bias and asymmetry, and these designs can be easily adapted for use in the missing data problem. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the feasibility of using the mean squared error as a criterion for estimator selection. Our investigation also emphasizes the importance of considering the specific structure of the parameter space when designing experiments and provides a systematic approach to achieve specified levels of bias. Furthermore, the study illustrates the applicability of the proposed framework in non-parametric statistical analysis by examining the properties of two estimators of population entropy. Our analysis is comprised of both theoretical and numerical sections. The theoretical part reviews established results and presents the new assessment method, while the numerical section is devoted to illustrating and validating the findings through simulation studies and real data examples. The study concludes by outlining potential areas for further research and investigation. Additionally, the associated R code is provided for ease of use in practical applications. Specifically, the code includes functions for calculating the mean and variance of estimators, determining the effective complexity, and selecting the best estimator. Thoroughly understanding gas disk evolution is crucial for predicting planet formation. In this study, we analyze the CO emission from the AS 209 disk, utilizing high-resolution data from 12 CO and 13 CO j = 2-1 and 5-1 transitions. AS 209 exhibits a distinctive CO j = 2-1 gap at 84-120 AU, primarily caused by 13 CO emission outside this area. This leads us to suspect that 12 CO is being removed through chemical processing rather than outflow activity. We support this claim by observing various lines, including those from CN and HCN, which are also affected by the CO j = 2-1 gap. Additionally, we find that the 13 CO emission does not originate from streams or jets, but rather from a region with higher dust emission and stellar irradiation. Our findings are consistent with a model where 12 CO is converted into 13 CO through non-self-destructive reactions, particularly astrophysical radiation processes. We further propose that this region may serve as a reservoir for volatile materials in the sub-stellar disk, while 13 CO from the inner disk could be driven outward by the photochemical reaction. Ultimately, this model provides a mechanism for reducing CO in gas disk models, thereby facilitating the preservation of volatile materials in the sub-stellar disk. Additionally, we observe that the 13 CO surface density exhibits a positive correlation with the 13 CO inner radius, implying that CO reduction is more efficient in disks with inner hot regions. We suggest that this trend is caused by the increased radiative energy from the star and inner disk fragments in the planet formation area. The goal of Visual Item Contrast, or VICTOR, is to identify unusual items in a collection by comparing their visual characteristics to those of similar items, either by matching individual attributes or by contrasting overall appearances. Our study introduces a novel dataset with 300,000 images and outlines a detailed analysis of the visual anomalies in online retail clothing sales. To improve the accuracy of visual anomaly detection, we suggest a distinctive pre-training approach that combines category-level visual similarities with expert reviews of clothing items. The proposed method, called FashionContrast, significantly enhances the model's global understanding of fashion trends and critical critique, as demonstrated by experiments conducted on recent image representation techniques. Finally, we evaluate the VICTOR approach on a range of transfer learning tasks, such as matching individual attributes and combining multiple attributes to identify unusual items. The results of these experiments, along with expert analyses, are presented in the study. The VICTOR code and dataset are available for public use at https://github.com/wgreenw2/VICTOR. As the complexity of distributed training increases, federated learning presents a viable option. Historically, FL has been implemented with synchronous data aggregation, but asynchronous accumulation has become a more efficient alternative. With asynchronous accumulation, each client collects gradient updates and aggregates them only when connection parameters are met, resulting in lower latency. Nonetheless, current applications of asynchronous accumulation rely on assuming that clients' devices are capable of sustaining connections, a premise that doesn't always hold in real-world scenarios where network connectivity can be unstable. This paper explores a novel approach that enables seamless connection to the main aggregator without the assumption that clients can maintain continuous connections. Our solution involves using the concept of dead zone to store gradient updates collected during periods of disconnection, allowing for a smooth and efficient flux of information to the aggregator and maintenance of accurate model representations. Experimental results show that our solution performs better than existing methods, supporting the use of asynchronous accumulation in scenarios unaffected by connection constraints. Moreover, we identify potential areas for improvement through additional analysis. This research provides the foundation for further investigation into the efficient application of asynchronous accumulation in FL. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/guiperrin/unconstrained-fl. Additionally, a pre-compiled version of our code can be found on PIP at https://pypi.org/project,unicfl,version=0.1.4. This research was supported by ANR-15-CE25-05.

A close look at raft mechanics shows that fracture-type failures occur when there's little give in the material. Research has mostly studied this phenomenon through detailed simulations. There's been relatively little hands-on testing to validate these findings. Our study aims to change that by examining how different loads affect raft mechanics in a lab setting. We used a specially designed system to apply forces to a group of objects held together by a floating mat. The results from these experiments match what the simulations predicted. We also found that the rate at which the loads increase has a significant impact on how the raft responds. When the loads rise slowly, the raft deforms smoothly but ultimately gives in all at once. On the other hand, rapid increases in load cause cracks to spread gradually at a constant speed. When the rate of crack growth equals the rate of deformation in the surrounding material, the cracks stabilize and the raft can handle more load. This behavior turns out to be a general trend, applicable to a wide range of materials. We based our understanding of this phenomenon on a simplified theory that represents the mechanics of this type of failure. This theory is similar to one used to explain how ice forms and grows in water. It suggests that the rate at which the cracks spread is controlled by the rate at which the surrounding material deforms, or by the rate at which the fluid inside the raft has time to move away from the cracking area. When the rate of crack spread equals the surrounding material's deformation rate, the cracks stabilize and the raft can handle more load. This study provides a new level of understanding of how and when fracturing failures occur and offers a simplified theory to explain this phenomenon. Additionally, our research offers a practical method to predict when such failures might occur. This could be especially important in situations involving floating solar panels or other critical applications. Our work also confirms that the phenomenon of gradual failure is a common one, occurring not just on floating solar panels, but also on sea ice and other materials as well. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In this study, a novel approach is taken to explore whether the anisotropic strain from co-grown binary and ternary nitride materials can enhance hole mobility in the GaN buffer. To investigate this, ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ polymorphs with lattice parameters closely matched to the wurtzite structure are examined as strain sources. These investigations show that growing ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ on top of GaN changes the p-type buffer material into n-type, causing a significant increase in carrier concentration but a significant decrease in hole mobility in the GaN buffer. Notably, a high hole mobility of 1500 cm$^2$/V*s is achieved with MgSiN$_2$ on SiC substrate, significantly surpassing the conventional Si-doped GaN process. The notable improvement can be attributed to the novel polytype of MgSiN$_2$ with a Si-Si $dz$ bond, facilitating the mobility of Si ions in the material, thereby reducing the spatiotemporal variability of the anisotropic strain. In contrast, ZnGeN$_2$ with a Ge-Zn $dz$ bond cannot provide such excellent performance, as its bond stiffness and anisotropic strain are insufficient to boost hole mobility in p-type GaN. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the anisotropic strain in nitride materials with Si-Si $dz$ bonds in the wurtzite structure has the potential to significantly enhance hole mobility in the p-type GaN buffer. Moreover, it is speculated that this technique can be applied to other III-V semiconductor materials, such as InN and AlN. Ultimately, it is anticipated that this approach will contribute to the development of highly efficient integrated gallium nitride transistors and enable the anisotropic strain to play a significant role in III-Nitride electronics.

To accomplish tasks that require understanding of temporal information, systems can utilize knowledge in the form of sequential timelines rather than concurrent events. However, existing representations, which depict temporal relationships as a whole, fail to reveal the sequential nature of time. In contrast, we propose representing temporal information in a sequential manner by dividing the circular time circle into equal parts and assigning specific indices to these segments. By doing so, we demonstrate that traditional recurrent neural networks, which excel at processing sequential data, can effectively acquire and utilize temporal knowledge inherent in the modified time representation. Through theoretical analysis and experimental validation using the MABenchmark and Rail-Route problems, we illustrate how RNN can learn to recognize temporal patterns even in scenarios with loops, thus showcasing the advantages of our temporal representation over alternative methods that represent time as a whole. Furthermore, we highlight the additional benefits of this representation in reducing data requirements for temporal feature engineering. Our work provides a unique solution to the question of how to represent temporal information in a sequential manner and showcases the capabilities of traditional recurrent neural networks in acquiring and utilizing temporal knowledge. Moreover, we illustrate the practical implications of our approach by applying it to real-world problems, such as modeling rail routes and hospital admissions. In particular, we demonstrate that our temporal representation, combined with long short-term memory (LSTM), can achieve a 99.7% accuracy rate in predicting hospital admissions based on sequential time representations, thus outperforming a baseline model by 3.7%. Our approach offers a novel and efficient strategy to model temporal relationships and has the potential to be applied in a wide range of domains. With a maximum memory footprint of approximately 12KB, our long-term memory model, which is based on LSTM and trains on the MABenchmark for 100 episodes, successfully predicts 97.5% of the next event's attributes in a sequence. Additionally, we illustrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to real-world problems in different domains, such as rail routes and hospital admissions for children. Our temporal representation, which is designed to learn sequential patterns, achieves a 94.5% accuracy rate in predicting rail service schedules and a 97.5% accuracy rate in predicting children's hospital admissions, thus outperforming baseline models by 5.5% and 2.5%, respectively. In summary, we offer a novel approach to representing and modeling temporal information in a sequential manner and illustrate its efficiency and effectiveness using real-world datasets. Our work has the potential to a wide range of applications in which temporal relationships need to be understood

To mitigate the severity of a pandemic, governments implement non-pharmaceutical measures such as mobility restrictions, which entail trade-offs between lives saved and economic preservation. We find that, to achieve a specified economic recovery target, the optimal policy is to ease restrictions in proportion to the decline in virus-transmitting cases, thereby allowing a controlled balance between health concerns and economic considerations. This strategy is applicable not only because the shape of the virus transmission rate fits well with exponential distributions, but also due to the nature of economic activity itself. The underlying structure of the problem, rooted in the combination of Gaussian processes and utility functions, yields the widely applicable solution. The proportionality rule is further validated by comparison with results from established econometric models. We illustrate the relevance of our findings through analysis of the 2020 pandemic in seven countries. The simplicity and general applicability of our approach make it suitable for use in data-poor environments. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in the antiferromagnetic triangular compound Mn$_3$Sn. At ambient pressure, this material exhibits a small anomalous Hall effect due to its contamination with a ferromagnetic phase. However, our research reveals that by subjecting Mn$_3$Sn to pressures exceeding 1.50 GPa in a helium gas medium, the contamination can be eliminated, allowing for a pure antiferromagnetic phase to develop. The resulting analysis shows that pressure's impact on the band structure around the Fermi level leads to an increased anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, our theoretical models suggest that this increase arises from pressure-induced changes in the electronic structure, particularly at the Fermi level, rather than spin-polarization around the Fermi level. In contrast, our models disagree with previous studies suggesting that pressure's impact on Mn$_3$Sn's band structure is caused by lattice distortion effects. Instead, our analysis points out that pressure's impact on Mn$_3$Sn's band structure resembles a typical band inversion phenomenon, often seen in materials exhibiting anomalous Hall effect. In conclusion, our research demonstrates that pressure can regulate the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn by controlling the contamination from a ferromagnetic phase. Additionally, our study identifies key factors contributing to Mn$_3$Sn's anomalous Hall effect, including band inversion and ferromagnetic contamination. Given a hyperbolic 3-manifold with a non-trivial Euler characteristic, we establish that most of its tight contact structures fail to possess the desired property of being representative in the context of the norm. In addition, we present examples illustrating two distinct scenarios where representative tight contact structures in the norm do not coincide with the set of all tight contact structures. Additionally, we identify a characteristic that distinguishes representative from non-representative tight contact structures in the norm. It is worth noting that this distinction is inherently defined by the properties of the manifold and does not rely on the presence of a Euclidean structure. Lastly, we present an open question concerning the existence of a single tight contact structure that is representative in the norm for all hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a non-trivial Euler characteristic. If such a structure exists, it would likely be a universal contact structure. In support of this assumption, we prove that any universal tight contact structure is representative in the norm. Furthermore, we present an alternative expression for the Euler characteristic in terms of the norms of tight contact structures, drawing parallels with previously established results by Masmouche, which applied to Chern-Simons gauge theory and were later extended by Sarig, and relating to the volume of pseudo-Anosov maps as studied by Farb and Johnson. We establish that the set of norms from tight contact structures achieves its maximum value when the Euler characteristic is at its minimum value. In the process of achieving this goal, we derive a formula for the determinant of the intersection matrix, which is known to be equal to the square of the Euler characteristic. Additionally, we present an open question concerning the existence of an integral, non-trivial universal contact structure. We establish that the set of intersection numbers achieves its minimum value when the Euler characteristic is at its maximum value. In the process of achieving this goal, we derive a formula for the intersection number of a universal contact structure, which is equal to the square of the Euler characteristic. We propose an innovative method to analyze anisotropic emission patterns in microcavity lasers. This method leverages the entropic index of light to quantify leptocrite and plectocrite components, providing a concise measure of beam quality. The technique's initial validation is achieved through numerical simulations of two common microcavity laser designs: a rectangular cavity and an elliptical cavity. The outcomes demonstrate that the entropic gauge effectively identifies both isotropic and anisotropic emission conditions, differentiating them from more complex cases. Furthermore, a method to determine the anisotropic degree of emission is introduced, along with a method to identify the axis of emission. The techniques offer precise analysis of beam quality and allow for the identification of anisotropic characteristics in a wide range of microcavity laser configurations. This study provides a framework for evaluating anisotropic emission in a variety of optical sources. Anisotropic emission is a crucial characteristic that influences the accuracy and efficiency of optical communication systems. Consequently, we expect this research to contribute significantly to the development of vision-corrected emitters, enabling new applications in arthropod bionics and optoelectronic microsystem technology. Our research addresses the cost effectiveness of using cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Drawing on the concept of Lyapunov stability from mathematics, we develop a framework to assess the relative stability of cryptocurrencies. This involves mapping the behavior of transaction costs to the cryptocurrency's price, using a Lyapunov function to determine its stability. Theoretical calculations using Lyapunov stability analysis reveal that the stability of cryptocurrencies may be susceptible to mathematical singularities and asymptotic instability. Consequently, we propose an alternative approach to evaluating the stability of cryptocurrencies, based on the behavior of their percentage price fluctuations over time. By applying this method to the most widely traded cryptocurrencies, we investigate their stability and analyze the results. Interestingly, our investigation reveals that the stability of cryptocurrencies may decline over time, with some showing a higher rate of instability than others. Furthermore, we identify a positive correlation between the changes in the daily price volatility of cryptocurrencies and their stability, suggesting that more widely traded cryptocurrencies tend to be less stable than less widely traded ones. Overall, our study provides a novel approach to evaluating the stability of cryptocurrencies, offering a valuable perspective for investors and practitioners. A novel approach to fault detection in textile images is introduced, focusing on detecting flaws in fabric samples. Textile faults appear as irregular patterns in image symmetry, making edge-based features ineffective. To address this challenge, a proposed method combines GHOG (Generalized Horizontal Ordinate Partition) with low-rank decomposition to accurately identify flaws in textile images. First, low-rank decomposition reduces the spatial correlation in texture features, followed by the extraction of GHOG features to represent the irregular pattern. Finally, binary segmentation is applied to distinguish flaws from the image background. Experimental results demonstrate the high precision of the proposed method in flaw detection, with a precision of 98.95% achieved. To evaluate and validate the approach, a large dataset of 200 textile image pairs was used, along with statistical analysis to assess reliability. Additionally, the simplicity and efficiency of the proposed method were verified through computational experiments. The low computational complexity of the approach enables real-time application in industrial settings, enhancing the overall quality of textile production processes. The proposed method has been made available on GitHub for public access. With its high precision and efficiency, this framework provides a valuable reference for both research and industrial use in textile fault detection. By employing modern tools such as higher k-theory, categorification, and stable homotopy theory, we outline a comprehensive approach to wrapping these concepts in a coherent framework. The tutorial concludes with a concise overview of pretopological k-theory and the Fredholm theory of elliptic operators on topological insulators. This tutorial is designed for students and young researchers to gain a thorough understanding of the theoretical foundations of topological insulators. Specifically, given a non-constant rational function on a variety and a number field in which the function's denominator is contained, we demonstrate that the function's values are indeed contained in a finite set. This result generalizes the known finiteness theorems for linear systems and applies to function fields as well, yielding a Tsen-Dedekind theorem for finite extensions of $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-1})$. Furthermore, we derive applications to the study of number fields and algebraic tori. In particular, we resolve a question of Neumann-Beyer and Garcia-Ramos-Beyer by showing that there are only finitely many number fields of a given degree containing a given finite subgroup of the circle, and we establish an arithmetic analogue of Faltings's theorem for degree-$d$ finite subgroups of $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$. Additionally, we address a question of G. Wüstholz, showing that the rational function field of a certain degree-$d$ curve over a number field has only a finite number of elements in the function field of another degree-$\delta$ curve, provided $d>\delta$. Finally, we demonstrate that the function field of a certain degree-$d$ variety over a number field has only a finite number of homomorphisms to the rational function field of a given degree-$\delta$ linear algebraic group, provided $d>\delta$. Throughout the article, we use the finite-basis theorem for finitely generated $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-vector spaces, which we refer to as the finite-basis theorem, to achieve these results. This new result has the potential to be applied more widely. A key issue in current robotic systems is efficiently allowing humans to grasp and move objects, especially when their hands or eyes are in unusual positions. To address this limitation, we're taking a data-driven approach, focusing on adapting task models to accommodate variations in human hand positions. Our approach uses a new optimization technique that synchronizes pose and shape adjustments, ensuring smooth and informative results. To ensure the results remain within the limits of what's physically and visually possible, we've developed a way to incorporate constraints from what's known as a "visuomotor terrain". This terrain represents the set of all feasible visual and motor states, taking into account factors like the limitations of human vision and motor abilities. When translating the task model, we use a special algorithm to move information from one position to another, while maintaining consistency. To make sure the results are consistent when viewed from different perspectives, we've developed a special version of the Point Cloud Registration algorithm, ICPhum. This algorithm uses the connectedness of the visuomotor terrain to ensure that rotated and translated points remain connected, and allows multiple perspectives to solve the registration challenge simultaneously. Finally, we've developed a way to evaluate and compare the feasibility of different task models, using simulations of various robotic systems, their corresponding hand-mounted RGB-D cameras, and a set of randomly generated poses. This tool, called ROPLAN, represents the set of all feasible robotic systems, allowing us to evaluate the feasibility of different task models and compare their performance, even when viewed from different perspectives. With ROPLAN, we've shown that ICPhum outperforms other algorithms, and that making small adjustments to the hand position significantly affects the feasibility of the task models. This means that even small variations in hand position can greatly affect the ease of performing a task. To confirm this, we conducted a real-world experiment, where participants performed a simple reaching task while their hands were mounted with small, light-detecting sensors and cameras. The results of this experiment matched our previous findings, showing that small adjustments in hand position significantly affects the ease of performing a task. This means that robotic systems should be able to adapt more easily to small changes in hand position, and that incorporating this adaptation into task models significantly improves their feasibility. This research has potential applications in areas such as industrial robotics, space exploration, and search and rescue, where robotic assets are used to perform tasks despite varying hand positions. This is an difficult problem because the amount of information in a single image is limited.  Most existing methods assume either that the object remains unchanged or that its location can be calculated without considering its appearance.  However, these assumptions are not applicable in situations where a robot needs to navigate through unfamiliar environments and observe changing objects in 3D.  A new algorithm has been developed that uses observed objects rotating as a reference point for calculating their three-dimensional position without any initial assumptions.  This algorithm is based on the idea that rotating objects appear in a circular pattern, and by capturing images of this movement, a robot can determine the 3D distance between itself and the object.  This method was tested using realistic simulations and real-world experiments and achieved an accurate distance of less than 0.1 meters.  The only requirement for this algorithm to work is that an observable part of the object rotates, meaning it can be applied in a wide range of scenarios. The rapid dissemination of misinformation regarding COVID-19 vaccines necessitates immediate attention, as social media platforms are inundated with user inquiries. In contrast to conventional misinformation detection approaches, which focus on individual posts, this study recognizes the interactive nature of online conversations by incorporating retweets into the analysis. By integrating SOT (Staircase OT) for anomaly detection and fine-tuning a pre-trained BERT model on a small dataset, this study successfully identifies tweets indicating skepticism towards COVID-19 vaccines, thereby separating retweets from original tweets. Furthermore, we apply OT-based anomaly detection to identify user groups propagating misinformation, and conduct case studies on the retrieved tweets to uncover the causes of misinformation dissemination. By quantifying the spread of misinformation, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing debate on social media platforms' responsibility for combating misinformation. Overall, this research highlights the significance of online conversations in the dissemination of misinformation and suggests a possible strategy for social media platforms to address this issue. The code for this project is available on the GitHub repository.

The production of isolated attosecond pulses, which enable the observation of electron movement in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, relies heavily on the coherence between different harmonic components generated in a recircating laser field. Our research demonstrates, however, that even in incoherent XUV fields emitted by ions, a comparable level of coherence can be observed, leading to the generation of attosecond pulses, as shown in the case of Ne9+ ions. By implementing a real-time optimization technique based on the optimal control method, we were able to enhance the coherence of the XUV field and utilize it to generate isolated attosecond pulses, regardless of the incoherent nature of the field. It is anticipated that the implementation of coherent manipulation in a complex system such as ionized neon would open up new avenues for the efficient generation of attosecond pulses in a broad range of ions and lasers. Additionally, the technique could be used to generate specific ultrashort pulse patterns that are resistant to disturbances and could be used in the development of attosecond technology. It is also possible that this technique could be adapted for use in the coherent manipulation of more complex systems. The present study shows that coherent manipulation can be achieved in a system that is not coherent, thereby expanding the applicability of this technique. Our research further reveals that, from an engineering perspective, it is more beneficial to generate attosecond pulses in a laser field that recircates rather than in a linearly oscillating field. It is also demonstrated that generating attosecond pulses in a linearly oscillating field is only feasible if the energy of the pulse is increased significantly. Our research provides new insights into the underlying mechanics of attosecond pulse generation and recircation and these findings may contribute to the development of new approaches in this field. The implementation of coherent manipulation in a system that is not coherent has also been shown to significantly reduce the requirements of any underlying coherent mechanism necessary for attosecond pulse generation. Our research demonstrates that it is indeed possible to manipulate the coherence of a system that is not coherent by optimizing the behavior of the harmonic components of that system. The experiments presented in this study were performed using the ATLAS three-stage laser system, with a wavelength of 800 nm, a typical pulse duration of 160 fs, and a repetition rate of 10 Hz. Our research shows that it is possible to enhance the coherence of the XUV field emitted by Ne9+ ions through the optimal manipulation of the harmonic components of that field, regardless of the incoherent nature

The detection of a low-mass companion orbiting the ancient star Algol, a key figure in the story of stellar evolution, has significant implications. Algol's characteristics make it ideal for studying mass exchange and planetary formation in globular clusters, particularly if it has a companion less massive than previously thought. Recent studies suggested the presence of a 0.12 solar mass companion at a distance of 0.16 astronomical units from Algol. This would have been one of the lowest mass ratios identified for a binary star system in a globular cluster and less massive companions of fresh counterparts, such as those in the Clusters-@-n, could be harvested by stellar winds during their main sequence period. However, a thorough examination of the 0.12 solar mass companion's orbit revealed that it was likely much closer to the star than previously thought, which would have resulted in the companion's loss to the star's Roche lobe and eventual absorption long ago. This would mark the end of hopes for finding fresh counterparts in the Clusters-@-n using Algol as a prototype. The accumulation of material from dissolved companions could explain features of Algol's mass distribution, including its wide range of mass ratios and its uneven distribution across the binary phase, which had previously been attributed to mass exchange between companions. This study also highlights the limitations of relying on long-term observations of a single star to make generalisations about the properties of all low-mass companions in a globular cluster. The wide range of orbital distances and companion masses that could account for Algol's characteristics have made it difficult to identify the original location of the companion, particularly since features of the mass distribution could be explained by the loss of smaller companions. This loss could also result in the reduction of orbital distances in the remaining companions and could lead to the detection of the companion's mass loss in the vicinity of the star. The possibility of harnessing the energy produced by the absorption of the companion by the star, which had previously been a key feature of fresh counterparts, has also been ruled out. This ruling out of a well-known theory has brought an end to hopes for a new source of energy production, such as that proposed by the Clusters-@-n, where fresh counterparts, such as those in the Clusters-@-n, could be harvested by stellar winds during their main sequence period. The concept of harnessing energy from the dissolution of companions in the Clusters-@-n, which had previously been a key feature, has also been dismissed.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for solving partial differential equations. Despite the advantages of continuous representations, they can be difficult to train, especially with pointwise data. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various point-discretization methods that convert PINNs to function approximators. However, adaptations of these methods are rare for mesh-free coordinate systems, which are widely used in physics simulations. To fill this gap, we propose Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, a novel mesh-free point-discretization method that automatically creates new nodes to enhance function fitting. We compare the performance of RANG, mesh-based discretization, and continuous representations on three challenging problems, including a nonlinear Schrödinger equation, a heat equation with boundary conditions, and a nonlinear wave equation. The results demonstrate that RANG surpasses mesh-based methods and closely approaches continuous representations, while also providing interpretable node generation outcomes. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of RANG in solving real-world problems, such as sea ice dynamics and traffic flow, extending its application to problems with moving boundaries. Given its simplicity and efficiency, RANG presents a viable option for training PINNs with mesh-free structured points, enabling its adoption in numerous physics-inspired applications. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yusongzhang1989/RANG.eyJ.

For analyzing stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to understand irreducible Markov processes, which can be applied to systems governed by random disturbances. In this study, we verify that stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations with discrete-event disorder are irreducible under specific conditions, thereby demonstrating that these systems maintain irreducibility for various applications, such as those involving random force or pure jump noise. Additionally, we establish that these systems have a single invariant measure and are ergodically maximal, meaning they exhibit ergodic behavior. Importantly, our findings encompass famous real-valued stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, as well as their hyperbolic and supercritical versions, which indicates that these systems remain irreducible even in the absence of imaginary components. Our study also includes an example illustrating the applicability of these results to systems with periodically modulated linear parts. In another example, we demonstrate that these results can be applied to systems with randomly changing linear parts that are not necessarily periodic, which in turn implies the ergodic behavior of systems with periodically changing nonlinear parts, as seen in the case of quadratically coupled complex Ginzburg-Landau equations. Overall, our findings provide a foundational understanding of the Markov process generated by the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations, which in turn enables researchers to analyze the ergodic behavior of these systems. In doing so, we utilize the spectral theory of transition operators and the decomposition theorem for Markov processes. Since these systems exhibit ergodic behavior, we discuss how to extend this behavior to solve certain partial differential equations, such as those involving the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, which may also include randomly changing coefficients and aspherical boundaries. Additionally, we outline potential future research directions in this area. These studies could involve examining the ergodic behavior of systems with periodically and randomly changing linear parts and pure jump noise, as well as those that couple quadratically. In doing so, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the ergodic behavior of these systems and clarify the interplay between their nonlinear and linear components. Furthermore, we hope to establish the ergodic behavior of these systems through the selection of appropriate Lyapunov functions. In doing so, we may be able to generalize our results to other stochastic systems, such as those described by the Stochastic Hamiltonian system, the Stochastic KdV equation, the Stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equation, the Stochastic wave equation, the Stochastic heat equation, the Stochastic Allen-Cahn equation

The success of Deep Learning methods in computer vision tasks has created a high demand for efficient and adaptable neural networks designed for point cloud processing. Due to the unique characteristics of their input, such as sparsity, variability, and regression challenges, current frameworks face substantial obstacles. This study addresses these issues by introducing a novel graph convolutional network, GCN2, which combines graphical and convolutional components. GCN2 employs an optimized graph construction method from dynamic graph networks to create a semi-implicit graph framework, thereby ensuring fast and seamless assembly of the graph within deep network training. The proposed graph construction method balances accuracy and computational efficiency by using a parameterized technique to determine the nearest neighbors for each node, thereby reducing computational complexity. The results of GCN2's performance in various point cloud processing tasks, such as semantic segmentation, oriented bounding box detection, and centered bounding box detection, demonstrate its superiority over alternative graph convolutional networks. As deep learning technologies advance, deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a crucial component in various AI applications. Nevertheless, research has uncovered a critical security threat called Trojan attack, which can enable backdoor access to DNN models without compromising their original performance. Traditionally, Trojan attacks have focused on compromising the trust of trustworthiness assessors through maliciously trained models. Existing approaches to detecting Trojan attacks typically rely on analyzing distorted or modified input data, which is not applicable to naturally occurring data. To address this issue, we propose a new approach to Trojan attacks, in which we exploit the semantic relationships between inputs and outputs in DNN models. Specifically, we employ a zero-watermark technique to hide semantic patterns within model weights and a detection algorithm that extracts and analyzes semantic representations from test data. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach, while preserving the original performance of DNN models, can effectively detect Trojan attacks with high accuracy across various attack types and configurations. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we also conducted a detailed comparison with traditional detection methods and achieved superior results in multiple scenarios. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI). Recent research suggests that incorporating attention mechanisms (AMs) into DNNs can significantly boost performance. However, the existing literature lacks thorough assessments of AMs on CSI-based localization. To fill this knowledge gap, we compared the effectiveness of various attention mechanisms for localization. Our experiments involved simulating room environments with mobility using ray-tracing and gathered CSI data from Bluetooth 5.1 devices. Notably, our findings indicate that attention can enhance the training efficiency of DNNs, specifically by reducing the required snapshots and training iterations. Moreover, attention is found to be beneficial when the signal power of CSI channels is low. Although attention mechanisms exhibit potential, they often fail to surpass conventional DNNs with double-layer DNNs (DLDN) in localization accuracy. Our work provides a comprehensive evaluation of attention mechanisms for CSI-based localization, offering valuable insights for practitioners. Ultimately, the choice of attention mechanism is depicted as being dependent on specific localization conditions. Code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Infotech-NUST/Attention_enhanced_wireless_localization.

In cubic bipartite graphs, an edge-tinting refers to a coloring of the edges where each pair of adjacent vertices receives the same color. The problem of determining if a given cubic bipartite graph can be edge-tinted has been proven to be polynomially solvable. However, we demonstrate that this is not the case for all cubic graphs by providing a counterexample. Moreover, we show that a special class of cubic perfect square-octahedral graphs cannot be edge-tinted if they contain specific subgraphs known as K_4^--saddle graphs. Additionally, we propose an algorithm to determine if a given cubic perfect square-octahedral graph can be edge-tinted. If it cannot, the algorithm identifies a K_4^--saddle graph that is part of the graph. If it can, the algorithm provides an edge-tinting. All of our results and findings are documented in this article. Finally, we conjecture that a given cubic perfect square-octahedral graph can be edge-tinted if it does not contain any K_4^--saddle graphs. If this conjecture is true, it would allow us to develop a polynomial-time algorithm for determining if a given such graph can be edge-tinted. The article also discusses the relationship between this problem and other well-known graph coloring issues. The algorithms proposed in this article use techniques from graph homology and Betti number analysis. The idea of K_4^--saddle graphs and edge-tinting was first presented in the authors' previous paper and is further developed here with new findings. The concept of K_4^--saddle graphs can be seen as a special case of K_4^-saddle graphs, with the difference being the position of their vertices. The question of determining if a given K_4^-saddle graph is part of a given cubic perfect square-octahedral graph is shown to be solvable in polynomial time. This is achieved by projecting the graph's vertices onto their corresponding coordinates and examining the resulting images for signs that indicate the presence of a K_4^-saddle graph. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to rely on a local installation to utilize its full range of features. Despite being available in open-source form, accessing these features required significant technical expertise. To address this limitation, we have developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based user interface that makes COPASI's tools easily accessible to a broader audience within a web browser. Built with R using four interdependent packages, ShinyCOPASI allows users to import, run, and analyze COPASI models through a simple and intuitive web interface. It offers a range of functional tools, including model validation, parameter estimation, equilibrium and pathway analysis, and single-trajectory simulations, among others. To ensure compatibility with the widest possible range of models, ShinyCOPASI includes a model conversion function, enabling users to upload and analyze models in multiple formats. Furthermore, our web application includes a comprehensive guide with Frequently Asked Questions to assist users who are new to COPASI or biochemistry modeling in general. Achieving accuracy in scientific predictions is a crucial challenge for researchers in the field of predictive modeling. One major area of uncertainty arises from incomplete knowledge represented as ambiguity in the prediction outcome. To address this ambiguity, researchers use various techniques such as ambiguity-reducing probabilistic neural networks to generate more precise forecasts. However, the efficacy of these methods is heavily influenced by the performance metric used to evaluate them. In this study, we provide an exhaustive review of techniques employed to quantify ambiguity in machine learning-based prediction, alongside a comprehensive comparison of six distinct metrics, including PM2K and PofM K-entropy on simulated and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark to facilitate reproducibility of our findings. Our analysis shows that PM2K and PofM K-entropy achieve superior performance compared to other metrics in identifying the optimal prediction threshold and evaluating model generality, alongside providing unique benefits. We also propose a novel metric called specific ambiguity that complements existing ambiguity measures. Our work has potential implications for researchers and practitioners to select suitable metrics for practical applications. The datasets, code, and NNM2K implementation for this study are publicly available at https://github.com/fortuitousAI/AmbiguityQuantification. Additionally, the results have been posted on the AIVault data repository at https://aivault.org/index.php/SVA-2023-04.04.003. When dealing with a limit case, traditional Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) methods may result in an infinite number of iterations, which is unacceptable for applications such as large-scale Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). To address this, researchers have introduced modifications to the Quadratic Programming (QP) formula and algorithms such as Full Policy Iteration (FI) with a quadratic objective function. However, these modifications require computing a GMRES approximation at each iteration, which can be costly. To improve performance, we have developed an iterative scheme that generates a sequence of feasible policies without requiring GMRES approximations, starting from any full policy. Each iteration consists of two parts: first, a GMRES approximation is obtained, and then the policy is updated. We prove that this method converges to the first order optimal policy when using the first GMRES approximation and offer further optimizations. Moreover, we present a novel direction of thought - imposing a constraint on the shift in policy - and demonstrate its benefits through numerical examples. Our proposed method has a lower computational cost compared to existing algorithms and outperforms them in terms of efficiency, especially for large-scale MDPs. Computer experiments often involve running expensive simulations with various scenario assumptions, but it's difficult to determine which assumptions have the greatest impact, which is known as the inverse problem. By treating simulation outputs as time series data and employing a non-parametric approach in combination with techniques for analyzing patterns and trends, we are able to identify simulation inputs that significantly affect output patterns. This new method, known as High Dimensional Projected Extreme Coordinate Descent, enables efficient identification of multiple input variables driving distinct output patterns in large-scale simulation runs. Our approach significantly outperforms other methods established in the literature, as demonstrated by our analysis of 12 case studies from diverse fields. This research was facilitated by an open-source software framework, PyTSE, which enables the efficient calculation of multiple extreme coordinates. Furthermore, PyTSE includes an implementation of other established methods for resolving the inverse problem, allowing for a comprehensive comparison of these techniques. Our study also highlights the importance of projecting high-dimensional input spaces onto smaller dimensions using techniques like clustering or classical factorial projections. By resolving the inverse problem in this way, we are able to identify key output patterns and the corresponding input variables driving these patterns. This research was presented at three conferences: The 24th Annual Conference of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM), the 28th Conference of the International Society on Industrial and Applied Mathematics on Uncertainty Quantification (ISIUQ), and the 15th Annual Conference of the Conference on Uncertainty in Design (CID). This paper is a revised version of our original paper. Since the conferences listed above were held after the submission of our paper to this journal, we have updated it to include new examples and now present new results demonstrating the efficiency of MCET in handling multi-dimensional output data. This research was also presented at the 23rd SIAM Conference on Uncertainty Quantification. To improve the robustness of computer systems to data corruption, a concept called resilient learning has emerged, focusing on developing accurate models even when trained on unreliable data. This study adds to that effort by exploring how to enhance the robustness of neural networks through a simple yet effective technique - the use of regional queries. However, the conditions under which this approach can contribute to resilient learning, particularly when dealing with non-adversarial data corruption, have not been clearly identified. This research therefore investigates how the structure of the corruption, the location of the corrupted data, and the type of loss function interact to impact the effectiveness of regional queries in resilient learning. In particular, it is discovered that regional queries can significantly aid learning under specific circumstances but are generally unhelpful in other situations. Specifically, regional queries are found to be beneficial when the corruption follows a specific pattern but is unknown in its specific location, a scenario which is distinct from the case where the corruption is random and known across the entire dataset. This study establishes that regional queries can be useful in the latter situation as well, providing insights into when such queries might be advantageous. It is demonstrated that regional queries can be integrated into the SGD optimization process in a way that is equitable and takes into account the varying levels of reliability across different data samples, in contrast to earlier studies. The introduction of regional queries is shown to not only enhance the accuracy of models but also their robustness, in particular when certain loss functions are employed and the data corruption is unknown. Furthermore, the incorporation of regional queries is found to be compatible with existing robust learning techniques and can even further improve the robustness of models when combined with other methods. Finally, this study verifies that regional queries can be effectively applied to problems involving video data by implementing a robust learning experiment using the Corrupted-Cinema dataset, which was specifically created for this purpose. This study provides a preliminary examination of modifications to jet fragmentation in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV using data from the CMS detector. It focuses on high-pT jets associated with isolated photons, which are less susceptible to modifications caused by the medium and collective effects within it. By comparing the fragmentation functions and the average number of sub-jets in jet-photons between Pb-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions, it was found that there are noticeable alterations to jet fragmentation in the central region of Pb-Pb collisions. Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for this object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that it possesses remarkable proper motion, corresponding to over 1200 years in the recent past, as evidenced by its large angular separation of 13.3 arcseconds. Additionally, its brightness has undergone substantial fluctuations over the past three years, while its WISE and ZTF photometry appear to be consistently representative of a ~5000K brown dwarf. Nevertheless, its spectral energy distribution, observed through Keck/MOSFIRE, can be accurately modeled by a photosphere characterized by temperatures of 3400K, nearly six times lower than its WISE-estimated temperature of 4600K. Its large proper motion suggests that it is likely not in an equatorial star formation zone but instead may be an unusually fast-moving sub-stellar object or extreme PMBD. Further analysis of its motion, using the Gaia DR3 data, indicates that it may be sharing a trajectory with nearby objects, including a ~7000K white dwarf, whose provenance is unclear but could be linked to the unusual properties of WISEA J153429.75-104303.3. This association raises the possibility that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 could be a novel type of astrometric double star, featuring the aforementioned object, along with the aforementioned white dwarf. It is also conceivable that during its rapid motion, the Gaia DR3 may have captured a rare image of a binary system, with WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 acting as a "mishap" that has enabled researchers to identify unusual celestial entities whose existence would have gone undetected through observations of this object in a single state. In light of these new findings, the most plausible hypothesis is that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 is an extreme parasitic brown dwarf with a temperature of ~3400K and a mass of ~0.021~M. This type of object is expected to be extremely rare, with a mass ratio of 0.6 to 0.9, and would likely have a much longer and more irregular motion, deviating from the expected smooth trajectory, as it is thought to be an outlier in the equatorial plane of a nearby star

We propose an innovative method to derive parton distribution functions from initial conditions at a high temperature, achieving this through an effective interpolation technique. This method employs D'Alembertian operator eigenfunctions to connect high and low temperature scenarios. In our approach, the evolution of parton distribution functions is encapsulated within a general operator equation, which can be solved through eigenmode analysis. Notably, our strategy allows the parton distribution functions to follow quasi-static dynamics at high temperatures, while still enabling matching with cold nucleus distribution functions at lower temperatures. Additionally, our proposal facilitates the continuation of parton distribution functions to higher and lower momenta without being hampered by ultraviolet and infrared divergences. To illustrate the efficacy of our method, we can use various tools such as machine learning algorithms or simplified assumptions about the parton distribution functions behavior in the high and low temperature scenarios to solve the parton distribution functions directly. We discuss one such possibility where we assume the parton distribution functions follow quasi-static dynamics at high temperatures and use neural network to learn the distribution functions directly without solving the operator equation. In another possibility, we assume the parton distribution functions can be expressed as a sum of eigenmodes and use D'Alembertian initial conditions to derive the parton distribution functions explicitly. We discuss how our method can be applied to preheat parton distribution functions, quark-gluon plasma properties, and study recombination at high and low temperatures. We outline future research directions enabled by our method. Finally, we point out future research tasks to completely derive all the parton distribution functions. We then demonstrate how our method can be applied to preheat parton distribution functions, quark-gluon plasma properties, and recombination at high and low temperatures through numerical calculations. Our results show that quasi-static parton distribution functions at high temperatures are different from cold nucleus parton distribution functions at lower temperatures. We outline future research directions to completely derive all parton distribution functions, especially for color-singlet and color-octet parton distribution functions. We then discuss how our method can be applied to preheat parton distribution functions, quark-gluon plasma properties, and recombination at high and low temperatures through numerical calculations based on simplified assumptions and further improve them in future research. We propose future research tasks to completely derive all parton distribution functions. We then demonstrate how our method can be applied to preheat parton distribution functions, quark-gluon plasma properties, and recombination at high and low temperatures through numerical calculations

Press-molded specimens of simulated Martian and lunar soil were fired at various temperatures to develop a base material for 3D printing on other planets. X-ray computed tomography was used to image samples at different stages, revealing how heat affected their structure and properties. As temperature increased, porosity decreased and strength improved, with the optimal sintering temperature found to be 1100-1200 degrees Celsius for both types of soil. However, strength varied depending on the type of sintering process - either reduction or oxidation - with reduced porosity but different mechanical behavior. Mechanical testing showed that samples from Martian simulations had more resistant compressive strengths and Young's modulus at higher temperatures, while those from lunar simulations demonstrated better tensile strength and Young's modulus at lower temperatures. These findings indicate that 3D printing on other planets should be done using reduced sintering temperatures to produce parts with optimal mechanical properties, taking into account the type of environment and soil used. Additionally, the use of atmospheric pressure and in situ materials could lead to better mechanical properties by limiting porosity, making it a viable technique for building structures on other planets. Since lunar simulations had better results in tensile strength and Young's modulus at lower temperatures, this process might be more beneficial for building structures on the Moon, while 3D printing under reduced pressure or vacuum could be the best approach for building structures on Mars. Furthermore, using elevated temperatures in a reducing environment improved mechanical properties, justifying the use of heat treatment in 3D printing on other planets. Based on these findings and to expand on previous research, a new theory on the relationship between structure, property, and processing has been developed, incorporating data from this and other relevant studies. By applying this proposed framework, manufacturers can select the most suitable building techniques and materials to meet specific performance goals in future Earth-based and space-related construction projects. In the future, using this theory and incorporating more variables, even more precise controls can be applied to build structures on other planets with optimal mechanical properties. By doing this, buildings on other planets can be engineered to withstand any changes in their structure resulting from the unique conditions of other planets, ensuring a safe and durable presence on other planets. Also, using this theory and incorporating more variables, even more relevant mechanical properties can be accurately predicted, such as fracture energy, creep resistance and thermal expansion. By doing this, buildings on other planets can be engineered to withstand any changes in their structure resulting from the unique conditions of other planets, ensuring a safe and durable presence on other planets

By comparing various methods for estimating star formation rates (SFR) in galaxies, we found that some formulas produce excessively high results. For example, using dust-corrected H$\alpha$ emission and a specific observation, we derived SFRs that were often higher than the galaxy's total mass converted into stars. This was resolved by employing a novel approach to fitting spectral energy distributions (SEDs) or by relying on line fluxes like Br$\gamma$ to estimate SFR. In this study, we used 54 galaxies from the M81* star-formation rate survey to compare different SFR estimation methods and identified Br$\gamma$ as a reliable indicator of star formation rates. Furthermore, we developed a new template set and presented revised observations for all 54 galaxies in the survey. Additionally, we conducted statistical analysis to evaluate the accuracy of various other SFR estimation methods. These include using strong emission lines like H$\alpha$, [OIII], and [NII], as well as artificial neural networks and empirical equations, to reconstruct the SFRs derived from photometric data. Our analysis revealed that some of these methods yield excessively high SFR estimates, comparable to those derived from Br$\gamma$ observation, suggesting that these techniques may also produce unreliable results. Consequently, we propose using Br$\gamma$ as a benchmark test for SFR estimation and provide recommendations for improving other methods. To facilitate future research, we published our template set in starlight, a public code for fitting SEDs. We also provided corrected fluxes for the 54 galaxies in the survey and added our analysis of other SFR estimation methods. Furthermore, we published a paper showing that some of these methods may also produce unreliable SFR estimates in edge-on galaxies. These include using [OIII] or [NII] emission alone to estimate SFR and employing artificial neural networks. Additionally, we found that using photometric data alone can also yield unreliable SFR estimates compared to those derived from Br$\gamma$ observation. This led us to propose additional constraints based on galaxy orientation and other properties to improve the accuracy of SFR estimation. To make our results and data available to the public, we published them in https://git.lna.observationalastronomy.net/AnaGarcia10/SFR_fails/-/tree/master. This includes the data, the Python code for our analysis and the template set in starlight. We have also made pseudocoded available at https://git.lna.observationalastronomy.net/AnaGarcia

Species distribution analysis is a key aspect of ecological research that has been extensively single-species focus but is now being used for multi-species studies due to the advancements in statistical methods and software availability. Our R package, spOccupancy, offers a comprehensive approach to fitting and evaluating various types of spatial occupancy models for both individual and combined species studies. Key features of spOccupancy include the capability to estimate model parameters, calculate uncertainty, integrate multiple species occurence models, and identify important covariate factors, in addition to offering a range of simulation options to assess model performance and reliability. This guide provides a step-by-step introduction to using spOccupancy for single-species and combined species research, as well as utility functions to assist in data import, model selection, and model checking processes. Furthermore, spOccupancy is designed with user friendliness in mind, offering a simple and intuitive interface to utilize the fundamental simulation, model estimation, and post-processing tools. This guide also includes case studies on single-species and multi-species occurence models, along with a detailed examination of the theoretical underpinnings of occupancy modeling. Lastly, we present a comparative analysis of species distribution models, including those offered by spOccupancy and well-established software such as unmarked, to illustrate the diverse range of distribution models that can be fit with spOccupancy. Ultimately, spOccupancy is intended to support and supplement existing software while providing a unified approach to integrating single and multi-species occurence models. To establish a reliable model of type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) spectral evolution, 
we must consider both temporal variations across the spectrum and time-dependent 
shifts in wavelength. Most existing quantum mechanical models struggle to account 
for the complex observations, especially the time-dependent spectral shifts which 
are as important as the radial velocity in understanding SNe Ia evolution. In this 
research, we use a stochastic autoencoder to model the temporal series of spectra 
with built-in time-gating and spectral shift mechanisms. By introducing an extra 
gating module, our approach can prioritize the extraction of temporal features, 
spectral features, and time-dependent shift information from the spectral data. 
By back-projecting the encoded variables, we can also determine the critical phase 
of SNe Ia evolution and employ the extracted features to distinguish between SNe Ia 
and other astronomical phenomena. Our artificial neural network model is compared 
to the widely used quantum mechanical models through both synthetic and real data 
tests, revealing its superiority in extracting relevant features from the spectral 
temporal series and its potential to be integrated with existing phyiscal models to 
further improve our understanding of SNe Ia evolution. Additionally, our model is 
showed to provide accurate predictions of time-dependent shift trajectories, 
confirming its potential to be a useful complement in the deep learning-based 
classification of SNe Ia phenotypes. Our research provides an innovative approach 
to extracting key features from the spectral temporal series of SNe Ia, as well as 
a reliable model of the radial motion of SNe Ia ejecta across phase. Our findings 
also offer an efficient and simple way to incorporate the time-dependent shift 
information of SNe Ia into quantum mechanical models to further improve their 
accuracy and precision. Our research code is publicly available at https://github.com/tzhuang621/SNAEAE. Our research has significant practical implications for the understanding and classification of SNe Ia based on spectral observations, as well as the development of more accurate quantum mechanical models that take into account the time-dependent shift information of SNe Ia ejecta across phase. Additionally, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of stochastic autoencoders in modeling temporal series and has significant practical implications for the deep learning-based classification of SNe Ia phenotypes. Our research has also successfully integrated the time-gating and spectral shift mechanisms of SNe Ia evolution, offering an innovative approach to extracting key features from the spectral temporal series of SNe I

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming geometrical relationships between individuals may provide a more accurate representation of the spread, akin to modeling infections within spatially organized environments. Hypergraphs capture these connections by encapsulating higher-order interactions within the inherent structure of the graphed relationships. Our research explores the transmission of epidemics within hypergraphs, examining the critical thresholds at which the disease spreads through the network. Through an inversion of the spectral graph operator, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the extinction of the epidemic, and subsequently, the asymptotic critical threshold as the hypergraph doubles in connectivity. Additionally, we apply this method to investigate the epidemic dynamics within two specific hypergraphs: hypercubes and complete k-partite hypergraphs. In the case of the cube, we show that a simplified approximation of the spectral limit, derived from the generalized Lubotzky-Weisfelter theorem, is asymptotically equivalent to the exact critical threshold as the dimensionality of the cube increases. For the complete k-partite hypergraph, we demonstrate that the spectral limit achieves an exact match with the asymptotic critical threshold, and further, that this value represents a generalized universality for all hypergraphs with equally distributed vertex degrees. The methodology employed in this research is expected to contribute to future investigations in the field. All of the code used to generate the figures in this paper may be found at the link: https://github.com/dsustudio/Hypergraph_Epidemic_Critical_Thresholds.ddd. Moreover, an interactive visualization of the figures may be accessed at the link: https://dsu-studio.github.io/Hypergraph_Epidemic_Critical_Thresholds/index.html.

A particular focus is given to computing Euler-Roch numbers via the Gauß-Bonnet theorem, a strategy initially proposed by Suárez in the context of compact Kähler manifolds. This method's feasibility depends on the convexity of the hypersurface curvature, a property that remains unaltered under algebraic transformations. This paper's main contribution involves establishing connections between convex topology and the notion of log-terminal log canonical pairs. These connections are then leveraged to prove that Euler-Roch numbers for such pairs always equal zero. A related result is also derived for pairs with log canonical singularities. A key step in achieving this involves extending the evidence for dimension two to a general theorem for all dimensions greater than two. Furthermore, this proof relies on an interpretation of Euler-Roch numbers as measures of the pair's hyperbolity, a concept that decayed to zero in the two-dimensional case. A Gauß-Bonnet theorem for complex manifolds with an algebraic boundary would provide a substantial proof for the Euler-Roch theorem's positivity statement.
