A statistical approach is presented to analyze market trends from transaction records, including the date, price, and quantity of shares sold. A novel trend analysis metric is introduced, leveraging the concept of dissimilar trend sets, to investigate the influence of future events on past market trends. Studies from the NASDAQ transactions (2001-2019) reveal that major global events like the 9/11 attacks and the 2008 financial crisis had a significant impact on the trends, leading to distinct changes in market behavior compared to usual trading patterns. To quantify the effect of future events, a metric called Dissimilar Trend Set Influence (DTSI) is developed, measuring the importance of each event by analyzing its impact on future trends. As the algorithm generates future prices, it provides a basis for evaluating event influence. A comparison of the new approach with existing linear and nonlinear time series analysis methods using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) confirmed its effectiveness in predicting future trends. A comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, including statistical testing and unsupervised learning techniques, demonstrated its ability to detect and analyze event influences. A critical examination of the method and future research directions are also presented. Software and data used in the study are available for public access at the link. Several earlier studies used gradient backpropagation to train spiking neural networks, but they failed to consider the class of neural encodings that are most suitable for biological brains. A novel neural network called the spiking neural tensor network has been introduced, which allows for deep spatio-temporal learning using the white interior-point gradient method. In our research, we tested this learning method on four different biological brain-inspired spiking neural network architectures, demonstrating its effectiveness for sequence learning tasks. Our experiments showed that the proposed method outperformed traditional deep neural networks and other state-of-the-art spiking neural networks, while also maintaining biologically feasible parameters. For example, our model was able to learn important sequence features using 0.04 discrete time steps over the course of 150ms. A significant aspect of our study is that we explored the actual computational performance of our model, as well as its potential hardware implementation. Our findings indicate that the proposed model could achieve a 10 to 100 times faster inference speed compared to the best previous spiking neural networks. A further study of the generated spikes provided evidence of the significant role that temporal coding plays in the learned patterns. Our model, including the corresponding source code, is now made available for other researchers to study and apply the proposed approach. It is possible that the generated neural networks, with their other notable features, could be a suitable candidate for simulating specific aspects of biological brain function. Our study offers a new perspective on the field of spiking neural networks, which up to now has primarily focused on motor control applications. We believe that our work has the potential to stimulate new research in this area, particularly regarding the theoretical understanding of spiking neural networks and their relationship to biological brains. Moreover, our study is a first step towards developing neural networks that not only imitate but also match the capabilities of biological brains. The Riemann Hypothesis, a conjecture introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, states that the critical zeta function has non-zero values at all natural numbers. This article presents a new proof of a lesser known aspect, the Twin Prime Hypothesis, which stems from Riemann's Hypothesis. The Twin Prime Hypothesis proposes that there are infinitely many pairs of prime numbers with a difference of one. The article starts with a fundamental concept, the prime counting function, and explores its relationship with the zeta function. Then, it develops a crucial theorem, which demonstrates that the ratio of the prime counting functions for consecutive arguments approaches one as the upper limit approaches infinity. The Twin Prime Hypothesis can be derived from the assumption that this ratio remains close to one for large upper limits, which is itself a consequence of the Riemann Hypothesis. Building on this proof, the article derives mathematical expressions for key concepts such as the distribution of prime numbers and the Chebyshev function, and presents analytical solutions for these expressions. Finally, the article analyzes a particular function that arises from the division of the zeta function by the squared prime counting function, and shows that its first derivative meets specific criteria, ultimately leading to the derivation of the Twin Prime Hypothesis. This new proof, in addition to confirming the accuracy of Riemann's Hypothesis for all natural numbers up to a very large number, also provides a precise bound on the location of the first non-real critical zeta function zero. The article concludes by extending the Riemann Hypothesis to the Langevin function, which is closely related to the zeta function. The calculations in this article were performed using the mathematical software package Maple. A companion document provides the complete Maple code for these computations. The article also includes various property theorems, and analyzes the infinite prime triplets and their distribution. Furthermore, it derives the Chebyshev function and the prime counting function, and presents new expressions for these functions. The article then explores the behavior of certain infinite sums and provides new expressions for them. Finally, the article is supplemented by several additional theorems and analyses. The Riemann Hypothesis is not only crucial for confirming the Twin Prime Hypothesis but it is also closely related to other significant problems in number theory, such as the prime number theorem and the distribution of prime numbers. Pessimism is measured by the difference between the expected outcome under the best treatment strategy and the expected outcome under the worst treatment strategy. Building on theoretical frameworks since the late 2010s, numerous studies have established criteria for validating new learning methods. In this research, we introduce a novel theoretical framework tailored to learning in dynamic regimes. Our findings also provide a general validation for Bayesian learning methods. To illustrate the practical usefulness of our research, we conducted an experiment in the anesthesia field using data from 1,834 patients. The outcome of the study showed that the Bayesian learning method led to better clinical practices when compared to a conservative approach. Our proposed framework, Complementarily Learning for Salient Object Detection, tackles this challenge by employing a unique multi-context learning approach that integrates spatial and channel information to enhance feature extraction. This method comprises two main components: Contextual Block and Self-Occlusion block. The Contextual Block harnesses the context of different scales through contextual activation function to gather global spatial features, while the Self-Occlusion block incorporates self-occlusion information to capture complex object patterns. By combining these blocks with a bi-directional fusion strategy, our network outperforms state-of-the-art models on several public datasets and surpasses performance even when trained with ground-truth depth maps. This performance milestone represents a significant achievement in salient object detection. Our approach combined a BERT-based model pre-trained on Aggressive-Neutral tweets with a SVM classifier trained on labels provided by human annotators. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively employed in radiology for diagnosing tissue abnormalities, also providing information about tissue density and composition. Most CT systems produce images using multiple X-ray sources with varying energies. However, currently used reconstruction methods ignore this multi-source information, directly utilizing scanned projections to form polyenergetic X-rays. This approach can lead to inaccurate dual-energy (DE) image and material composition results. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a non-convex variational framework that jointly handles polyenergetic X-ray data, noise reduction, and material decomposition. Formulated as an optimization problem with constrained and unconstrained variants, this framework relies on iterative Total Variation regularization to process noisy data and a forward-simultaneous iterative reconstruction technique to accurately interpret multi-source CT data. Experiments with both simulated and genuine CT data confirm the proposed framework's effectiveness in producing high-quality dual-energy and material composition images even with corrupted data. Additionally, results indicate that incorporating noise reduction enhances image quality, particularly visible noise reduction in actual data. Lastly, comparisons with conventional filtered-backprojection and iterative reconstruction techniques demonstrate the proposed framework's superior performance. These findings validate the introduced framework as a reliable standard for processing CT data, addressing its inherent inaccuracies and producing high-quality dual-energy and material composition images. Additionally, this framework may also be utilized for single-isotope CT data, simply omitting the dual-energy and decomposition components. With this adaptability in mind, the introduced framework presents a more comprehensive approach to CT reconstruction. Furthermore, the study also conducted experiments to assess the influence of various numerical parameters on the reconstructed results, providing these findings in supplementary documents. Additionally, the study also proposed and conducted actual CT data acquisitions using the specially designed 'CT-Infinity' protocol to produce high-quality dual-energy and material composition images, presenting these findings in supplementary documents. These experiments involved shooting CT data through human subjects using the 'CT-Infinity' protocol for superior results. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and language-specific dictionaries. To overcome these obstacles, we concentrate on developing methods for single-shot data generation and dictionary learning. From a given handwritten page, our approach produces a collection of single-word sentences by assuming them to be compositional, meaning they consist of sequences of constituent parts such as prefixes, domains, suffixes, and letters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on the datasets "NLP-UA Text" and "AMT-Hilltop", which showcase notable performance enhancements compared to existing techniques. Notably, our results reveal a significant boost of up to 14 Character Error Rates with only 25% fewer annotations. We also introduce a new dataset, "NLP-UA Text", specifically designed to facilitate the development of compositional HTR models. Additionally, we provide a detailed evaluation of the "AMT-Hilltop" dataset, which consists of 13,610 pages of handwritten text collected through crowdsourcing. We further present a new word-sentence decomposition model based on Hidden Markov Models, making our code available at https://github.com/darthvader611/HTR_Composition. We successfully achieved training and testing on real-world data without any prior knowledge of the language, achieving a 12 Character Error Rates on the "NLP-UA Text" dataset. We also demonstrated that through pre-training on synthetic data generated using our approach, we could achieve a 10 error rate margin on real-world data. Recent advances have focused on theoretically quantifying the reliability of machine learning models, particularly those operating under uncertain conditions. This paper contributes to that effort by investigating the theoretical reliability of Bayesian learning frameworks that take into account constraints on model parameters with probabilistic guarantees. Our study considers two approaches: the first relies on the concept of probabilistic logic, while the second uses the reliability of probabilistic circuits. The major contribution of this paper lies in establishing the relationship between these two methods and identifying the consequences of relaxing the underlying constraints in the context of probabilistic logic. Additionally, we demonstrate that evaluating certain constraints in the context of probabilistic logic is a computationally intractable problem, while proposing a practical solution involving constraint programming. Furthermore, we show that propagating uncertainty over model outputs has promising applications in systems such as credit approval and travel planning, while highlighting the practical limitations and potential areas of improvement for theoretical reliability analysis. Lastly, we establish that approximating the confidence of predictive distributions can be achieved with high precision using few sample points, although this precision comes at a significant computational cost in practice. The paper concludes by proposing various directions for future research in theoretical reliability analysis. A permanent current can be established in a wavefunction when there is a uniform acceleration in a potential that varies linearly with position, leading to a moving oscillatory pattern over time. This moving oscillatory pattern is commonly referred to as Bloch oscillations. In this review, we will examine the phenomenon of Bloch oscillations within the context of Bose-Einstein condensates, primarily those occurring in optical lattices. A detailed analysis is provided, incorporating theoretical models and simulations, to explore the interplay between oscillations and other wavefunction features, such as sound waves and solitons. The review will also discuss observations of Bloch oscillations in superfluids, drawing from both numerical and experimental results in the field. In particular, we will examine case studies involving helium-3 in magnetic fields and Bose-Einstein condensates of Rydberg atoms. Finally, we will review the current state of research on Bloch oscillations in superfluids, identifying areas where further investigation is needed. These areas include the use of higher-dimensional lattices, the observation of oscillations in fermionic condensates, and the establishment of connections between Bloch oscillations and other phenomena in condensed matter systems. It is hoped that this review will facilitate new areas of exploration within the field of superfluids. A comprehensive list of references is included to support this review. It is expected that readers will gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between wavefunction features in accelerated Bose-Einstein condensates through the analysis presented here. Additionally, we anticipate that this review will illustrate the versatility of optical lattices as tools for investigating fundamental phenomena in condensed matter systems. A distinctive aspect of this review is that it does not provide an in-depth examination of a particular theoretical model or experimental technique, but rather offers an exhaustive exploration of the application of a particular concept, namely Bloch oscillations, within the context of Bose-Einstein condensates and fermionic and spinodics. It is our hope that this review will serve as a comprehensive introduction to the application of Bloch oscillations in superfluids, showcasing their potential to illuminate fundamental principles in the field through simulations and experiments. Developing accurate models for all steps in the photoexcited process is crucial to fully
understand the complex behavior observed in high-fluence X-ray absorption edge (XAE) spectra.
In this study, we present a simplified rate-based model for electron population dynamics
that is an extension of initial models proposed by other researchers. Our analysis is specific
to 3d transition metal compounds and includes confinement effects, residual lattice effects
and core-hole decay in the final step. We apply our model to the case of nickel in a oxide
material, using a mean-field approximation to calculate time-dependent system properties.
Our results for the modulations in the XAE signal around the absorption edge match experimental
data, demonstrating the significance of electron correlations and lattice effects in this
regime. Additionally, we discuss how our model can be applied to other systems to
interpret experimental results. Our analysis code is open-sourced for community use. It
enables the calculation of time-dependent electron populations for any 3d transition metal
in any crystal structure via a web-based interface. In the long term, we envision it to be
integrated into more comprehensive ab-initio codes. Our model positions the XAE signal as
a sensitive probe of electron correlations in strongly interacting metals. Our analysis
also points out the limitations of linear-scale density functional theory in describing
non-linear effects observed in high-fluence XAE spectra, explicitly demonstrating the
need for non-linear theories to explain them properly. Conversely, our results indicate
that nonlinear theories can outperform density functional theory in explaining certain
experimental results. Our model is now available at https://dxwatch.pythonanywhere.com. We
invite the community to test our model by providing and comparing their own calculations
with available experimental results. In the future, we intend to expand our model so that
it can be applied to elements beyond 3d transition metals and to develop more sophisticated
ab-initio models that describe all steps in the photoexcited process. These future models
will likely require more sophisticated computational resources to accurately describe
all interacting components in the system. Our model serves as a starting point, connecting
electron population dynamics to observed modulations in the XAE signal around the absorption edge. It
reveals that certain phenomena, previously not fully understood in experiments, can be
inently explained by electron correlations and lattice effects. Our results suggest a
distinct boundary between linear and nonlinear behaviors in XAE spectra, corresponding to
different fluences of photon absorption.

Achieved through the innovative use of a Gm-Rs process-driven temperature extraction technique and a reference voltage generator capable of 80ppm accuracy, this design excels with a measurement area of 0.033mm^2 and features a power consumption of 1.5μW at 0.6V, alongside a power efficiency of 14.6nJ per conversion at 1.8V. This pioneering system enables the reliable measurement of microcontroller temperatures in diverse applications, such as ultra-low power systems, to a level of precision that was previously achievable only through external diode temperature sensors. This capability is exemplified by a demonstration in which the system accurately measures the temperature of an AVR microcontroller attached to the sensitive detector's signal output. This remarkable achievement marks the first known instance of a single CMOS circuit capable of temperature measurement across such a broad voltage range. We introduce a novel technique, the Distorted Resolvent method, to construct Nash equilibria in various game-theoretic applications. This method leverages the properties of the Nash equilibrium-like solution concept, the Distorted Resolvent, which outperforms traditional perturbation techniques. By utilizing the Distorted Resolvent, we develop local and global analysis tools that can be applied to a broad range of situations, including infinite and finite games, as long as they meet specific criteria. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate the efficiency of the Distorted Resolvent method in constructing accurate Nash equilibrium approximations. Furthermore, we show that this method can be efficiently implemented when the games it originates from have a particular structure. We anticipate that the Distorted Resolvent method will serve as a vital tool in contemporary game theory and dynamical systems. Additionally, we believe that it will contribute to the development of novel approaches in both fields. of training images has a notable impact on the development of property-based PTs

To address this challenge, we present a novel approach called reversible concealment, which utilizes learned probability distributions to protect images from forensic analysis through undetectable modifications. To underpin this concept, we establish a theoretical framework based on mutual information to quantify the effects of concealment on revealed features. Experimental investigations into reversible concealment are conducted within the context of diffusion model-based image processing, where we compare the performance of traditional and neural network-based approaches, the latter drawing on a Bayesian framework. While traditional approaches may excise modified regions to maintain consistency, this can lead to noticeable gaps in the reconstructed images. In contrast, we propose an algorithm that integrates Bayesian sampling and RNS-based reconstruction to maintain image quality. Experimental results verify the superiority of the proposed method, which outperforms the competitor in terms of performance and visual quality. Solar regions with extreme magnetic fields, known as bright spots, are characterized by a high rate of energy conversion, which can be attributed to their distinct two-part distributions of magnetic field strengths. 

 1. The weak-field portion adheres to statistical noise, while
 2. the strong-field portion exhibits a pattern of power decrease at a rate of d^(-5), consistent with the predictions of non-potential field models. 

  Our analysis of a microwatt bright spot, as observed by the SOLIS project, yields a power spectrum that supports the existence of two distinct areas of magnetic field distribution. From this analysis, we derive essential parameters, including the separation between these two parts (approximately 100 Gauss), the strength of the strong-field area's magnetic field (around 1500 Gauss), and the coefficient of the power decrease (approximately 2.6), all of which show notable consistency with previous studies of bright spots. Additionally, we find that the areas of the weak and strong-field distributions are, respectively, 1000 to 3000 times and 20 to 50 times larger than those observed in a typical granule. We hypothesize that bright spots may serve as a primary site for the heat loss that mitigates the solar atmosphere's temperature drop. We recognize that further research is necessary not only to validate our findings but also to gain a deeper understanding of the unique solar structures known as bright spots. We propose the use of future telescopes, such as the ELT, to investigate the general characteristics of bright spots, as well as their impacts on the solar surface and the overall energy balance of the Sun. In brain tissue, the regulation of substance distribution is essential, with excessive accumulation indicating abnormal conditions, such as brain disorders or drug overdoses, that can lead to cell damage. With its versatile structure, our model can be applied to various brain disorders, providing a general framework for understanding substance regulation and addressing potential shortages or imbalances in brain tissues. Modern single-image deblurring methods rely heavily on clear image datasets for training, 
which creates a discrepancy between blurred images and real-world deblurred images.
To address this limitation, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes a pseudoblur 
generator to incorporate knowledge from motion-blurred images.
By cross-training on paired blurry-nonblurry image pairs, the pseudoblur generator 
learns to generate realistic blur patterns, including those caused by human and scene 
movement, which are often difficult to simulate synthetically.
This unique feature enables our approach to better tackle a broader range of blur 
patterns, particularly those resulting from non-stationary objects.
Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method, 
especially when dealing with deblurring long-lasting motion and mixed blur patterns. 
Although computationally efficient, our method also achieves state-of-the-art performance 
when evaluation metrics such as PSNR and SSIM are used to measure accuracy. 
Furthermore, qualitative analysis confirms the ability of our approach to remove 
artifacts and achieve sharp, natural-looking images.

Deep Learning's extension into graph-based datasets led to the development of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), which are widely used today. GCNNs mimic the principles of classical convolution operations to process graph-structured data. The graph convolutional operation's mathematics was initially unclear, hindering a deeper understanding of the network. This work proposes a new matched filtering approach to elucidate the graph convolutional operation, revealing it as an application of spectral convolution to x-ray transforms of the input graphs. The proposed method illustrates how GCNNs can effectively learn high-level graph properties through the translation of graph-structured data into the x-ray domain. The matched filtering approach provides a unified understanding of various graph convolutional operations, such as spatial and multi-headed graph convolution operations. The method allows for the equivalent representation of GCNNs using the Fourier domain and reveals the graph parameterization's influence on the graph convolutional operation. The derived insights enable the creation of simplified synthetic graph datasets that challenge GCNNs to effectively capture high-level graph properties. The datasets, called 'forests', challenge GCNNs to emerge from the graph domain, revealing their limitations to capture high-level graph properties. The analysis demonstrates that forest datasets can be successfully handled by GCNNs with an added Fourier domain pass or with an extended training period. The proposed matched filtering approach offers a new perspective on GCNNs and enables the continued use of these networks to process graph-structured data. The derived insights may also contribute to the development of future GCNN variants. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. We examine the feasibility of discrete gauge symmetries in theories involving bosonic string vacua, specifically in scenarios where D-branes give rise to non-abelian discrete symmetries in line with stringy considerations. To understand the implications of open string states, we establish restrictions on the spectrum resulting from stringy interactions, emphasizing the difference between reversible and non-reversible symmetries. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that discrete gauge symmetries in string theory contexts are inherently dimpled, a notion we justify through a simplified example in the context of bosonic string compactifications. Furthermore, our study reveals that, in string theoretical settings, any accrued discrete gauge symmetries are contingent upon supersymmetry, a requirement we expect would also apply to theories constructed from state spectra alone. Additionally, our investigation into non-reversible symmetries yields insights into the potential constraints such symmetries impose on the spectrum, potentially leading to new theoretical developments in the field. In a related context, we explore the possibility of discrete non-invertible symmetries arising from stringy 3-form states, discovering that these symmetries are subject to constraints equivalent to those of stringy 't Hooft operators. Finally, our study establishes that any discrete gauge symmetries in string theory are diminished by stringy crossings, a phenomenon we illustrate through a simple example. Lastly, we speculate that discrete gauge symmetories in string theory may be entirely eradicated by stringy crossings, a possibility we expect would hold true for non-reversible symmetries as well. In a supplemental analysis, we examine the phenomenon of stringy dimpling in the presence of fundamental type IIA D-branes, determining that any resultant non-abelian discrete symmetries are accompanied by fundamental strings, a consequence of the Stone-Von Neumann theorem. Furthermore, our study reveals that the stringy dimpling giving rise to non-abelian discrete symmetries in this context is distinct from the one generated by NS5-branes, a distinction we expect would also apply to theories constructed from state spectra alone. Finally, our investigation makes connections between fundamental strings, 1-form states, and p-form states in type IIA string theory, ultimately demonstrating that the dimpling phenomenon can be reversed through the addition of NS5-branes, a distinction we anticipate would also be reflected in theories constructed from state spectra alone. Our research demonstrates that if a graph can be recognized with a two-way logarithmic distance, it can be recognized in polynomial time on a symmetric network, which implies it can be recognized with a quadratic time on an unordered network and in linear time on an ordered network, all under the same complexity constraints. This leads to the discovery that if a graph can be recognized with a two-way logarithmic distance, it can be recognized in polynomial time on a symmetric network, specifically when the network's degree is bounded by O(n^k) for any constant k. Furthermore, our study shows that if a graph can be recognized with a two-way logarithmic distance, it can be recognized in polynomial time on a symmetric network with the specific property that each node's children are far apart from each other. These findings demonstrate that the space requirements of a graph's recognition can be translated into polynomial time constraints on its symmetric network representations, depending on specific geometric constraints. This framework combined propeller-like information propagation with optical flow-based feature alignment to gather spatially distinct information. However, the original method had its limitations in handling motion patterns and the incorporation of teacher-student learning. To overcome these shortcomings, a refined approach called BasicVSR++ has been developed, featuring a more effective teacher model with aligned propagation and a revised student model with improved alignment mechanisms. The teacher model utilizes more efficient 3D corral propagation and asynchronized synchronous alignment to facilitate the learning process. Conversely, the revised student model utilizes alternative alignment mechanisms such as PFT and CFA in addition to reducing the parameter count of its counterpart. Experimental analysis of BasicVSR++ reveals its ability to produce superior results, particularly at intermediate scales, when compared to its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. This refinement further solidifies the reliability of teacher-student learning in the field of video super-resolution. The proposed model achieved top-notch performance in various benchmark tests and demonstrated efficient computational complexity, making it a suitable choice for practical use. The code for this model is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IngeMinho/BasicVSR++.yv3.0.0.0.0.0.py. It has been successfully used in the validation phase. The results of our research have been uploaded to the ECCV conference website. When employing teacher-student learning with aligned propagation, it is crucial to select appropriate alignment mechanisms to achieve the best possible results. To address this challenge, different alignment mechanisms including PFA, CFA, PFT, and CFT have been evaluated and compared to determine their relative effectiveness. The integration of BasicVSR++ into the test pipeline demonstrated its ability to produce superior results, particularly at intermediate scales, when compared to its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. The intermediate scale is where the majority of visible videos reside. The use of BasicVSR++ resulted in a significant improvement in the PSNR and SSIM metrics at this scale, outperforming its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. Furthermore, the computational complexity of BasicVRS+ was evaluated and demonstrated to be much lower than its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches, making it a highly efficient model. The efficiency of BasicVRS+ was confirmed through the analysis of its parameter count and FLOPs count, revealing its superior performance in this regard.

In order to prevent destructive interference in multi-task reinforcement learning, we suggest learning independent modules for each task. Using a simple grid-world example, we observe that model-based multi-task reinforcement learning often suffers from destructive interference and that using independent policy representations can prevent this issue. Additionally, we propose a method to select the most beneficial tasks for each new situation and demonstrate that using this approach when training a multi-task State-Action Value function Approximation (SAVMA) agent can improve performance by a large degree compared to traditional multi-task reinforcement learning methods. Finally, we observe that the benefits of training separate modules and task selection can be even more significant when the number of available tasks is high. Overall, our findings emphasize the importance of proper organization and cooperation among multiple learning components in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. Traditional methods for evaluating heat engines consider infinite operation times and
neglect the effects of work done by the engine. In reality, these assumptions are
reasonable only over the engine's equilibrium lifetime. This study takes a more
precise approach to examine ideal heat engines with limited control options and
finite lifetimes. Regardless of the restricted control, we demonstrate the existence
of an optimal strategy that achieves maximum efficiency and use this strategy to define
an improved method of evaluating heat engines known as the quasi-static method. The
engine's maximum efficiency and work output are expressed as the minimum value of
a function with multiple local minima, and these efficient values can be achieved by
applying the quasi-static method. This technique also enables the determination of the
temperature range over which the maximum efficiency and work output are valid. For
the Otto cycle, we derive closed-form expressions for the optimal strategy, efficient
values, and temperature range, and our results indicate that the efficiency and work
output are sensitive to the engine's lifetime and rate at which heat bath temperatures
change. Furthermore, the engine's behavior undergoes three distinct changes as its
lifetime varies. When the lifetime falls below a critical value, known as the e-fold time,
the efficiency and work output exhibit asymptotic behavior. In addition, we study an
extended version of the Otto cycle that incorporates a second non-touching state with
a different temperature, and apply the quasi-stochastic method to this scenario as
well. Our analysis reveals how the multi-level structure of the energy levels impacts the
efficient strategy, work output, and efficient temperature range. Finally, we
illustrate our findings with numerical simulations that compare the performance of an
ideal heat engine with limited control to a thermodynamically optimized engine with
unrestricted control. Our analysis shows that the efficiency and work output of these two
engines exhibit similar asymptotic behavior for large system sizes and that the
differences in efficiency and work output are more pronounced for smaller system sizes. 
In particular, we found that the relative difference in efficiency and work output
decreases exponentially with increasing system size. We hope that this study will
inspire the development of a more general quasi-static picture of finite-duration heat
engines. This new framework may be applied not only to idealized systems but also to
real-world heat engines that undergo finite-state changes. As such, we believe that
our results will be relevant to the operation and optimization of macroscopic heat
engines.

Extreme weather events like hurricanes and storm surges have devastating effects on power delivery systems, causing widespread outages that can stretch into days. To help utility companies prepare and improve recovery efforts, a new computational framework is being introduced to analyze the impact of these storms on the distribution of electricity. This framework utilizes a flexible mesh to represent the spatial distribution of faults and enables the calculation of economic losses, allowing utility companies to assess the financial consequences of their actions. In addition to advancing knowledge in this field, this framework also paves the way for the development of more effective storm-hardening strategies. Detailed simulations of actual storm events have been conducted and the resulting loss estimates have been compared with industry expectations, offering valuable insights that can be used to inform decision-making in the electricity sector. The framework's meshing algorithm has also been refined to improve computational efficiency, enabling the rapid simulation of various storm scenarios while minimizing processing demands. The development of this innovative framework marks a significant breakthrough in the field of power engineering, enabling the precise estimation of power delivery losses due to hurricanes and storm surges for the first time. The advanced computational framework is based on the distributed computing platformes (DCP) technology, commonly used in the electricity sector, making it easily integrable into existing DCP systems. The versatility of this framework means it can be applied to various domains, extending its utility beyond power delivery systems to other infrastructure domains. The results of our simulations suggest that the expected loss estimates reported in industry studies may be underestimating the actual consequences of these storm events. Consequently, this framework offers a valuable tool for utility companies to assess their exposure to the financial consequences of hurricanes and storm surges, helping them to refine their risk management strategies and inform decision-making processes. To evaluate the performance of our meshing algorithm, comparisons with actual outage data from the 2017 Hurricane Irma event have been conducted, offering valuable insights that can be used to refine our meshing algorithm and improve its accuracy. The comprehensive framework developed in this research study is comprised of three key components: (i) storm modeling, (ii) meshing algorithm, and (iii) computational evaluation process. The storm modeling component involves the representation of spatial domains and objects to assess the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on power delivery systems. The meshing algorithm component involves the generation of flexible meshes to calculate the economic losses of these storm events. The computational evaluation process component involves the use of sensitivity analysis to estimate the likelihood and severity of these storm events. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the model's pitch control relies heavily on the selection of a mean pitch, which can result in pitch-related inaccuracies and the production of unwanted harmonics. To overcome these limitations, QPNet is combined with a prior distribution that utilizes a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution network to model quasi-periodic signals. This modification enables WN to accurately represent signals with complex pitch patterns, resulting in improved waveform generation at low sample rates. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms WN in generating quasi-periodic signals at 22050 samples per second, particularly in speech and instrument contexts. Furthermore, QPNet demonstrates superior sample rate capabilities compared to WN, with a 22050 sample rate being the lowest tested frequency for this model. WN, in contrast, exhibited degraded performance at frequencies below 11025 samples per second. WN achieved only marginal success at 16000 samples per second. Based on these results, the model is named Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet). While this model shows great promise for generating quasi-periodic signals, it does not perform as well as WN at higher sample rates, particularly in music-related contexts. Future work will focus on developing a more versatile model capable of producing high-quality signals at both low and high sample rates. To facilitate this research, the proposed model's code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aliuts/QPNet. Assessment demos are available at https://aliuts.github.io/Ali-Utsaudio-QPNet.html. To evaluate the effectiveness of this model, a comprehensive set of steady-state vowels and consonants were generated using QPNet and WN with various sample rates and mean pitch values. These signals were then analyzed through confusion matrices and spectrogram metrics to assess pitch-related inaccuracies and harmonic contamination in both models. Additionally, magneto-acoustic features were utilized to train prior distributions for both models, demonstrating the superior performance of QPNet over WN in speech and instrument contexts, particularly at lower sample rates. Finally, the model was tested on letter-to-sound tasks to evaluate its ability to learn quasi-periodic signal properties through end-to-end training, with results showing the superior performance of QPNet over WN in modeling both periodic and non-periodic signal

However, the traditional collaborative filtering techniques have been less successful in dealing with the issues of data sparsity and subjective user preferences. In real-world settings, users' opinions on movies are not uniform and can vary greatly. Additionally, the subjective nature of preferences poses significant challenges to traditional collaborative filtering methods. To address these limitations, a novel CF approach called user-specific bicluster-based cooperative filtering (LSBCF) is introduced. This innovative method leverages biclustering to co-cluster users and items based on local patterns in order to address the issues of preference locality, sparsity, and subjectivity. By using a data-driven approach to identify cohesive groups of users with similar preferences for specific items or item preferences for particular groups of users, the algorithm models each pattern's overall rating trend. When an unrated movie is involved, the algorithm selects the most relevant bicluster groups that share similar patterns with the target user's profile and uses their estimated ratings to predict the missing rating. To achieve subjectivity management, the algorithm incorporates subjective factors into the prediction model by scaling individual bicluster ratings proportionally to the target user's overall rating for the corresponding item. Existing image enhancement techniques primarily focus on improving perceived image quality in a forward direction (original image $\rightarrow$ aesthetically pleasing image) but disregard how this quality can be manipulated in reverse (aesthetically pleasing image $\rightarrow$ higher quality image). In this study, a general approach is developed to apply style extracted from image pairs to new test images in both the forward and reverse directions. Additionally, to enhance the versatility of the style extraction method, a new pre-training strategy is proposed. To validate the universality of the extracted style, a suite of 4000 image pairs from 40 categories is created and used as a style repository. It is demonstrated that the extracted style can effectively capture the characteristics of a particular image pair while disregarding the details of the original and resulting images. Furthermore, it is shown that the extracted style can be applied to multiple images without compromising its coherence. Last but not least, it is shown that the extracted style can be employed in both the forward and reverse directions with minimal loss of quality. All code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/HzShy/Universal_Tone_Mapping. Experimental findings show that the proposed universal tone mapping approach surpasses state-of-the-art aesthetic enhancement methods in both the forward and reverse directions in terms of comprehensive metrics. Specifically, it is shown that the proposed approach yields an increase of 3.46\% and 3.14\% over current techniques in terms of CLIME and LPIP metrics, respectively. It is worth noting that the proposed approach is only outperformed by domain-specific techniques (i.e., techniques trained on specific image pairs) but surpasses them in dataset-agnostic techniques (i.e., techniques that are not trained on specific image pairs). Conversely, it is shown that the proposed approach is an improvement over existing universal techniques. Specifically, it is shown that the proposed approach yields an increase of 4.53\% and 2.24\% over current universal techniques in terms of CLIME and LPIP metrics, respectively. All code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/HzShy/Universal_Tone_Mapping. By conducting detailed analyses of high-resolution images, researchers found evidence supporting the preferential selection theory. They observed that water droplets initially accumulate on narrow features such as branches and then widen due to the increased water volume. This process recycles small water droplets towards the core, resulting in a self-reinforcing cycle that enhances the peak water accumulation. Alternatively, large water droplets may bypass the initial accumulation site, widening and shaping the snow cluster in an irregular manner. By simulating the atmospheric turbulence using a computer algorithm, researchers found that the preferential selection hypothesis could explain the formation of disk-shaped snow clusters, typically seen in high-altitude mountains. We introduce an innovative form of active inference that enables robots to independently gather information needed to make informed decisions.  This unique method is built upon recent enhancements to the standard active inference process, incorporating discoveries from 'free-energy' anatomy and anatomy-by-descent.  As a demonstration of its effectiveness, we successfully integrated it into a simple robot navigation system, proving that information seeking can significantly improve performance when compared to a more traditional passive approach.  Furthermore, our method excels in uncertain environments, outshining even optimized passive strategies.  This pioneering application of active inference marks a significant breakthrough in using Bayesian inference for predictive information guidance in robotics.  Key features of our solution include its ability to be fully automated, to adapt to changing environments, and to make decisions without external input or guidance.  This breakthrough sets the stage for future utilization of active inference in more complex tasks, such as collaborative navigation and object detection. In experimental nuclear physics, the Telescopic Particle Counter is a widely used instrument. It's capable of measuring the volume flow rate of particles in a four-dimensional spacetime. There are two components to the TPC - a main section and a sparse section. Data from the sparse section is particularly difficult to process because its sensors only cover a limited portion of the particle flow. However, this part of the instrument is crucial for detecting particles that pass through the detector's center. We've developed a new method using a autoencoder to combine data from all sensors on the partially enclosed section, effectively combining multiple limited-view images into a complete view. This approach involves using a dual convolutional network that learns from the partial images and their translations, demonstrating better reconstruction quality and more accurate particle identification when compared to existing methods. Overall, this new method compresses data from the partially enclosed section into a more manageable format, allowing for more efficient data transmission. Once transmitted, the data can be fully reconstructed to its original size. We've verified the effectiveness of this approach through simulations of particles moving through the detector, capturing key images, and analyzing these images for nuclear particle types. With this new method, we've reduced the data transmission requirements for the TPC by up to a factor of 23. Additionally, the reconstructed data shows over 90% accuracy for particle type identification. These results indicate that the proposed approach is an efficient way to compress and process data from the partially enclosed section of the TPC, preserving key information for accurate analysis. We've confirmed the reliability of this approach through extensive statistical testing, verifying its stability under a wide range of operating conditions. Furthermore, we've explored the ability of the autoencoder to generalize to other operational scenarios, verifying its ability to do so. Ultimately, we've demonstrated that the proposed approach is a valuable tool for the efficient operation of the TPC, allowing for more effective use of detector bandwidth and improved accuracy of nuclear particle types in experimental data. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub. We've also performed a detailed study of the performance of the autoencoder, verifying its capabilities and providing important insights for future development and improvement. One key area for future improvement is the integration of flow rate information into the compression algorithm, potentially allowing for even better transmission efficiency and reconstruction quality. We've outlined a plan for this future work, including the development of a new compression algorithm that incorporates flow rate information. This will likely lead to a more efficient data transmission, allowing for higher particle collection rates and better accuracy of nuclear particle types

This paper outlines a novel approach for identifying the most effective treatments in medical care, with specific emphasis on cancer treatment. We begin by developing a mathematical model that describes how the immune system responds to a particular treatment. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the connection between the probability distribution of the internal body environment and the treatment's duration, with the aid of a customized Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. To illustrate the practical utility of our approach, we focus on colon cancer treatment and employ a Fokker-Planck equation to optimize the probability distribution of the internal body environment. In doing so, we utilize the first two components of the probability distribution, along with the Hamiltonian, to develop an optimal control strategy that maximizes the colon cancer patient's survival rate while maintaining a high quality of life. The feasibility of our approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations, with specific results showing the optimal treatment duration in months. Importantly, our technique allows for the treatment of multiple cancers to be optimized independently, thus facilitating more effective treatment protocols. With the continued advancement of medical technology, our framework is well-positioned to facilitate personalized treatment customisation. The proposed approach, based on the probability distribution of the internal body environment, offers a valuable tool for clinicians in their quest to develop tailored treatment plans. Current estimates suggest that the remaining eccentricity of neutron star-black hole mergers detected by LIGO is about $10^{-4}$, which may imply significant survival of inspiraling binary black holes with eccentricities as high as $10^{-3}$. In order to make more accurate predictions, we used post-Newtonian theory to model the orbital evolution of the binary system and found a more precise estimate of the remaining eccentricity. We conducted extensive computations that accounted for various assumptions and found that the remaining eccentricity is less than $5\times10^{-5}$ for equal mass systems and less than $1.5\times10^{-5}$ for unequal mass systems, which may imply that the remaining eccentricity is generally lower than $10^{-6}$. Our work led to a new model for the remaining eccentricity, and we used it to determine that the majority of detected binary black hole events with detectable eccentricities have remaining eccentricities below $10^{-4}$. Additionally, we found that the remaining eccentricity of inspiraling binary systems depends strongly on the masses of the objects, leading us to conclude that the distribution of remaining eccentricities is skewed, which may imply that the majority of surviving inspiraling binary systems have eccentricities below $10^{-6}$. Furthermore, we verified that the remaining eccentricity of binary black holes is closely related to the characteristics of the gravitational wave signal, particularly its frequency and duration. Our work enabled us to determine that the remaining eccentricity of binary black holes typically falls within a specific range, and we found that the distribution of remaining eccentricities is not uniform, which may imply that the majority of surviving inspiraling binary systems have eccentricities between $10^{-7}$ and $10^{-5}$. Lastly, we used our model to make more accurate predictions about the characteristics of future gravitational wave detectors, which may be capable of detecting highly eccentric binary black hole systems at greater distances, such as those resulting from dynamical interactions in dense stellar environments. In particular, we found that the upcoming LISA detector may be capable of detecting highly eccentric binary black hole systems at greater distances, such as those resulting from dynamical interactions in dense stellar environments. Dynamic networks represent a type of network that changes over time, commonly observed in various systems such as power grids, social media platforms, and biological networks. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to accurately diagnose and prevent potential precancerous lesions. The process typically involves expert pathologists examining stained tissue samples, which are then linked to corresponding patient medical records. Since the visual analysis required is highly complex and sensitive to expert variability, there is a need to leverage deep learning methods to aid accuracy. However, the development of effective models relies on high-quality datasets that include annotated information and are specific to the application at hand. Such specialized datasets are rare for the task at hand, so we introduced UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 2850 annotated histopathological images, stained and staged according to the Jarowenski protocol, to facilitate the training and testing of deep learning models for classification and adenoma evaluation tasks. We provide detailed technical information and guidelines on using the dataset to contribute to the advancement of applications in histopathological settings. Data leakage occurs when an adversary is able to obtain additional knowledge beyond what is publicly disclosed during the encoding process. This paper specifically examines zero-error source encoding methods, seeking to identify methodical approaches for an adversary to derive inferences from the encoded data without being explicitly supplied with the source sequence itself. Utilizing graph theory, we devise various graph-based models to tackle distinct forms of data leakage, followed by the derivation of fundamental capacity characteirizations for each model. This paper focuses on zero-error source encoding and seeks to develop systematic methods for an adversary to derive inferences from the encoded data without being explicitly supplied with the source sequence itself. Utilizing graph theory, we will devise various graph-based models to address different forms of data leakage and derive the fundamental capacity characterizations for each model. This paper introduces an innovative method to identify areas where two ellipses intersect. Our approach avoids intricate calculations commonly associated with this problem. Instead, we utilize a straightforward geometric technique that relies on basic arithmetic to determine intersection regions. The method's simplicity makes it suitable for teaching and modeling purposes in computer science. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a tangible example, solving a long-standing inquiry regarding the intersection of two specific ellipses. The solution employs our proposed method to pinpoint the areas where these ellipses intersect. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted to calculate the volumes of shapes formed by merging these ellipses through the cut-slice method. Specifically, we demonstrate how to accurately calculate the volume of a solid formed by taking a segment of one ellipse and slicing it with another ellipse. This adaptation not only enhances the simplicity of our initial method but also makes it more versatile, yielding a general technique that can be applied to a broad range of scenarios. The areas where the ellipses intersect, as well as the volume of the resulting solid, are illustrated through graphical visualizations that provide a tangible representation of our solution. The proposed method is likely to have far-reaching implications in fields such as calculus, geometry, and computer graphics, facilitating the development of innovative algorithms for manipulating 3D shapes, merging objects, and estimating errors in geometry. In particular, this approach is expected to broaden the systematic development of geometric programming, a programming paradigm that mimics the manipulation of geometric shapes to solve algorithmic problems. This paper presents a new tracking challenge, continuous duration q-learning.
The classic discrete duration q-learning framework is modified to accommodate
real-time measurements. We propose a novel approach to tackle this problem by
expressing the continuous state as a probability mass function (PMF) in the q-learning tensor network framework. As a theoretical exploration, we apply the umbrella framework to derive useful inequalities for analyzing this problem. Additionally, we provide a straightforward method for initializing the q-network. Our initial experiments have yielded positive outcomes with the simple deep continuous duration network (DCDN) approach. Furthermore, we have observed that the umbrella framework can effectively handle situations where observations become sparse. Although these results are preliminary, they indicate that the q-learning approach in continuous duration can achieve a satisfactory level of performance with relatively few samples. Moreover, the DCDN method outperformed the traditional deep duration network (DDN) in the tested scenarios. We have tested these methods on both the simple mobile robot simulation and the real TX2 robot platform. A significant outcome of these experiments was the detection of the mobile robot and the tracking of its movement using the DCDN method, where the observed success was surprising and caught our attention. Conversely, with the real TX2 robot, we encountered several obstacles, such as electrical interference and motion smoothness constraints, which hampered the efficient evaluation of the DCDN method in real-time. Consequently, we plan to undertake further investigations to optimize the DCDN performance on the real TX2 robot platform. Additionally, we aim to carry out more comprehensive comparisons between the umbrella DCDN and the DDN methods. Accurate vertebral segmentation in CT scans is essential for various clinical applications like spinal surgery planning, radiation therapy, and evaluating metabolic bone diseases. Despite significant research, fully automated vertebral segmentation remains a difficult task due to challenging conditions such as similar density with the surrounding environment, variability in size and shape, and the presence of pathological and external instruments. This study proposes a new, automated approach to localize and identify vertebras in 3D CT data, which involves correcting the spine's curvature to allow for lateral visualization, followed by the application of anatomically-informed optimization to select suitable vertebral centers, and finally, leveraging neural networks to determine vertebral body and head boundaries. Our evaluations revealed our method to be the most accurate compared to currently available state-of-the-art methods, including SiamNet, SpineTracker, and Spine-CF, in terms of Dice Similarity Coordinate (DSC) score, with a significant improvement from 83.2% to 89.7% for 35 vertebral bodies, or an 8.5% improvement. The proposed approach also successfully corrected spinal curvature and identified vertebral body and head boundaries in all cases, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) increasing from 0.785 to 0.940. Furthermore, we found that our approach significantly reduced the reliance on expert annotations, with the results showing an increase in difficulty (from 0.785 to 0.942) when the expert's influence was limited. Our study demonstrates that spinal correction and anatomical constraints are essential for full spine segmentation, with the optimized vertebral body and head boundaries contributing more to accurate identification compared to state-of-the-art methods. We derive coherent conditions for the Milnor fiber of a generic hypersurface singularity in two contexts: for arbitrary complex bases and for $\mathbb{C}$-bases that satisfy a specific cohomology condition. Our approach relies on demonstrating the coherence of the Milnor fiber as a consequence of the flatness of the critical set, which is achieved through the development of novel keys for Milnor fiber coherence and a comparison with an alternative construction of the Milnor fiber coherence set proposed by B. Fry. Additionally, we prove that the coherence of the critical set implies the coherence of the secure set, thereby extending a known result from B. Fry and M. Ulmer. Furthermore, we establish that the conditions for coherent Milnor fibers have a significant implication – the compatibility of the semisimple decomposition of the rational singularity's vanishing cycles with the Hertling-M. Lejarraga decomposition of the critical points' monodromy, which is a novel connection in this field. Our paper also provides a mathematical interpretation of G. L. Ormsby and M. Ulmer's observational findings about the relationship between the Milnor fiber and the critical points of a hypersurface. Moreover, we formulate two conjectures based on our comprehensive analysis: (1) demonstrating that the Milnor fiber is topologically coherent in the classical sense, and (2) establishing the existence of a semi-algebraic critical component that isomorphic to the Milnor fiber, which would provide a constructive proof of its coherence. Finally, in the appendix, we establish that for a $\mathbb{Q}$-base, the coherence of the secure set implies the coherence of the Milnor fiber, addressing an inquiry initially posed by B. Fry. Our study has far-reaching implications for research in the fields of Hertling-M. Lejarraga decomposition, monodromy, and topological invariants of singularities. Ultimately, this work significantly expands our understanding of the secure set, allowing us to assert that it is larger than the critical points and flat t*-secant set in certain scenarios. Our work has the additional effect of bridging the gap between the theory of complex singularities and the semi-algebraic topology of flat singularities. The transition from a neutral, matter-dominated universe to a photoionized one is a pivotal real-time process governed by Saha's ionization equation. To investigate the dynamics of this equation, we treat the number of neutral particles as a Gaussian distribution centered on the number of electrons, effectively making the impact of Saha's equation non-Gaussian. Assuming that electron neutrinos are always ionized, we find that late-time universality is influenced by two critical parameters: the initial electron-proton separation, which determines the shape of a peak in our probability distribution, and the initial ionization level, which dictates the location and height of this peak. When the initial separation is small, this probability distribution is narrow and symmetrical, but as the separation increases, it becomes broader and asymmetrical, leading to a second mode appearing at low-density values. If the initial ionization level exceeds the initial electron density, it results in a discontinuity in our distribution, with a steep drop at high-density values. Through numerical simulations, we observe that these non-Gaussian impacts of Saha's equation lead to deviations from Gaussian distributions in neutrino density, bispectrum, and non-commutative magnetic field correlations, indicating that these phenomena may be detectable during the cosmic reionization era. Additionally, we find that if the initial ionization level is too high, it would contradict observational evidence that the neutral fraction during the reionization period cannot exceed 10^-2. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose the existence of additional physical processes. Finally, we suggest that our findings could be explored using observations of the cosmic neutrino background and magnetic field measurements at various scales. The corresponding modified magnetic field correlations could be tested using observations of CMB, Galactic magnetic fields, and cosmic structures. The initial conditions of our scenario could also be tested using neutrino data from future experiments such as JUICE and future observations of cosmic structures with the Square Kilometre Array. In turn, these tests could help us understand early universe dynamics between 10^-12 and 10^6 s. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive equations that can only be effectively solved with the aid of sophisticated numerical simulations. In this research, a Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-In-Cell model is utilized to study the quantitative aspects of magnetic island merging in both linear and nonlinear scenarios. The incorporation of a finite-size current collection zone into the Magnetohydrodynamics equation significantly enables the simulation to accurately capture the interaction between contrasting plasma populations. The resulting simulations successfully replicate the key characteristics of island merging, including the conversion of magnetic energy into plasma kinetic and thermal energy, as well as the formation of a collisionless shock. The findings also illustrate the precise timing of collisionless stages and the separation distance between plasma populations. Furthermore, the model is validated through a comparison with analytical estimates and by examining the distribution of plasma densities and temperatures. The application of this advanced Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-In-Cell model to study magnetic island merging in various astrophysical settings is discussed. The model has potential applications in understanding various complex, magnetically charged phenomena in general. The research delves into comparing different models of collisionless magnetic reconnection and notes that the outcomes vary significantly based on the level of numerical detail. The simulation code is found to be versatile and adaptable, allowing for simulations of various reconnection scenarios with embedded magnetic loops, non-uniform current distributions, and realistic boundary conditions. We propose a novel system called Scribe, which acts as a reliable assistant for
low-level programming tasks, essentially functioning as a reliable replacement for
these tasks. Scribe's capabilities include generating code based on a user's
description, as well as providing the user with suggested code configurations.
Levers, a specialized knowledge base, drives Scribe's functioning; it is
composed of annotated examples of successful code configurations, each accompanied
by a brief description. When a programmer supplies a description of the code
requirements, Scribe utilizes this information to identify a relevant pattern in
Levers and offers the associated code configuration as a suggested starting point
for the user's program. In addition to these tasks, Scribe aims to facilitate
communication among programmers by providing a standardized language for describing
code configurations and supporting collaborative programming through the sharing
of customized configurations, ultimately aiming to integrate a team of programmers.
This paper serves as a introductory foundation for Scribe, presenting the system,
its component Knowledge Base of code configurations, and introducing two methods by
which Scribe navigates the space of possible configurations to suggest useful
patterns. Two case studies with real-world participation are presented to
demonstrate Scribe's efficacy in two distinct programming domains. Experimental
results showing Scribe's performance are presented, including data from its
initial deployment with 28 participants. This research was partially funded by
